I pray you take care of yourself.
The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature; the illusory and empty body is itself the Dharma-body. O people! If you have faith...
One may depart; this is not without its economy of effort. It may be said that when Sudhana enters Maitreya’s pavilion, he fully pervades immeasurable dharma-gates and attains great non-obstruction.
He awakens to the non-arising of dharmas; this is the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Within the realms of boundless lands, self and other are not separated by even a hair’s breadth; throughout the ten ages of past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment. And so it is.
I ask you all: which of these is the "present thought"? It is simply this: the nature of your ignorance is none other than your own fundamental, wondrously luminous nature of awakening.

It is only because you fail to understand the root source of birth and death that you grasp at delusion as reality, follow along with delusions, and consequently fall into saṃsāra to undergo all manner of suffering.
If you can turn the light back upon yourself and reflect inwardly, you will spontaneously awaken to your original state.
The true nature is neither born nor extinguished; therefore it is said that the actual nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature, and the illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
Just as the four elements and five aggregates—this impure body—are entirely devoid of substantial reality, being like a dream and like an illusion.
Like shadows and echoes, since immeasurable kalpas past, they have wandered through birth and death, driven by craving and attachment without a moment’s rest.
Emerging from here and entering there, the bones they have accumulated are like Mount Vipula, and the milk they have drunk is equal to the waters of the four great oceans. Why is this?
Because they lack wisdom and are unable to realize that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty and entirely devoid of reality; thus, they pursue delusions and undergo suffering.
Beings are bound by craving and lack self-mastery. Therefore, the World-Honored One said: "Craving is the root of all suffering;
if craving is extinguished, there is nothing upon which one depends. If you can thoroughly understand that this illusory body is false and provisional, [you shall attain liberation].

Originally empty and still, no views arise; there is no self, person, sentient being, or life-span. All phenomena are thusness (*tathatā*); therefore it is said: "The illusory, empty body is itself the Dharma-body.
The Dharma-body is awakened and aware that not a single thing exists; there is only hearing the Dharma and preaching the Dharma.
This is the vast and profound Great Way, the unattached True Teaching; therefore it is said: "The original source and intrinsic nature is the heavenly Buddha. It is also said:
The five aggregates are like floating clouds, empty as they come and go; the three poisons are like bubbles on water, vainly appearing and disappearing.

If one is thus, this is called crossing over all suffering and calamity, even unto the immeasurable and boundless. When afflictions and cognitive understandings are entirely purified, this is the pure *dharmakāya*.
If one reaches this state, one is able to emerge from here and enter there, casting off this body to receive another.

Throughout the body, the hells, the heavens, this realm, and other directions, he moves with sovereign ease, floating and sinking at will. He radiates light in response to things and imparts teachings according to the capacities of beings.
To call this "the manifestation of a thousand, ten-thousand, or hundred-million transformation bodies" is, as such speech goes, nothing but speaking a dream while dreaming;
it is like mixing mud and water, or spitting out excrement and urine—utterly failing to recognize what is good or bad. Then, he let out a great laugh, saying: "He-he!"
If you approach the gate of the patch-robed monk, even the "one hundred and eight thousand" [paths] have not yet allowed you to dream of the stench of his sweat.
Nevertheless, though this is so, matters are never one-sided; it is merely by means of provisional names that sentient beings are guided. (He lets out a shout.)
The medicine is abundant, yet the illness is grave; the net is fine, yet the fish are dense.
When Daowu beats the drum, the four great continents participate together. His staff is held crosswise, encompassing the entire universe and the great earth.
The almsbowl turns, overturning worlds as numerous as the sands of the Ganges. Now I ask you all: where do you establish yourselves and sustain your lives?
If you know the place where one establishes oneself and sustains one's life, then even in Uttarakuru, one eats porridge and rice.
If you do not know this either, then while sitting on the long bedsteads, eating gruel and rice, and leaning upon your staff, [I say]:
"Winter after winter, day after day; for those who practice Chan by the Five Lakes, do not bring up such fine scenery. He lets out a shout.

Entering the Record of Shishuang, it says: "The mountains are green and the waters are blue; beholding the scenery, I think of the man. The eras are far apart, yet his voice and countenance seem as if present before me.
I recall when those former practitioners lived at the Liu-yang Hermitage; they would simply act on behalf of the Chan guests of Dongshan by delivering a single turn of phrase."

Upon hearing this once, Wuben immediately recognized him as one of the fifteen hundred virtuous spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra). That year, he was invited by the assembly to leave and reside at Shishuang.
Later, it proved exactly as he had said, and his fame spread throughout the world. This is what is meant by "discerning the field from its sprouts."
I am known as a man of words. This mountain monk has never lived in a hermitage, nor have I ever offered a single turning phrase on behalf of others.

Nevertheless, I was moved by a worthy lord to reside at Shishuang, where I receive travelers and provide for them with nothing but coarse gruel and plain rice, using whatever is available according to the season;
thus, I do not fail to act appropriately. Even if someone comes seeking me in such a manner, I recognize them all; even if they do not come in such a manner, I am no less present.
"Little Yi, when you arrive here, naturally one does not beat this drum or blow this flute; one simply brings an end to strife and conflict. It is said:
'Like a single strand of white silk, it goes to the incense burner in the ancient temple. Now tell me, is there any intimacy or distance between this and the ancients?
After a long silence, he said: 'Before the hall of the withered tree, the flowers bloom even more brightly in spring.'"
The wind howls vast; the rain falls incessantly. Ancient halls and old shrines are all pierced through. My peak stands solitary and high, towering into the azure sky.
Zen practitioners who arrive here all find it detestable; even before the snow falls, they all say it is cold. How much more unbearable when the snow falls and the incense smoke burns?
"Transforming afflictions. "Drink tea and go. "Take care.
"The great sun rises. "Running north and south. "The night moon is full. "Before the sky has dawned. I do not ask about the phrase "hiding one's body within the nostrils.
But as for you all: how do you speak the phrase "hiding one's body beneath the heels"? Is there anyone who can say it?
“Dimo. After a long silence, he said: “Familiar faces fill the world; how many can truly know one’s heart?
The sky has already brightened, the drums have already sounded, and the assembly of noble ones has arrived. All join their palms together. Is there anyone present now who does not join their palms?
If there is, the Nirgrantha will rejoice; if there is none, Gautama will be displeased.
If the mind is free from affairs, the myriad dharmas do not arise; when the intellect is cut off at the profound and subtle, how could even a speck of dust stand?
The path that goes beyond is not transmitted by the thousand sages; students weary their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections. I, this mountain monk, am not thus:
the path that goes downward is not practiced by the thousand sages; students weary their bodies like monkeys grasping at reflections. (He lets out a shout.)

"The Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind. Now tell me: how do you explain the phrase "walking by day and sleeping at night"?
After a long silence, he struck the ground once with his staff and said, "Deshan provides the certification."
[The Master] strikes the rope-bench once with his staff and says: "Striking the grass is only to startle the snake.
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, a thousand sages gathered together; the Lord of Śākyas raised his eyes, and Kāśyapa smiled. Within the school of the patch-robed monks—

"You are still only halfway there. Now tell me: how do you speak this single phrase of total presentation? After a long silence, he said: "Out of love for one's child, one does not notice their ugliness.
On the occasion of the end of the summer retreat, he said: "Yesterday I was an infant; today my years are old. Without clarifying the three eights and nine, it is difficult to tread the path."
The Way of the Ancient Sovereign: With his hands he grasps the Yellow River until it dries; With his feet he kicks Mount Sumeru until it falls. This floating life is a dream-like illusory body;
Human life is difficult to preserve even for a single evening. Heavenly realms and hells are both created by the mind.

Pines on the southern mountains and northern ridges, Grass on the northern ridges and southern mountains— A single rain moistens them boundlessly, Strengthening the roots and sprouts while reviving the withered and parched. You practitioners of Chan at the Five Lakes, you may ask:
Investigating the void: dying, one sheds the summer shirt; living, one dons the winter robe. Clearly, this is a person of no affairs, yet they needlessly give rise to affliction. *A shout.*
The World-Honored One’s samādhi, Kāśyapa did not know; Kāśyapa’s samādhi, Ānanda did not know; Ānanda’s samādhi, Śāṇakavāsin did not know.
Thus, the samādhis of these successive sages were mutually unknown to one another. Then, he picked up his staff.
He drew a circle and said, "What is this? After a long silence, he said, "When meeting a swordsman on the road, one must present one's sword;
if you are not a poet, do not offer your poem."
To go about in such a manner already constitutes a great deal of trouble; what more could one do? It is merely mixing mud with water.
Therefore, on Vulture Peak, Kāśyapa heard it directly from the Buddha; before the cliff of Shaoshi, the Patriarch cut off his own arm. But tell me, for what purpose did he cut off his arm?
[He] strikes the meditation staff once and descends from the seat.
Last night, the sky was filled with snow; the great earth was at once bright and pure. This morning, there is no one in the courtyard.
Do not say that this mountain monk has nothing to say.
If we discuss this matter, you have already attained it; there is nothing further lacking. It is no different from the Buddha; there is no other dharma.
After a long silence, he said, "O worthy ones, have you even had a glimpse? The ancients, for no reason, buy high and sell low.
Entering Xinghua’s hall, he struck his meditation seat once with his staff and said, "Does the assembly understand? Have you not heard it said?"
With a single blow, all that was known was forgotten; there was no further need for cultivation or maintenance. Those who have attained the Way in all quarters say this is the highest capacity.
Xiangyan’s awakening was indeed clear; he awakened to the Buddha-dhyāna, yet he had not even dreamed of the Patriarchal-dhyāna.
Now tell me: what excellence does the Patriarch possess? If you seek a standard within his words, you will lead later generations astray;
even if you can take responsibility under the staff, you have failed the former sages.
The myriad dharmas are fundamentally serene; it is only people who create their own clamor. Therefore, when this mountain monk dwells at Fuyan, he perceives only the realm of Fuyan:
rising late and sleeping early, sometimes clouds rest upon the azure ridges, and the moon sinks into the cold pool. The singing birds fly and call out before the Prajñā Terrace;
the *śāla* flowers disperse their fragrance beside Mount Zhurong. Grasping my slender staff, I sit upon a flat rock and—
The five-lake monks often discourse upon the profound and subtle. With ash on their heads and dust on their faces, they dwell at Xinghua, where they witness the house style of Xinghua:

welcoming and seeing off guests; the monastery gates connected to the city, with carriages and horses thronging together; the fisherman’s songs of Xiao and Xiang, and the cries of monkeys at Mount Lu;

the sounds of strings, flutes, and singing entering the ears at all times. Furthermore, they spend their days discussing the ancestral Way with Chan practitioners from the four seas. Year after year...
The moon has been forgotten for a moment. Now tell me: is there a difference between dwelling in the deep mountains and residing in the city walls?
Try to say something. After a long silence, he said: "In every place is Maitreya; there is no gate, and no Sudhana."
In the kingdom of Magadha, there is no passage for water; before the peaks of Shaoshi, he personally issued this command.
What is this command? Is there anyone who can state it? Bring forth a single phrase—muddling the mud and blending the water—is there one?
After a long silence, he said: "The traveler has just returned, his travel-sleeve damp; the fair lady has barely begun to sing, her green brows droop. With a shout, he struck.
Striking the meditation seat with his staff, he said: "A single leaf falls; the whole world is autumn.
A single speck of dust is just raised, and the entire earth is fully encompassed. He held up the staff, struck the meditation seat once, and said:

"Ten billion Mount Sumerus, ten billion suns and moons, lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges—all dissolve like crumbling walls or melting ice. He let out a shout.

An investigation of the Venerable Ming of Xingjiao Monastery in Junzhou. A messenger arrived bearing a letter. Upon receiving the letter, the Master asked, "Did you come by the main road or the side path?
Ming replied, "Try saying it yourself, Master," and then struck a sitting mat. The Master said, "Blind fellow! You are talking nonsense."

"What are you doing? [The Master] blew a loud "xu" sound and struck him. When the new Abbot Xin arrived, the Master asked, "An ancient said, 'If we do not meet for three days, do not view me as I was before.
We have been separated from the Abbot for an entire summer; how do you view me now?
Xin replied, "It is no easy matter for the Master to maintain the monastery. The Master said, "If that is so, then the Western Patriarch has not..."
[The Master] transmitted the news of the faith in the land of Tang. At Shaolin, they vainly established distinctions between the distant and the near.
Xinyun asked, "Why did the Master speak in such a way? The Master said, "Nanyuan is at fault. He questioned a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "It is already quite late.
The Master said, "Without traversing the journey, how do you express a single phrase? The monk said, "Seven times nine is sixty-three."
The Master said, "It is evident. The monk said, "This will kill me with suffocation. The Master then struck him. He asked a monk, "Venerable, how old are you?
The monk said, "Twenty-six. The Master said, "That makes my staff the same age as you.
The monk said, "Yes. The Master said, "Tell me, how old is my staff? The monk was speechless. The Master then struck him. He questioned another monk.
"What is the elder’s name? The monk replied, "Haiman (Ocean-Full). The Master said, "The ocean neither increases nor decreases;
why is it 'full'? The monk said, "Master, do not deceive Haiman. The Master said, "I, this old monk, am at fault.
The Master asked a monk, "Where have you been this summer? The monk said, "At Xingjiao. The Master said, "Is Master Zhi well? The monk said, "He is well."
The Master said, "I grant you twenty blows. He asked a monk, "Everyone possesses their own self; which one is your own self, Venerable?
The monk replied, "My sitting mat is made of seven-foot cloth. The Master said, "Regret that you asked such a question. The monk hesitated.
The Master struck him and asked a monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "Clouds pass over a thousand mountains, all green.
The Master said, "Why are you in such a hurry? The monk said, "The wild geese have flown away; the sound of the water is long. The Master gave a shout. The monk also shouted. The Master struck him.
The monk also struck him. The Master said, "Look at this blind fellow! He originally should have been driven out through the main gate, but I spare you because..."
"A newcomer. Sit for a moment and drink some tea. The Master saw the monk approach, picked up his staff, and said, "Why have you been swallowed by my staff?
The monk said, "I dare not [speak]. The Master said, "How can you be so reckless? The monk said, "It is so.
The Master said, "Give me back the money for my straw sandals! "How do you say the single phrase upon entering the gate? The monk—
The monk said, "There is no road leading up to heaven. The Master said, "Go well. The monk said, "There is no gate for entering the earth.
The Master then gave a shout. The monk pushed the Master once and then departed. The Master called out, "Venerable! The monk did not look back.
The Master said, "Today Nan-yuan has failed. When meeting, one does not bring it forth; when a thought arises, one already knows it exists. What is this 'not bringing it forth'?"
[The monk] made a gesture of departing. The monk spread both hands. The Master said, "Nanyuan has burned incense; you have gone to make offerings. The monk said, "I have passed through.
The Master asked, "In what way did you pass? The monk pointed with his finger. The Master said, "How very far you have come!
The monk was speechless. The Master then struck him.
A special messenger from Jiufeng arrived with a letter. The Master said, "Xuansha sealed it in white paper; why does Jiufeng trouble himself so much?
The messenger said, "The birds warble in the deep peaks. The Master said, "If you do not walk the path beneath the mountains, how can you see the person weeping at the crossroads?"
The messenger said, "At noon, they strike the evening bell. The Master then shouted and said, "If you wish to observe the one who sends, first observe the messenger.

He asked a monk, "A traveling mendicant must know that there is the business of traveling. What is this business of traveling? The monk said, "I know it. The Master said, "What is the thing that is known?
The monk said, "The mountains are high and the waters are cold. The Master said, "I take pity on you for having come from so far."

"Come. Sit for a moment and drink some tea. The monk replied, "Yes, yes. The Master asked the monk, "You who travel through clouds and across waters without disturbing the waves—try and say something about it.
The monk said, "The tip of the Governor’s brush has slipped; it falls to the ground, and no one is there to pick it up.
The Master said, "Why do you speak so recklessly? As the monk hesitated, the Master gave a shout. The monk said, "The sun is at its zenith; looking up, I see the blue sky."
The Master drew a line across the space before him with his hand and said, "What is this? The monk said, "It is finished. The Master struck him.
He then asked another monk, "Where have you recently come from? The monk said, "From Beichen. The Master said, "Without traversing the journey—how do you express this in a single phrase?
The monk said, "Shut that dog’s mouth! The Master said, "Where does the fault lie with this mountain monk? The monk said, "Both."
A heavy koan. The Master then gave a shout. The monk hesitated; the Master struck him. Regarding this karmic occasion:
when the Master was traveling on pilgrimage, he met with Li, the Commandery Governor. As soon as he had presented his visiting card, Li invited him to the high-ranking official’s quarters.
He sat. He ordered a young page to come and ask: "If you can speak, then we shall meet. The Master said, "I have come specifically today to pay my respects.
The Commandant again ordered the page to say, "The characters on the stele are white; one should plant green pines along the road.

The Master said, "Were it not for this day of the festival, such an occasion would truly be difficult to encounter on other days. Again he ordered the page to say, "In that case, [you are] with the Upādhyāya."
"Let us meet," [the official] said as he was leaving. The Master replied, "From head to foot. Thereupon, [the official] requested an audience.
As soon as he was seated, the Master asked, "I have heard that there is a golden-maned lion in West River; is this true? The Master asked, "Where did the Commander obtain this news?
The Commander gave a shout. The Master said, "A jackal howling. The Commander shouted again. The Master said, "Exactly so! The Commander clapped his hands and laughed loudly.

The Master had been there for several days when he took his leave of the Commandant. The Commandant asked, "What is the one phrase for the moment of departure? The Master said, "Take good care of yourself.
The Commandant said, "If that is so, then it is no different from other places. The Master asked, "How is it at the place where you, Commandant, see things?
The Commandant said, "I grant you twenty blows. The Master said, "Solely for the sake of its circulation. The Commandant then gave a shout and clapped his hands.
[The messenger] bowed once. The Master said, "Blind. The messenger said, "May you go well. The Master said, "Yes, yes.

While the Master was in Hedong, he carried a letter for the Venerable Tang Ming-sōng to Yang Yi, the Palace Secretary. As soon as [Yang] unfolded the formal letter of introduction, he invited him to meet.
During their conversation, the Palace Secretary asked: "We face one another yet do not know each other; from a thousand miles away, we are as one."
Feng said, "I have been invited by the Monastery. Han said, "That is truly a lie. The Master said, "I left Tangming last month.
Han said, "Just now I regretted not asking you a question. The Master said, "An accomplished one. The Vice Minister (Neihan) then shouted.
The Master said, "Exactly! The Vice Minister shouted again. The Master drew a line across the air with his hand. Yang stuck out his tongue and said, "A dragon and an elephant!"

The Master said, "What words are these? He summoned the guest master and ordered fine tea to be served. [The Official] said, "It turns out he is one of our own. The Master said, "That too is unnecessary.
When the tea was finished, the Palace Secretary asked again, "What is the phrase by which Chan Master Yuan benefits others?
The Master said, "Cut! The Secretary said, "If that is so, it is like a long-skirted bride running through the mud. The Master said, "Who could attain this?"
The Inner Secretary (Nainhan) said, "A master, a master! The Master replied, "I grant you twenty blows. The Secretary struck his knee and said, "What kind of place is this?
The Master clapped his hands and said, "One must not let this pass. The Inner Secretary laughed heartily.
He then asked, "Do you remember the circumstances of the initial awakening of Preceptor Tangming, when you were his special envoy? The Master—
[The Master] said, "Have you ever seen the Master [Zhaozhou] bring this up? The Secretariat Scholar said, "I request that you do not withhold your compassion.
The Master said, "I have seen the Master bring it up. There was a monk who asked Master Nian, 'What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma?
Nian replied, 'At the edge of King Chu’s city, the Ru River flows east. The Scholar said, "As for 'At the edge of King Chu’s city, the Ru River flows east,' what is the underlying intent?"
"What? the Master asked. Wen-han replied, "A lantern hanging upon the water. The Master said, "If that is so, you have failed the ancients.
Wen-han said, "If you doubt it, Inner Secretary, you must seek elsewhere. The Master said, "A three-legged frog flying up to heaven.
Wen-han said, "Feel free to leap about as you please. The Inner Secretary then laughed heartily. After staying for ten days, the Master was taking his leave. Wen-han said, "I have something—"
A turning phrase was sent to Tang Ming; will it be returned? The Master said, "The bright moon shines upon the traveler at night.
Han said, "But that does not quite fit. The Master said, "It may still be bearable when the night grows deep, but after midday, it is even more distressing for people. Han said, [silently].
"Vajrapāṇi before Kaibō-ji Temple, why are you sweating these days? The Master said, "I know.
Hàn said, "As you are about to depart, do you have no word for the sake of others? The Master said, "The layered mountain passes and roads.
Hàn said, "If that is so, then I shall follow you, Master. The Master let out a single sigh. Hàn said, "A true lion cub making a lion’s roar! The Master [nodded].
The Master said, "I let him go, yet he comes back again. Han said, "Just now, I tripped and fell, and then I was helped up by my servant.
The Master said, "When will there ever be an end to this? The Palace Secretary laughed heartily.
Because Zhang Jie had introduced the two Great Masters, the Duwei’s letter arrived.

The Master wrote a reply, and at the end of the letter he drew a pair of feet, writing the names of the two Great Masters beneath them, and sent it to the Duwei. The Duwei replied with a verse, saying:
"The black brush-tip has traveled more than a thousand li; The golden coffin reveals a pair of feet. Humans and devas can fathom neither of these; Take care, O red-bearded barbarian!"
When Commandant Li was on the verge of death, he drew a circle and presented it along with a verse to the Master:
"The world has no dependence; mountains and rivers offer no obstruction. The great ocean contains a mote of dust; Mount Sumeru holds a mustard seed.
Picking up my turban and unfastening my sash—if you ask about birth and death, ask of this leather bag. The Master then asked, "What is the Commandant’s original Buddha-nature? The Commandant—
The Magistrate said, "Today it is as hot as yesterday. The Master replied, "When you depart, how will you speak that one phrase?

The Magistrate asked, "What do you say? The Master said, "Originally there is no obstruction; wherever one is, one may act according to the situation. The Magistrate said, "I am weary by evening and will no longer engage in conversation.
The Master said, "Where there is no Buddha, manifest Buddhahood."
Yangqi asked, "The dark birds warble and chatter; leaving the clouds, they enter the tangled mountains. What is it like at such a time? The Master said, "I walk amidst the wild weeds;
you, again, have entered a deep village. Yangqi said, "The official does not allow even a needle;
may I borrow another question? The Master then gave a shout.
In the ancient verse:
"The two Hall Heads both let out a shout. *Courtyard Cypress* The mechanism of the old woman’s "cracking" and "pecking" was like an arrow meeting a spearhead;
in a flash, guest and host were distinguished at that moment. The Master, pitying sentient beings, bestowed the black robes.
Plainly so. The waters of the Yellow River in the northern lands are thoroughly turbid.
The cypress tree in front of Zhaozhou’s courtyard—throughout the world, Zen seekers run to it. Do not let your child grow too large; once grown, he becomes a master thief.

Zhaozhou thoroughly exposed the old woman; when the leaves fall, one naturally knows autumn. How many Zen practitioners there are throughout the world, drifting aimlessly across the Five Lakes and Four Seas!
Yunmen’s Dharma-body: You are Huichao.
North, south, east, and west—ten thousand, ten million; heaven and earth, above and below, vast and boundless. Meeting and seeing one another, they laugh "he-he";
counting on their fingers and lifting their heads, the moon is halfway up the sky.
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "You are Huiqi. [The monk] prostrated, approached, and joined his palms;
ten thousand miles of distance passed in a mere thought.
Why did the Great Sage of Sizhou manifest in Yangzhou? Dongshan said, "The gentleman loves..."
Wealth. Take it by the right way. Under the Zhulin Mountain, bamboo-vein whips;
Lingyun saw peach blossoms;
Sizhou suddenly manifested at Yangzhou. The discourse-paths of the world’s masters are dense. A gentleman loves wealth, but takes it by the right way.
The Way! In the South Sea, the Persian’s nostrils are coarse;
beneath Mount Zhulin, there are whips made of bamboo sinew. There are myriads upon myriads of Chan practitioners from the south and north.
Do not be surprised that we do not dismount when meeting; east and west, each has their own path ahead.
In the third month, peach blossoms are fresh everywhere; once Lingyun saw them, he had no further kinship with the world.
Everyone they meet says, "I shall retire from office," yet beneath the forest trees, not a single person has ever been seen.
The Monk Requests Instruction on the Three Secrets and Three Phrases:
The First Secret: The great earth, mountains, and rivers overflow; Vimalakīrti merely nods his head, and Mañjuśrī immediately becomes loquacious.
The Second Secret: Unfolding and extending, one observes the opportune moment; speech and silence—how could they possibly interfere? It is like the autumn moon at midnight.
The Third Secret: The mountain is distant and the road difficult to traverse; one rows a boat upon dry land. Picking out the sun and moon with one’s eyes—this is the first phrase.

Above the heavens and in all other directions, none can find a way; the various schools of thought turn like wheels, proliferating in many ways. Lofty and majestic, yet one has not yet reached the Nyagrodha tree.

The second phrase: Linji and Deshan set out on their journey; before they had even crossed into Silla, the staff was already brandished. The one who attains realization points wildly along the way. The third phrase:
Vimalakīrti manifested illness and Mañjuśrī went to visit him; their dialogue of mutual silence shook heaven and earth. It is straight to the point.
Now I shall provide a source of laughter.

Regarding the first of the Three Mysteries and Three Essentials: how could the Buddhas of the three periods of time possibly proclaim it? To bestow compassion while dreaming is to treat it with levity; sit upright and return [to the source].
This constitutes falling into the extreme of annihilation.

Second, the profound mystery: even for a sharp-eyed monk, the eye has not yet opened; the spark of a flint and a flash of lightning are known to be dull. Raising an eyebrow or blinking an eye is already traversing the mountain passes.

The third mystery: The myriad phenomena are arrayed as the universe expands; clouds disperse into the vast void and the mountains and peaks are still; fallen flowers and flowing water fill the long river. The first essential:
How can the wondrousness of the sages and worthies be spoken of? To deliberate upon it is to travel a long road; to raise one’s eyes is to fall into seven perversions.
The second essential: Striking the *keng-kan* at the peak of the mountain summons those with sovereign spiritual powers; they come. At the gate of much learning, one shouts.
The third essential: Rising and falling makes people laugh; within the palm, one grasps the universe (*qiankun*), illuminating all myriad differences as one.

General Verse: I report to you, O Master of Penetrating Mystery: The staff and the shout must be applied according to the occasion. If you clearly understand the direct intent, At midnight the sun shines its brilliance.
In praise of the True One, the Commandery Governor.
A bubble, an illusion, born of conditions; the marvelous brush of the Venerable Sengyao [reveals] the moon in water, cold and deep in the pool—[yet it seems] solid and real.

He came to manifest his transformation in the imperial capital; he departed for other lands under the bright sun. The Duke of Longxi appeared as a prodigy between the ages of image and dharma; complete in both civil and military arts.
The Buddha-dharma is hereby complete. I prostrate to Avalokiteśvara. Who fully knows the Golden Grain?
The words of Chan Master Zhen of Cuiyan. Preface by Huang Tingjian of Nanchang, successor to Ciming.
In the mountains of Shishuang, there was a tiger with three horns that roamed alone and sat solitary amidst ten thousand trees stirred by the wind.
Even at a distance of a thousand *li*, there was no human being; the grass grew a fathom deep. One man stroked its whiskers and attained the Way—he was Huanglong Huinan.
Another man stepped upon its tail and attained the Way—he was Cuoyan Zhenke. These were the descendants of Huinan.
In Jiangxi and Hunan, [the Dharma] was like the sun and moon being raised high; yet it was not until late that he truly found his son. The child he nurtured was the man of Mount Wei, Muze.
Dwelling in forests and hiding in valleys, steadfast, dense, profound, and still, when the frost and dew ripened the fruit, the various sages brought him forth.
Like withered wood and rotten stumps, through which clouds move and rain falls, the Way of Cuiyan then shone forth and was put into practice. Indeed, it was Cuiyan who [did so].

Upon entering Shishuang, he happened to encounter a single roar, whereby all sentiments of ordinary and sage were exhausted. Through his inquiry and resolution, he penetrated to the very essence of Buddhas and Patriarchs;

whether walking, standing, sitting, or reclining, throughout past and present, he was like water flowing through a valley that never fails to fill its channels, or a pearl rolling on a platter that leaves no trace of its shadow.
Even when the Ten Sages and Three Worthies stand in the way, they must bow like grass before the wind. In the four directions...
From all eight directions, they have come; there are none who do not seek refuge in this land of old age and dispersal. Their golden chapters and jade verses are fully present and may be known.
Yet, as for the bright moon and its luster, they often meet with those who brandish their swords; as for the "Yangchun" and "Bai-xue," it is difficult to find one who can appreciate the sound.

To the guests who have ceased formal inquiry at Huanglong, he must surely dismiss them by saying: "True gold refined a hundred times must enter the furnace and bellows of Cuiyan. Now, he sits firmly presiding over [the assembly].
Throughout all quarters, those who hear the dragon’s roar and the tiger’s cry do not fail to praise the verses from within the chamber of Cuiyan.
These were used to receive ordinary people of great capacity; thus, the monastic communities have designated him as one who has truly "marked his chest.

Several elders of the same lineage, though their gaze was fierce and their literary brilliance was radiant—appearing as if they had emerged from the Dharma-cave of Ciming—actually did not understand the meaning of Shishuang’s verse.

It is merely the mechanism of the tree. Each dreams of sharing the same bed, yet this does not hinder their different melodies. Like beans popping in cold ashes, I offer this as a mere excuse for self-exoneration.
[Ascending the hall: "Sentient beings are bound by conceptual obstructions; Bodhisattvas always awaken and do not abide. Holding up his staff, he said: "The staff..."
This "son" is an obstruction. What, then, is awakening? If you understand it, you will mistake the obstruction for an obstruction and lack freedom.
If you do not understand it, the source of return is non-dual; though there are many gates of expedient means.
Xuefeng presented a wooden snake to Xiyuan, inscribing upon it: "The wood is already perfected; there is no need for the axe.
Upon receiving it, Xiyuan said, "A man who dwells in the mountains in his true nature, yet bears no marks of the blade or axe. The Master remarked, "Frail and withered;
one would not call this fine timber."
A monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "In the same pit, there is no different soil. "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master said, "Deep plowing and shallow sowing. "What is the great meaning of the Buddha-dharma? The Master said, "The worthies and sages of the five supernatural powers.
The monk said, "I, this student, do not understand. The Master said, "The tongue reaches up to the Brahma Heaven; such is the student."
At the point where he turned his body, the Master said: "One wall; a hundred walls are harmonized. "How is it that this student exerts effort? The Master said:
"Chopping wood for a thousand days, burning it on a single day. "What is the student’s point of intimacy? The Master said: [Silence].
The wife sends him off to the ferry; the Master then says: "Above, it reaches the peak of existence; below, it extends to the void of space.
If you let this pass, it is all a muddy mess of water; if you do not let it pass, not even a blade of grass can survive. Raising his staff, he said:
He churned the waters of the eastern great ocean and shook the palaces of the dragon kings until their souls were scattered and their courage failed, causing them to recite the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā*.
Shanglan unified the eight directions and brought peace to the four quarters.
He then recited this mantra: *Oṃ huan pen huan pen. Do not be angry; I know your true nature. Hūṃ.*
HŪṂ SVĀHĀ. He plants his staff and descends from the seat.
"To not see a single dharma is a great affliction. Mountains, rivers, and the great earth; sun, moon, and stars; form and emptiness, light and darkness."
It is not a single dharma. [The Master] raised his staff and said: "Ordinary people see the staff and call it a staff.
Śrāvakas see the staff and recognize it as mere empty space, thereby negating the staff. Bodhisattvas see the staff—when has it ever caught on their teeth?
When hungry, they eat; when weary, they sleep; when cold, they approach the fire; when hot, they seek the cool."
"I do not see the Way. All-knowledge wisdom is pure. Speaking thus, he laughs until the nostrils of the local earth-spirit burst.
He strikes the meditation staff and descends from the seat.
King Prasenajit raised a question to the Buddha: "Within the Noble Truth of Ultimate Reality (*paramārtha-satya*), is there also the Conventional Truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*)?
If one says it exists, then wisdom should not be singular; if one says it does not exist, then wisdom should not be dual. What is the meaning of this duality of 'one' and 'two'? The Buddha said:
"Great King, in the past, during the time of Dragon Light Buddha (*Nāgaprabhāsa-buddha*), you once asked about this very matter. I have no [need to] repeat it now."
[The Master] said: "You have neither heard nor spoken. To have neither heard nor spoken—this is called 'one meaning' and 'two meanings.
The Master said: "King Prasenajit understands the question but does not understand the answer; the World-Honored One understands the answer but does not understand the question. Why is this?

King Prasenajit is biased toward phenomena (*dharma*), while the World-Honored One is biased toward principle (*li*). If Shanglan had seen this at the time, he would have taken a torch and shone it upon them.
How thick is the skin on the old fellow Śākyamuni’s face?
Brothers, add a cross; together, apply a single rite. The local deity is called Songshan; the egg-shaped stupa is named Nandī.
There is further the "Hu Family Tune. You must all know this well: I sing the bellowing of the clay ox, and you respond with the neighing of the wooden horse.
The Master said: "The Emperor’s decree within the realm; the General’s command beyond the passes. Xuefeng did not reach the village in front, nor did he encounter the inn behind.
If it were Shanglan, he would have mixed mud and water. For now, let it be so; do not be negligent thirty years from now!"
The cold wind blows piercingly; the withered grasses are mottled. The general who has emerged from the ranks—his heart is like iron. Is there anyone such?
If there is, then with a single horse and a solitary spear, I invite you to meet me. After a long silence, he said: "If there is none, look back to the place where the eagle was shot down:
the evening clouds stretch level for a thousand miles."
The Buddha preaches the Dharma with a single voice, yet sentient beings each attain understanding according to their kind. [The Master] strikes the meditation staff and says:
"Is this not Śākyamuni the Old Man? If you all know how to go about it, you can move freely in every direction—eating porridge, eating rice."
If you do not know this either, you are merely prattling on about this and that inside the brazier; wait until after the winter solstice to see it. He planted his staff and descended from the seat.
He then cited the story of Mazu, together with Baizhang, Xitang, and Nanquan, while they were gazing at the moon. The Master asked, "Right at such a moment as this..."
At that moment, what was it like? Zhaozhang said, "It is precisely the time for cultivation. He then asked Xitang, who said, "It is precisely the time for making offerings.
He then asked Nanquan, who shook out his sleeves and walked out. The Great Master said, "The Sutras have entered the Canon;
Chan has returned to the sea. Only Puyuan alone transcends the mundane world. Master Shending said, "It is simply because his grandmotherly heart is so earnest. Shanglan then—
Not so. Lowering a hook ten thousand *li* deep, he halts the black steed of a thousand *li*. Spreading a net across the heavens, he gathers the giant fish leaping through the waves.
Is there anyone? If there is, come forth through the waves and meet me. If not, return for now to the base of the cliff and wait until the moon is bright.
He cited the Prefectural Governor, Master He, who asked Yunmen, “I request your instruction. Yunmen said, “Before one’s eyes, there is no grass other than this.
The Master said, “The world is one foot wide; the ancient mirror is one foot wide. If you do not believe this Way, who knows that beneath the scholar’s hat?”
Originally, these were but sorrowful people of old.
Clouds conceal the valley mouth; waters flow into the vast ocean. All phenomena are thus by nature, yet it is man who creates his own clamor. Beyond this, there is nothing more.
Furthermore, how is it so? [The Master] picks up his staff and says: "This staff leaps up to the Thirty-three Heavens and strikes the nose of Śakra.
The Earth Deity becomes incensed and reports it to the Sky Deity; the Sky Deity reports it to the Celestial Deities.
Now it is back in the hands of Shanglan. Do you all see it? If you do see it, then the Vinaya follows its direction. If...
Nor will it [hinder you]. Let him leap as he pleases.
Take the case of Devadatta, who slandered the Buddha and was cast alive into hell. The Buddha commanded Ānanda to convey his message:
"Are you at peace within the prison? Devadatta replied, "Though I am in this prison, it is as pleasant as the fourth dhyāna heaven. The Buddha then again commanded Ānanda to inquire further.
“Will you come out? Da said, “I will wait for the World-Honored One to arrive before I come out. Ānanda said, “The World-Honored One is the Great Master of the Three Realms;
how could he have a portion [of karma] that leads him into hell? Da said, “How could I have a portion [of karma] that leads me out of hell? The Master said:
The words of a parent come from the parent’s own mouth.
When this old monk carries Mount Sumeru on his back, everyone else holds up the sun and moon in their hands;

when the old monk retreats three thousand paces, everyone else advances eight hundred. Therefore it is said: there is the provisional and there is the real; there is the contrary and there is the compliant. Depart!
Beyond this, what else is there? [The Master] strikes the meditation staff and descends from his seat. He then cites Panshan’s saying:
"Like the earth supporting a mountain, it does not know the mountain's loftiness; like a stone containing jade, it does not know the jade's flawlessness.
The Master says: "Panshan’s strength is exhausted and his spirit weary; he too is merely looking at the clouds while climbing a tree. Do you understand?"
"Is there anyone who, without traversing the various stages of the sages, alone transcends the mundane world? He then let out a great laugh and descended from his seat.
He then cited an episode: One day, Zhaozhou and Wenyuan were walking in the garden. With his staff, Zhaozhou pointed to a stalk of vegetables.
Wenyuan lowered his head and pulled it out. Zhaozhou struck him. The Master said: "Those who know me grieve for my heart; those who do not know me..."
"What do you seek from me? O distant, azure Heaven! Who is this person?
A monk asked Dongshan, "What is it like when Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra come to visit? Dongshan said, "Drive them into the cowpen.
The monk said, "Entering hell, Master, would be like being shot by an arrow. Dongshan said, "It depends entirely on your own strength."
The Master said: "The Founders of our school close and open [the gates of truth]; for this reason, they drive away the oxen of the plowmen and snatch the food from the hungry.
Yet, as for those who have attained insight—how would they act? An old man like me will now decide whether such an act is appropriate or not.

At that time, had I been this monk, I would have prostrated myself with my five limbs touching the ground like the collapse of Mount Tai, performed three bows of ceremony, and returned to the midst of the pure assembly."
He taught Dongshan to know when to advance and when to retreat; was he not a sage indeed?

His sharp and novel path of speech sweeps across the realms of humans and devas. If you attempt to deliberate upon it, you will find it difficult even to look down upon it; it does not fall within the reach of mere stylistic flair.
How would you say it? Is there anyone who can say it? If there is, bring forth a single phrase from the time before the black bean had even sprouted.
If not, then the road north and south of the gate will meet with spring tomorrow.
"A single shout distinguishes guest and host; illumination and function act simultaneously. To understand the meaning within this, it is like striking the third watch at noon.
He then let out a shout and asked, "How do you distinguish them? Even if you could distinguish them, you must not overstep the gate of the patch-robed monk. He struck the ground with his staff.
Clouds rise on the Southern Mountain; rain falls on the Northern Mountain. Meeting by day, they hold torches to light their way. Holding up his staff, he said:
"The staff leaps and bounds up to the Thirty-three Heavens, striking the nose of Śakra and piercing through the skulls of you all.
Do you all know the sensation of pain? If you do, there is porridge upon the long benches."
[The Master] ate his rice. Not knowing [what else to do], he took up his alms bowl and went into the city of Hunan to eat porridge and rice.
He set down his staff and descended from the seat. He cited the case where a monk asked Baling, "What is the Way? Baling said, "A clear-eyed person falls into a well. He also asked Baoying.
"What is the Way? One should reply: "Before the Five-Phoenix Pavilion. Again, he asked Shoushan, "What is the Way?
Shou replied, "Three feet deep beneath one's feet. Regarding these three turning words: one phrase stands like a cliff ten thousand fathoms high; one phrase is rowing a boat on dry land;
one phrase is the mutual interpenetration of guest and host. Is there anyone among you who can discern them? Come forward and speak!
As there is no [self], one practices the compassion of an Arhat to destroy the thieves of the fetters; one practices the compassion of a Bodhisattva to bring peace to sentient beings;
one practices the compassion of a Tathāgata because of attaining the mark of suchness.
To resist the enemy on the battlefield without fear of life or death is the courage of a general.
To enter the mountains without fear of tigers or rhinoceroses is the courage of a hunter. To enter the water without fear of crocodiles or dragons is the courage of a fisherman.
But what is the courage of a monk? [The Master] picks up his staff and says, "This is the staff; you can pick it up and hold it."
If you can move it, the three thousandfold world-system will shake all at once; if you cannot move it even by picking it up, then Mañjuśrī remains Mañjuśrī and liberation remains liberation.
A monk asked, "What is the Way? The Master said, "As soon as you step out the door, you see it. The monk pressed further, "What about one who is on the Way?
The Master said, "Carrying the cangue, passing through the legal proceedings. The Master then said: "Day after day it rises in the east; day after day it sets in the west."
Do you understand? That which is before is the front mountain; that which is behind is the main mountain. Thirty years hence, do not err in your citation.
It is not above in heaven, nor below in earth, nor in between among men. [The Master] picks up his staff and says:
"Now it is in the hands of Cuiyan, acting as the Bodhisattva Anantagātra. Do you all see him? If you see him, then truly you do not see."
Come forward to the top of the hall. If you do not see it, today we shall go on a tour of the quarters to inquire after one another.
Holding up his staff, he said: "Cuiyan’s staff harmonizes its virtue with Heaven and Earth; it harmonizes its brilliance with the sun and moon; it harmonizes its sequence with the four seasons;
it harmonizes its auspiciousness and misfortune with the ghosts and spirits. But tell me, with what does it harmonize for the patch-robed monk?"
What is this? I tell you: do not travel the path beneath the mountain. Indeed, the cry of the monkey is heart-rending.
Studying the Way is like drilling for fire; when smoke appears, one must not yet desist. Only when the golden star manifests does one finally reach home.

Later, Shendǐng said: "Studying the Way is like drilling for fire; when you encounter smoke, you should stop immediately. If you wait for the appearance of the spark, you will burn your hands and then your head.
The Master said: "If we speak in terms of the sudden (dùn), Shimen is still halfway there. If we speak in terms of the gradual (jiàn)..."
Even the divine cauldron still lacks awakening; regarding this, how can one proceed? O virtuous ones, this year we encounter falling leaves;
at how many places shall we sweep them and return home?
The ancient verse says:
"Old Master Lu Zu sits facing the wall;
ten thousand peaks and myriad mountains surround him. He exhorts people to eliminate the difficulties of right and wrong. Recently at Chi Yang, there has been no news."
Rest. By chance, one does not personally observe the events of that year.
Mazu said, "Mind is Buddha"; later he said, "Neither mind nor Buddha.
A million brave soldiers march forth; the general hunts at Wei City. Unfamiliar with the strength of bow and arrow, the crescent moon rises over the slanting Milky Way.
The National Preceptor called the attendant three times;
how could the attendant not have responded? The National Preceptor raises wind and thunder upon dry land.
Had they met at that moment, the ninefold elixir would have been reduced to ashes.
Baizhang’s Wild Fox:
The words are blunt and coarse. *Tatsaha-kya*: "I have my own thatched hut.
Dongshan’s Three Pounds of Hemp.

Nanquan, Guizong, and Magu went together to pay their respects to the National Teacher.
When three people travel together, there must be someone who can be my teacher; one should choose what is good and follow it, and what is not good and [reject it].
Correct this:
Xuan Sha’s three types of sick people—one, two, three—are seeing, hearing, and cognizing. Who is it that suddenly dissolves them? Where the flowers cluster, the partridge cries; the grass...
In the fragrant air, mandarin ducks fly. "Old Xuansha, Old Xuansha! Relying on past years, he lacked but one move;
these words of ultimate truth are merely empty assent. In the midst of it all, half the tree’s fruit has fallen.
When Lingyun saw the peach blossoms, Zizai asked about the ford. The world is vast and flowing, yet the man stands tall.
If meeting and encountering one another were like this, there would be spring wind after spring wind, year after year.
Heishan strikes the drum; he knows how to strike the drum. How many times does he strike? Four times he strikes the drum and breaks it. In the realms of heaven and earth, do not be reckless!
Take this clearly to heart and investigate it well. Li Ling once entered the households of the barbarians; he sent a letter back to report to the ministers of the Han court.
The yellow sands stretch far and wide, with no way to stay.
—From the words of Chan Master Huanglong Nan, successor to Ciming, speaking from the hall:
"The monk’s hall has been seen through; look at the kitchen. The osprey and hawk have pecked the ridgepole of the Buddha Hall to death. Clearly and plainly, I tell you."
Shang still did not understand. How much less could he have anticipated what was to come? [The Master] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.

"The nature of wisdom-sea is formless; by awakening to delusion, one becomes an ordinary person. Since awakening to delusion is fundamentally void, one perceives the Buddha within the very mind of the ordinary person."

Simply let it rest as it is. Then one says: "Tongan has no way to settle the matter. Let your desires run wild and upside-down as you wish: "The Southern Dipper is seven; the Northern Dipper is eight.
The green vines entwine themselves straight up to the summit of the cold pines; the white clouds, pale and limpid, appear and disappear within the vast void.
The myriad dharmas are fundamentally tranquil; it is only people who create their own clamor. What is there to clamor about?

*Duh!* To stroke a tiger’s whiskers in accordance with its grain, one must look back at oneself; to grasp a scorpion’s tail upside down, let others do the guessing. A barbarian comes and a Han appears—this is but an ordinary matter.
Do not hang a bright mirror upon a high dais. [He] strikes the meditation seat and descends from it.
The moonlight blends with the white clouds; the sound of pines carries the chill of the dew. What a truly authentic message! Rely on you to examine it closely.
At the summit of Mount Zixiao, black clouds gather thickly; within Poyang Lake, white waves surge to the heavens. All phenomena arise without being acted upon by a single breath;
all dharmas manifest without being produced by a single cause. If you further attempt to deliberate or conjecture, you will be separated by a distance of eighty thousand miles.
Holding up the staff, he said: "Held crosswise or used upside down, it plucks out Maitreya’s eyes; moving from darkness to light, it knocks off the Patriarch’s nostrils.
At such a time, Maudgalyāyana and Wuzhuo would swallow their breath and silence their voices; Linji and Deshan..."
He laughs out loud. Now tell me, what is he laughing at? He lets out a shout.
Though he explains it in a thousand ways and instructs in ten thousand manners, his sole purpose is to make you return home early. Where do you go? After a long silence, he says:
"Last night the wind arose, filling the courtyard with fragrance; it blew down three or five peach trees."
To discourse on the marvelous and discuss the profound is the work of traitors in a time of Great Peace; to employ the staff and the shout is the practice of heroes in a chaotic age.
Heroes, traitors, the staff, the shout, the profound, and the marvelous—all these are superfluous accoutrements. Under the gate of Huangbo, none of them are of any use.
Now tell me: what do they usually use under Huangbo’s gate? (He lets out a shout. Everyone holds the pearl of the divine serpent;
each person embraces the raw jade of Mount Jing. Yet, failing to turn the light back upon themselves to reflect, they harbor their treasures while remaining lost in their own lands.
Have you not heard it said: "When the ear responds, it is like an empty valley; great and small sounds have no [inherent] self."
It is insufficient. When the eye functions, it is like a thousand suns; the myriad forms cannot escape their shadows and substances.
If one hesitates or seeks through sound and form, even Bodhidharma’s coming from the West would be a great failure.

The ancients gazed upon this moon; the people of today gaze upon this same moon. How can the mind of the ancients be explained to the people of today? The ancients sought the Way by seeking within their own minds;
having attained the emptiness of mind, the Way became naturally intimate. The people of today seek the Way by seeking outwardly through sounds;
chasing after sounds and pursuing forms, they only exhaust their spirits further and further. Exhausting the spirit again and again, how chaotic is this delusion! Strike the meditation seat!
The seat. The lower seat. There are five things in the world that are difficult to do: first, it is difficult for one who transforms [raw materials]; second, it is difficult for one who gives;
third, it is difficult for one who changes the raw into the cooked; fourth, it is difficult for one who eats while sitting upright. There is yet another thing that is difficult to do; what is it?
[The Master] said, "What kind of person? After a long silence, he said, "Hmm. He then descended from his seat. At that time, Zhen Dianxiong was the head seat (śrāmaṇera).
The Librarian asked, "Just now the Master said, 'The fifth type is not easy. Who is this person? The Head Seat replied, "If you see the cheek behind the head, do not associate with him."

Addressing the assembly: When body, speech, and mind are pure, this is called the Buddha’s appearance in the world; when body, speech, and mind are impure, this is called the Buddha’s passing into extinction.
This is a fine piece of news. The ancients employed a single expedient means for you all to open up a path of entry.
Once you have entered, you must also exit; only then is it complete. To climb a mountain, one must reach the summit; to enter the sea, one must reach the bottom.
If one does not reach the summit when climbing a mountain, one will not know the vastness of the universe.

If one does not reach the bottom when entering the sea, one will not know the depth of the dark blue ocean. Once one knows its vastness and knows its depth, with a single kick one overturns the four great oceans;
with a single shake one topples Mount Sumeru. Reaching home with hands cast loose, people do not recognize it; magpies chirp and crows caw among the cypress trees.

There was one person who, in the morning, would study the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* and in the evening, the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Day and night he applied himself with diligence, never ceasing for even a moment.
There was another person who did not practice Chan meditation nor discuss the meaning of the teachings; he simply took up a tattered mat and slept in the sun.

These two people arrived together at Huanglong—one practicing with effort (*saṃskṛta*), the other without effort (*asaṃskṛta*). Tell me, which of these two would be considered right? After a long silence...
It is said: "The Goddess of Merit and the Woman of Darkness—should a wise host encounter them, he accepts neither.
He treads lightly upon the ground for fear that others might notice; his speech and laughter are clear and beyond doubt. One who understands this simply seizes it with vigor;
do not wait for dawn, lest you lose the rooster."
The mind-king does not move falsely; the six realms are simultaneously penetrated. Lay aside the three-foot sword; cease playing with the single bow.
(He strikes the meditation seat with his whisk and descends from the seat.)
"Active thought and tranquil thought constitute duality. Neither active nor tranquil—this is the entrance into the Dharma-gate of non-duality.
Having thoroughly mastered this path, he questioned Bodhisattva Red-Crested King, struck the meditation seat, and descended from it.
Upon returning from his visit to Zhuang, he said: "When I went, a stream of flowing water saw me off; on my return, a valley full of white clouds welcomed me.
My single body’s coming and staying are neither coming nor staying; these two things are insentient, yet they seem sentient. He then struck the meditation seat with his whisk.
When the sunbird cries, the sky is brightly dawned; where the white clouds part, the moon is full. O practitioners of meditation beneath Vulture Peak:
cease attempting to thread the golden needle in the dead of night.
"Sometimes Huangbo walks the straight path; sometimes he runs through the weeds. You people must not see the sharpness of the chisel's tip and lose sight of the squareness of the chisel's handle.
Have you not seen the ancients say: 'Opening it, one cannot block it; inviting a thief, one ruins the house.
If one hesitates to sever when it should be severed, one will instead suffer the resulting chaos. Descend from your seats."
Entering the sea to count its sands is but a waste of effort; polishing a brick to make a mirror is a futile exertion of skill. Do you not see?

The clouds upon the high mountains roll up and spread out of themselves—what intimacy or distance is there? The water at the bottom of the deep ravine flows along curves and straight lines—there is neither "that" nor "this.
The daily activities of sentient beings are like these clouds and waters; though the clouds and waters are thus, people are not. If...
It is so. Where does the saṃsāra of the three realms arise?
The Old Verse:
Changli Meets Dadian; Beimoyan Meets Huoshan.
The Founding Master displays his family style in a peerless manner; he deploys every means for the sake of Lord Han. Within the lion’s den there are no other beasts;
where the elephant king walks, the tracks of foxes are severed.
Uncle and nephew meet, neither suspecting the other; in the end, they pat each other’s backs like simpletons. Looking back, fearing people might mock them as strange, he reports:
"You have enticed me here from a thousand miles away."
Yanyang asked Zhaozhou: "I have brought nothing. Zhaozhou called to his attendant three times, saying, "I have brought nothing.

This is a statement of essence—essence being you, the master of the house, who, having finished eating your rice, does nothing but talk in your sleep, saying, "I have realized the Buddha-dharma.

"Rest? There is yet another kind of person who, as soon as they hear it said that there is a place of rest, immediately closes their eyes within the realm of darkness and makes their living inside a rat's hole.

What kind of fault is this? To call this "striking first without meeting a master" is, in the end, nothing but being a hollow charlatan.
If you truly have a point of view, bring it forth and show it; let us deliberate together. Do not let it pass in vain.
You do not recognize good from evil, yet you chatter and clamor together, gathering around to discuss tangled vines. Do not let the old monk catch you and bring you before me for interrogation.
"It does not match! I shall break your waist with this staff. Do not say I have not spoken! Is there any blood beneath your skin?

What are you all doing here? With his staff, he drove them all away at once.
From the beginning until now, what exactly has this been? Now, being constrained by necessity, I shall speak to you all:
throughout the entire earth, what object exists that could serve as an opponent or a condition for you?

Mountains, rivers, and the great earth; the sun, moon, and the stars—what do you take these to be? Are they the four elements and five aggregates?
When I speak thus, it is called the talk of an old woman in a village of three households.

Changqing said, "They are growing! The Master said: *Note: The term "舉" (jǔ) indicates that this is a formal presentation of a kōan or recorded dialogue for study.*

Guang: "Sometimes it is said that when light does not penetrate through, there are two kinds of illnesses. First, there is a lack of clarity in all places, as if there were an object directly before one's face.
Second, even if one has penetrated through so that all dharmas are empty, there is still a lingering sense, as if there were some kind of thing remaining."
The light does not penetrate through. Furthermore, the Dharma-body also has two kinds of illnesses. First, having attained the Dharma-body, one fails to forget the attachment to dharmas;
one's own views still persist, and one remains seated within the precincts of the Dharma-body. This is the first.
Even if you manage to penetrate through the Dharma-body, do not let it pass unexamined. If you scrutinize it closely, what trace of scent remains? That too is an illness.
Sometimes he would pick up his staff and show it to the assembly, saying: "This staff has transformed into a dragon and swallowed up heaven and earth.
Where, then, do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth come from?"
Case: Xuansha addressed the assembly, saying, "The venerable elders of all quarters all say they 'receive things and benefit beings.
But suppose three kinds of sick people were to come—how would you receive them? For one suffering from blindness, you raise your staff or brandish your whisk, yet he does not see.
For one suffering from deafness, you employ the samādhi of speech, yet he does not hear. For one suffering from muteness, you try to teach him to speak, yet he cannot speak. Now then—"
"How do you receive him? If you cannot receive this person, the Buddha-dharma has no efficacy.
A monk requested instruction from the Master. The Master said, "Prostrate yourself. As the monk rose from his prostration, the Master struck him with his staff.
The monk stepped back, and the Master said, "You are not blind. He then called him forward again. When the monk approached, the Master said, "You are not deaf."
He then raised his staff and said, "Do you understand? The monk replied, "I do not understand. The Master said, "It is not that you suffer from muteness.
At these words, the monk attained realization.
[The Master] raised [the topic]: Great Master Mā (Mazu) said, "All speech and language is the school of Deva; take this as the master.
The Master [Baizhang] said, "Excellent words, yet no one asks about them. A monk then asked, "What is the school of Deva?
The Master said, "Of the ninety-six types in India, you are the lowest type."
[The Master] raised [the topic]. Dharma Master Zhao said: "If all dharmas were not different, one could not shorten a crane by cutting it or lengthen a duck by adding to it;
only after leveling a mountain and filling a valley could they be said to be without difference. The Master said: "The long is naturally long;

the short is naturally short. He further said: "This dharma abides in its own station; the characteristics of the world are eternally present. Then, picking up his staff, he said: "The staff does not..."
"This is the eternally abiding Dharma.

[The Master] raised his staff and said: "When the World-Honored One was first born, he pointed one hand toward heaven and one hand toward earth, walked seven steps, and looking around in the four directions, declared:
'In the heavens above and the world below, I alone am the Honored One. If I had seen him at that time, I would have struck him with a single blow of my staff."
"Beat it to death! Give it to the dog to eat, so that the world may enjoy peace.
Case: Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "The world is ten feet wide; the ancient mirror is ten feet wide. The world is one foot wide;
the ancient mirror is one foot wide. Xuansha pointed to the brazier before him and asked: "How wide is this fire-donkey? Xuefeng said: [He beat him.]
Yun said, "It is like an ancient mirror, broad. Sha said, "This old fellow has not yet even touched the ground with his heels. Later, Dongshi took up this case and questioned a monk:
"Is it that the ancient mirror caused the brazier to be so large, or did the brazier cause the ancient mirror to be so large?"
Xiyuan said, "To ask such a question of a person—this is not yet permissible. The Master said, "Sour rice and a clay tea stove. He then cited the case:
A monk asked Yunju, "From what do the mountains, rivers, and the great earth arise? Yunju said, "They arise from deluded thoughts.
The monk said, "Can you give me a bar of gold produced by my own thoughts? Yunju then stopped speaking. The monk did not approve. The Master heard this.
To say "I have attained" is already a tangle that cannot be resolved. Wait for him to say, "Can one produce a bar of gold from thought?
and then take up the staff and strike him.

The Master, acting as a proxy for the previous speaker, ascended the hall and said: "Tell me, when it is said that 'the ancient Buddha intersects with the pillar,' to which level of spiritual capacity does this correspond?
No one answered. The Master said: "Ask me, and I will tell you. A monk then asked. The Master said: "A single cord costs thirty cash. This was his proxy response.
The saying goes: "Clouds rise over the Southern Mountain; rain falls on the Northern Mountain. A monk asked again, "What is this one strip of rope worth thirty coins?
The Master said, "Hit him! He ascended the hall and said, "Heaven and earth are tilted; sun, moon, and stars are all black at once.
How do you say it? [A monk] offered a substitute response: "Better not to have done anything good at all. One day he said, "Today is the fifteenth."
It is the beginning of summer. What does Hanshan say? [The Master] provides the answer: "When the Master asks about Hanshan, the student answers for Shigede.
Alternatively, he says: An ancient said, "Everyone possesses a radiant light; yet when one looks for it, it is dark and obscured. What is this light? [The Master] provides the answer:
"The kitchen, the storehouse, and the main gate. He also says: "A good thing is not as good as having none at all."
One day he said: "The Buddha-dharma is truly abundant; it is simply that the tongue is too short.

[A monk] offered in his stead: "It is long. He also said: "When the great axe has finished its work, one rubs the hands together. To the assembly he said: "Within there is a treasure, hidden within the mountain of form.
Take the lantern and place it inside the Buddha Hall; bring the triple gate and set it upon the lantern. What do you say to this? [A monk] offered in his stead: "Chasing after things."
[The Master] shifted his attention. He also said: "Thunder arises and clouds emerge. Or he said: "A-ye-ye!
While forging iron in the kingdom of Silla, a spark struck my finger. [A monk] offered a substitute response: "Not only my finger. One day he said:
"The eyelashes span across the ten directions; the eyebrows pierce upward through heaven and earth and downward through the Yellow Springs; Mount Sumeru blocks your throat."
[The Master] says, "Throat! Is there anyone who understands? If there is someone who understands, they would drag over Campā and wrestle neck-to-neck with the kingdom of Silla.
[Another] provides a substitute response: "A smile. He addresses the assembly, saying, "What is the phrase that does not reveal its sharp edge or bone? He provides a substitute response.
People of the present day must clearly and directly point toward the Way before they can succeed. The Master then offered this verse:
"A phrase that reveals neither edge nor bone, bestowed even before a word is spoken; When you step forward, your mouth chatters on— I know you are utterly at a loss."
Record of Wandering Journeys:
When the Master first visited Chan Master Muzhou Zong, as soon as Muzhou saw him approaching, he closed the door. The Master knocked on the door, whereupon Muzhou asked, "Who is it?
The Master replied, "It is I. Muzhou asked, "What do you want? The Master said, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg [for instruction]."
The Master pointed the way. When Master Zhou opened the door and saw him, he immediately closed it again. The Master went to knock on the door like this for three consecutive days.
On the third day, Master Zhou finally opened the door; the Master then pressed against him. Master Zhou seized him and said, "Speak! Speak!
The Master hesitated, and Master Zhou pushed him away, saying, "A cartwheel from the Qin dynasty. From this, the Master attained awakening. Later, the Master arrived at Xuefeng...
At Fengzhuang, he met a monk. The Master asked, "Elder, are you going up the mountain today?
The monk replied, "Yes. The Master said, "Entrust this kōan (in-yuan) to the Abbot; however, you must not say it was the words of another. The monk replied, "I understand.
The Master said, "When you arrive at the mountain, as soon as the assembly has gathered for the Abbot’s formal discourse, you should step forward and grasp [his staff]."
Wanlidi said, "This old fellow, why do you not cast off the iron cangue upon your neck? The monk followed his teacher’s instruction exactly.
Seeing the monk speaking in this manner, Xuefeng descended from his seat, seized him by the chest, and said, "Speak quickly!
Speak quickly! The monk had no reply. Xuefeng pushed him away and said, "These are not your words. The monk said, "They are mine."
[The monk] spoke. Xuefeng said, "Attendant, bring the rope and staff. The monk said, "This was not my words;
it was a senior monk from Zhejiang on the manor who instructed me to come and say this. Xuefeng said, "Everyone, go to the manor and welcome the five hundred virtuous teachers (kalyāṇamitra) there.
The next day, the Master went up the mountain. As soon as Xuefeng saw him, he said, "Why is this?"
Having attained such a state, the Master bowed his head; from that point on, they were in accord. Furthermore, because Shushan addressed the assembly, saying:
"Before the Xiantong era, this old monk understood the affairs of the Dharma-body; after the Xiantong era, I understood the matters above the Dharma-body. The Master asked:
"I have heard that before the Xiantong era, you, the Honored One, understood the Dharma..."
"Regarding matters of the phenomenal world: after the Xiantong era, did you understand the matter that transcends the Dharma-body?

Is it so? Shanshan said, "It is. The Master asked, "What is the matter of the phenomenal world? Shanshan said, "A withered stump. The Master asked, "What is the matter that transcends the Dharma-body?
Shanshan said, "Not a withered stump. The Master asked, "May I ask if you permit a student to speak of principle? Shanshan—
Xuefeng said, "I allow you to speak. The Master said, "A withered stump—is this not clarifying matters pertaining to the Dharma-body (dharmakāya)?
Is it not a withered stump—is this not clarifying matters above the Dharma-body? Xuefeng said, "Yes. The Master said, "Does the Dharma-body encompass all things?"
Shan said, "How is it that it does not encompass? The Master pointed to a water pitcher and asked, "Does the Dharma-body encompass this?
Shan said, "Do not interpret it from the perspective of the pitcher. The Master then paid his respects.

Later, because he saw Xinzhou Ehu ascending the hall and saying, "Do not say that those who have not yet attained realization are constantly in a state of restless agitation; even those who have attained realization..."
A person who clearly knows they have a destination still feels a sense of restless urgency. The Master came down from his seat, cited these words, and asked the Head Seat:
"Just now the Master addressed the assembly, saying, 'One who has not yet attained realization feels a sense of restless urgency;
one who has attained realization feels a sense of restless urgency. What is the meaning of this? The Head Seat replied, "A sense of restless urgency. The Master said, "Head Seat..."
"Having lived here for a long time, with hair white and teeth yellow, one speaks such words as these. The Head Seat asked, "I wonder, Senior Monk, what about you?
The Master said, "If you wish to speak, you may; if you see it, then you see it. If you do not see it, do not speak recklessly."
The Head Seat said, "As for what the Abbot said—that it is 'floating and pressing'—what does that mean?
The Master said, "A cangue upon the head and shackles upon the feet. The Head Seat said, "If that is so, then there is no Buddha-dharma.
The Master said, "This is the realm of the great beings Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra. When the Master arrived at Jiangzhou, the Minister Chen invited him for a vegetarian feast. They met...
Upon seeing him, [Zhaozhou] asked: "I do not ask about the Confucian classics; there are already masters for the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings.
What is the matter of a monk’s traveling pilgrimage? The Master said: "How many people have you questioned so far? Zhaozhou said: "I am questioning you, Venerable Sir, right now. The Master said:
"Setting that aside for a moment, what is the meaning of the teachings? Zhaozhou said: "Yellow scrolls and red axes. (Referring to the physical volumes of the scriptures.)
The Master said, "This is merely words and language. What is the meaning of the teaching? The Book [of Documents] says, "When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail;
when the mind wishes to contemplate, thoughts vanish. The Master said, "'When the mouth wishes to speak, words fail' is said in contrast to having speech.

'When the mind wishes to contemplate, thoughts vanish' is said in contrast to deluded thought. What is the meaning of the teaching? [The Master continued: "The *Shangshu* (Book of Documents) has no..."
The Master said, "I hear you say you have read the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* and studied the *Lotus Sūtra*; is that so? The Official replied, "It is so. The Master said, "The Sūtra says:
'All livelihoods and productive enterprises are not at variance with the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

Now tell me, how many people in the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception have fallen from their station? The Official was speechless. The Master said, "Official, do not be so hasty. Ten sūtras, five..."
The Master said: "A teacher-monk casts everything aside and enters the monastic groves; yet even after ten or twenty years, he may still be unable to cope.
How much less could a lay official (shangshu) ever understand? The official bowed and said, "I, this humble one, am guilty. The Master further related that when Qianfeng ascended the hall, he said:
"The Dharma-body has three kinds of illnesses and two kinds of radiance. You must penetrate each and every one of them; furthermore, you must know that there is more."

"Functioning through illumination is for the occasion; the one uppermost aperture remains. After a long silence, the Master stepped forward and asked, "Why does the person inside the hut not see what is outside the hut?
Feng laughed heartily. The Master said, "That is still where the student has doubts.
