Feng asked, "What kind of mental activity do you have? The Master replied, "I also wish for the Master to understand me. Feng said: [The text ends here.]
"You must simply be thus; only then can you sit securely. The Master responded, "Yes, yes. Qianfeng addressed the assembly, saying:
"If you bring up one, you must not bring up two. To let one pass is to fall into the second.
A monk stepped forward from the assembly and said, "Yesterday someone came from Tiantai and went on to Jingshan. Qianfeng said, "Head cook, tomorrow there shall be no communal labor."
He then descended from his seat. While Master Zhisheng was at Lingshu, he served as the head seat (shouzuo) in the assembly.
At that time, a monk asked Zhisheng, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West? Zhisheng said, "I have no words.

He then turned to the monk and asked, "If you were suddenly to inscribe something upon a monument, what words would you put there? At that moment, several monks offered their responses, but none were in accord with the truth. Zhisheng said:
"Go and invite the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera) here. When the Master arrived, Xing raised the previous conversation and questioned him.
The Master said, "Not difficult. Xing asked, "What words can you apply to it? The Master said, "If someone asks, 'What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
simply say, 'The Master knows. Xing deeply approved.
The Sayings of Chan Master Fachang Yu. Successor to Beichan Xian, ascending the hall:
Before Śākyamuni had passed away and before Kāśyapa had heard [the Dharma], one entered the holy from the ordinary; this merit was not bestowed in vain.
The texts of the Great Canon are like gold and like jade. Yet when the Golden-Colored Dhūta received the Dharma and the robe, the Dragon Palace and the Ocean Treasury [were opened].
There is no place for it to emerge. But tell me, what excellence does the Patriarch possess? A single pill dispels all ailments;
there is no need for many prescriptions.
If you retreat a thousand feet, I shall sprout right where you stand. If you present yourself face-to-face, I shall...
Hiding the body to play with the shadow: if you pick up pebbles from a spring pond, I shall scatter bright pearls.
Thus, it becomes such that water cannot wet it and wind cannot enter—like a solid iron hammer without a hole. Tell me, does Fachang still have a way to benefit others?
A sharp blade cuts the flesh, yet the wound may heal; But harsh words wound a person, and the resentment never fades.

The spring mountains are green and the spring waters are lush. Having awakened from a dream of the "South柯" (Nankuo), one’s spring-slumber is complete. Carrying my staff, I stride freely out through the pine gate;
everywhere the peach blossoms are fragrant and rich. Because of the old master Lingyun in days past, for thirty years there has been nowhere to seek it.
Now everyone vies to pluck the willow flowers; red fragrance fills the ground, yet no one sweeps it up.
Zen Master Huanglong Nan arrived and said: "Seizing the clouds and grasping the waves, they are as numerous as hemp seeds; once the coppery eyes are struck, they bloom with flowers.
Apart from the head and horns of the Yellow Dragon, everything else is nothing but a striped red snake. "Fachang is but a small monastery; the road is distant and the mountains remote.
The scenery is desolate and few travelers venture there. I did not dare to expect that Zen Master Huanglong would deign to grant his light [to visit us]."
It is fitting that not only do the springs and rocks increase in luster, but even the dragons and devas rejoice.

Yet, from antiquity to the present, while clouds move and rain falls, alas, the smelting furnaces contain an abundance of dull iron, and at the gate of the skilled physician, the sick are ever more numerous.
To cure an illness, one must seek the divine elixir; to dissolve stubbornness, one must rely on the golden hammer. Here at Fachang, there are several masters who have fallen into their roots.
Those who are ill have their ailments deep in the vital organs; those who are stubborn have their obduracy entered into the very marrow.
Had it not been for the arrival of the old man Huanglong, they would all have lived in vain and died in vain. He then raised his staff and said, "Do you understand? It is like striking flour."
Returning his native land’s wheat, one must be a man of the Imperial Capital to sing this song.
Wearing a flowered kerchief upon his head as he leaves Shaoshi, carrying a straw hat in his hand as he departs Chang’an.
We shall meet again beneath Vulture Peak; our nostrils have always been of one and the same kind. (Huanglong).
A winter melon hangs from a gourd vine; a shrimp is caught amidst waves of ripening wheat. Who is there at the painted tower where wine is sold?
Inviting one another to come and drink Zhaozhou’s tea. (Fachang)
Iron oxen, pair after pair, with golden horns; wooden horses, two by two, with white jade hooves.
Out of love for the fine fragrant grasses of the Snow Mountains, they ride the moon at night across the stream before them. (Huanglong)
The Jade Unicorn, girded by the moon, leaves the Milky Way; the Golden Phoenix, holding flowers in its beak, descends upon the painted pavilion.
The rustic old man takes no offense at the young lord’s intoxication; together they walk hand-in-hand through the Imperial Street. (Fachang).

On the eighth day of the fourth month, it is said: When our Buddha, the World-Honored One, was born in Kapilavastu, nine dragons spontaneously spat forth water and the heavens rained down four kinds of flowers.
Pointing one finger toward heaven and one finger toward earth, he declared: "Above heaven and below heaven, I alone am honored."
He acted as if he were completely unconcerned with others. When the old man of Shaoyang came forth and struck him once, everyone everywhere thought his position had crumbled like melting ice;
yet they failed to realize that when heaven intends to bring light, it must first be dark, and when a person intends to flourish, they must first decline.

It is like a drum smeared with poison: once struck, it brings immediate ruin. This has caused the land of the Patriarchs for a thousand years to compete in raising weapons, becoming a subject of gossip on people's lips.
Facha was not intimidated by the imminent danger; what a fine staff! But it was too late.
He should have been given a single thrust beneath the heels while he had not yet left the Tuṣita Heaven—how could it wait until today? Nevertheless, even so, it is very much like...

When bandits pass by, they draw their bows; none dare approach this place. To deliver a single turn of words that does not violate the principle of things is not only to vent one’s indignation on behalf of Gautama, but also to sever the entanglements of all quarters. Is there such a person?
Do not take offense at his great spirit; he has once trodden upon the highest barrier.
To awaken to the Way by hearing sounds is no different from climbing a tree to seek fish; to clarify the mind by seeing forms is much like mistaking a head for its reflection.
O worthy ones, there is no need to shorten the ducks or truncate the cranes, nor to level mountains or fill valleys. The Southern Dipper and the Northern Dipper have their distinct movements;
the sun is obscured and the moon is bright, each rising and sinking according to its own nature. Simply cease all military expeditions and warfare, and remain upright and inactive. From this—

However, having attained this point of entry, one stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs. If you further speak of discerning the intent within the midst [of words] and clarifying the mechanism within the phrases, you are like a person waiting by a tree stump under the clear breeze and moonlight;
the cool rabbit grows ever more distant while the spring grass turns green.
Today, Fachang opens the furnace. Not a single wandering monk is present. To inform the eighteen eminent practitioners: seal your mouths and sit in meditation around the hearth.

This is not because our rules are strict or difficult; it is to spare you all from falling into verbal pitfalls. Even if one’s mouth were like a scale-weight, one would still fail to escape being scrutinized by the lantern.
You do not realize that the Way is beyond achievement or merit, yet you recklessly cultivate causes and seek to realize fruits.

If one were to encounter Linji or Deshan, they would surely find it difficult to let such a person pass. Yet, if you simply know how to turn the mind for a single thought-moment, you will certainly escape the fetters of the Three Vehicles.

The bird-path on the green mountains—those who attempt to ascend it become lost; the azure void without waves—any movement therein violates the wind and shadows. This is not something before one's eyes.
Dharma. Do not give rise to various thoughts. Brightness and darkness are not related; space has no front or back.

Reaching this point, it is truly like the moon’s reflection in an autumn pond or the sound of a bell in a still night—yet these are still matters on the shore of birth and death. Do not treat them as trivial.

If you do not perceive the Way of the ancients, you must first shoulder the burden over there, and only then come back here to pack your gear, polish your consciousness, and exhaust the afflictions of the present moment.
Only when it is like withered wood encountering spring yet remains without moisture will you have a slight degree of resonance.
When the ancients spoke in this manner, what was their intent? What is it that one shoulders over there?
How, then, does one pack one's belongings here? Unless one is a man of great virtue who has long practiced, one cannot know this.
Do not merely remain thus, with a vast expanse of karmic consciousness, ignorant afflictions, and the egoism of human selfhood;

do not harbor private interpretations or give rise to groundless analysis, which would be like polishing a tile to make a mirror—how much superfluous error! You must quickly exert yourself; do not wait until the path ahead is exhausted before acting.
At first, I was preoccupied with busyness. One morning, my mind’s eye suddenly opened, and only then did I realize that Old Fachang took the Buddha-dharma as his sole concern.
On the sixteenth day of the fourth month every year, everywhere else observes the *kaṭhina* retreat; how is it here at Fachang?
One simply sees the mountains green and the waters clear.
The Master arrived at Beichan. Chan asked, "Where have you recently departed from? The Master replied, "Fuyan.
Chan said, "By how much has Sita’s nostrils grown longer? The Master replied, "They are exactly as they were when you first saw them, Reverend. Chan said, "Now tell me, then."
"When I saw you, how long had it been? The Master said, "The Abbot seems as though he has never been to Fuyan. Cuiyan said, "You are merely one who parrots the words of others.
[Cuiyan asked: "When you arrived, was Master Mazu well? The Master said, "He is well. Cuiyan said, "What did you say to him?
The Master said, "I told the Abbot not to be so nonsensical. Cuiyan said, "I am mindful that you are a newcomer; I cannot..."
[Zhaozhou] struck him. The Master said, "I, too, let the Master off. While drinking tea, Zhaozhou asked, "Where is your native place?
The Master said, "Zhangzhou. Zhaozhou asked, "What is Sanping doing there? The Master said, "He is preaching on Zen and preaching on the Way.
Zhaozhou asked, "How old are you? The Master said, "I am the same age as the pillar. Zhaozhou said, "As for having a pillar, that is one thing."
"How many years has the pillar been here? The Master said, "The pillar has not lacked even a single year. Càn said, "Letting loose a black chicken at midnight.
The Master visited the hermitage master Bājiā Quán and asked, "Is the hermitage master there? Quán replied, "Who is it? The Master said, "A traveling monk."

The monk asked, "What have you come for? The Master said, "I have come to pay my respects to the Abbot. Quan said, "It happens that the Abbot is not here. The Master said, "Then you yourself [should answer].
Quan said, "I told you he was not here. Why speak of 'you' and 'I'? He then seized his staff and drove him straight down the mountain, telling him to come back the next day.
The next morning, the Master went again and was driven away as before. Later, the Master went once more and asked, "Is the Abbot there? Quan—
"Who is it? the Master asked. The monk replied, "A traveling monk. He pulled back the curtain and entered.
Baizhang [Quan] grabbed him by the chest and said, "Here, where insects and tigers roam, what do you, a bed-wetting ghost-child, seek to come for three or two times?
The monk replied, "I have long admired your reputation for the Way. Baizhang then untied his robe and shook it out, saying, "You thought that Great Master Quan had some great wonders!"
Deshan asked, "What is the master of this hermitage? Nanquan said, "One must discern it upon entering the gate.

Deshan said, "Is it not simply this very thing? Nanquan said, "How many people have been deceived! Deshan said, "Where was your previous statement? Nanquan said, "Listening without clarity; calling a bell a jar.
Deshan said, "In that case, when the myriad dharmas are extinguished, the whole body is manifested. Nanquan said, "Your Majesty..."
"The subject should occupy the center; thus, the heterodox is eliminated. Yunquan said, "Let this donkey-headed fellow stop; why do you cause such confusion?
The Master asked, "I wonder, when a guest arrives, with what will you receive them? Yunquan said, "Yunmen’s *hubing* (millet cakes) and Zhaozhou’s tea.
The Master said, "If that is so, then I thank you for the offering. Yunquan said, "I have not even had the firewood yet, and you already speak of 'thanks'."
Offerings. At the North Zen Temple, during the year-end small lecture, he said: "The year has reached its end; there is nothing else with which to share this season with you all.
Tonight, I shall roast a white ox from the open field, boil a soup of wild vegetables, and burn firewood. Once we have eaten, everyone shall gather around the hearth."
They performed the *Sōden-gaku* (village music). Why? To ensure they did not rely on others' gateways or lean against others' walls, thereby allowing bystanders to call them "Mister.
When night fell, the *Rakan* (Venerable Leader) went to inquire, saying, "There is someone from the district office summoning the Master. The Zen master asked, "For what purpose?
The *Rakan* replied, "The Master killed an ox last night and has not yet paid for its hide and horns. Thereupon, the Zen master pulled off his hat.
The Master said, "This is not it. Shide then came out. Chan called to his attendant, saying, "Thief! Thief! Shide said, "It is cold;
please return the Master’s hat to me. Chan looked at the Master and asked, "How do you resolve this koan?"
The Master said: "Paper is in high demand in Tanzhou; one document suffices for all.

Generally speaking, brothers who study the Way, whose vision of the Path is not yet clear and whose minds are not yet at peace, must, upon entering a monastic community or leaving a spiritual society, draw near to virtuous friends and good companions.
Throughout the twelve hours of the day and night, they must take the Buddha-dharma as their primary concern and proceed directly [toward realization].
You must exercise discernment to make the mind’s eye sharp and clear. This is no small matter. Time passes easily;
it does not wait for anyone. Once you have lost this human body, there will likely be no way out.

Do not spend your time merely in such idle clamor, saying "today the third, tomorrow the fourth," staying here through the winter and passing the summer there, with nothing but a belly full of tangled confusion.

Fengtou Lubu studied the scholastic interpretations; wherever he went, he would rub his lips and stroke his beak, speaking in both Chinese and barbarian tongues, claiming, "I understand Chan, I understand the Way.
He treated good people with contempt and committed the karma of the Avīci Hell. You should know that this matter is not easily mastered.
Even great beings of immeasurable capacity, when they reach this point, cannot find their own heads and noses. Do not take it lightly and rashly open your big mouths—Old Farchang!
The people of Han have no human feeling; they do not love one another. When they stroke you or praise you, it is entirely not out of a kind heart.

One day, when wind and fire disperse and the light of the eyes falls to the ground, the karmic conditions of good and evil will bring retributions of beauty or ugliness within the realm of birth and death.
All at once it manifests before them; at that moment, they are like crabs falling into boiling water, their hands flailing and feet scrambling in confusion.
Their former livelihoods, spiritual powers, and Buddhist teachings all prove useless. Driven by frantic karmic consciousness, they have no one to rely upon, and their regrets come too late.
Receiving retribution according to conditions, shifting and revolving through various forms—none of this can be fixed. Have you not seen what the ancients said?
"O Bodhisattvas who study Prajñā, do not deceive yourselves; you must be most meticulous. If even a hair’s breadth remains unexhausted, you will not escape saṃsāra.
If a single thread of thought is not forgotten, you will all sink into the depths. Do you wish to recognize those who wear fur and carry horns? They are none other than yourself.
It is you who constantly act as the master of chaos. Do you wish to recognize the Hell of the Tongue-Puller? It is none other than you who deceive and delude your followers.
Do you wish to recognize the Cold Ice and the Boiling Cauldron? It is none other than you who unworthily accept the offerings of the faithful.
The three miserable realms and the eight difficulties are all created by your own mind; it is only because your Dharma-eye is not clear that you are thus.
It is so. If one were a person who has truly realized the truth, how could there be such news?

When Fachang speaks in this manner, it is entirely in accord with all the sages—not only you, my three elder and five younger brothers, but even Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained *kṣānti* (patience) all possess this fault;
how much more so for the eight classes of gods and dragons! Since you have come here and spent the entire winter and summer, do not take this lightly.
"By the side of this old monk’s hoe, I provide you with food. Let me speak a few words on the life of renunciation;

do not let yourselves be crushed by the delusions of self and others, lest your entire lives pass in vain. When the four elements finally disperse, it will be too late to employ any clever stratagems.
There are a certain kind of people who, upon hearing these things mentioned, give rise to thoughts of anger within their bellies and say: 'How could there be such a thing as Buddha-dharma?'"
Such matters as these—great enlightenment does not depend on minor details. Who else is there to ask? Let me ask you instead: what have you realized upon awakening?

Have you yet been able to cast off the consciousness and perceptions of the skull? Throughout the twelve periods of the day, you should at least remain in accord with the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.
At the assembly on Vulture Peak, have you ever seen a Buddha who lacked karmic conduct? Is there anyone here who still harbors delusions?
To speak of the Patriarch of the Source is much like comparing cow dung to sandalwood; what connection could there possibly be?

It may be said that while the supreme flavor of clarified butter (amṛta) is prized by the world, when encountered by such people as these, it turns instead into poison. If you wish for them to achieve resonance [with the truth], [you must first understand this].
But now, in a single thought-moment, in all places, let [the mind] be released into a state of withered detachment.

Throughout the twelve periods of the day and night, when facing the five desires and the eight winds, be like a blind person looking at objects; do not be governed by any phenomena, nor govern any phenomena yourself.
If you examine the gateway of the six sense-faculties and find not even a hair’s breadth of fault, only then will you have a slight measure of progress toward the goal.
When Fachang speaks in this manner, it is like taking a medicine that causes dizziness; though it is bitter to the mouth for a time, there will be great benefit later on.
Thus, the ancients said: "Even if a hundred thousand kalpas pass, the karma one has created will not be forgotten. This is the principle of cause and condition.
"When the time of meeting arrives, you must experience the karmic retribution yourself; no one can take your place. Each of you must exert yourselves.
— These are the words of Chan Master Xuedou.

Upon ascending the seat for the opening of the hall, the successor of Zhimen looked over the entire assembly and said: "The humans and devas have gathered here; together we should clarify and manifest [the truth]."
What kind of matter is this? How can one merely alternate between guest and host, racing through questions and answers, and take that to be the very vehicle of the school?
The vast and great tradition of our lineage possesses sovereign majesty and virtue; its brilliance transcends past and present. It holds fast the heavens and earth;

the thousand sages have said it can only be known by oneself, and even the five vehicles cannot establish it. Thus, though one may realize the essential meaning before a sound is uttered, one still remains lost at the point of the turning mirror. As for words...
Those below understand the school, yet they still remain dimly aware within the realm of emotional consciousness.

You all must know that to realize the true mark, you need only cease looking upward for something to rely upon and cut off your own personal efforts below. Then, the natural, eternal light will appear before you; each and every one stands like a cliff rising ten thousand fathoms.

Can you discern this clearly or not? If you have not yet discerned it, discern it! If you have not yet clarified it, clarify it! Once you have discerned and clarified it, you can sever the cycle of birth.

The stream of death flows on. Occupying the same station as the patriarchs and Buddhas, this moment of wondrous, perfect, and transcendent awakening is precisely when one can repay the unrepayable debt of gratitude and assist in the transformation of non-action.
Cui-feng received the letter of appointment, while the special envoys vied with one another; the clamor did not cease. Ascending the seat, [Cui-feng] said: "There is no need for such a fuss.
Furthermore, in the monastic life there is neither fixedness nor necessity. To stay, one is like a solitary crane perching coldly atop a pine peak;

to depart, one is like a fragment of cloud suddenly passing over the human world. It is surely not that our origins differ, nor that movement and stillness contradict each other's essence. Now, let us together recite the Three Refuges."

For two years, I have remained in seclusion at Dongting. Having received the gracious regard and the faith of those from afar, I have found harmony with the community and the restoration of the Tripitaka has returned to its former state.
How could I, moved by such profound gratitude, suddenly forget these things and hasten forward? This would truly be improper.

The Governor of Siming dispatched a messenger at full gallop, and his carriage and baggage soon arrived. Having already traveled across several provinces and traversed over a thousand li, he had come with such earnest and urgent sincerity that it reached this extreme.
Deliberating on whether to advance or retreat, he could not decide for himself: "Is it better to stay at Cui Feng? Or is it better to go to Xue Dou?
At that moment, the assembly of monks cried out in a loud voice, "It is better to go to Xue Dou! The Master looked back and said: [to the messenger].

Donor, there is no need for alarm; you should each know the proper time. Furthermore, the Buddha-dharma rests entirely upon kings and ministers, and moreover, the current abbot’s karmic conditions have come to an end.
Whether he remains there or stays here, there is fundamentally no contradiction. I hope you will peruse this letter to satisfy your request.
He then descended from his seat.
On entering the hall, a monk presented him with a walking staff. The Master picked it up and composed a verse, saying: "Pure and lofty, its solitary root possesses a distinct spirit."

The momentum contains mountains and waters, naturally distinct. Brought forth, it surpasses the sword of Fengcheng. When the retribution for the two injustices of the human world is complete—[the Master] spoke again:
"In general, to repay injustice with justice is the standard rule of righteous heroism; to repay injustice with injustice is the extraordinary regulation.
It is like using wisdom to dispel delusion, which is encountered quite often by those of inferior capacity. To use wisdom to..."
"O you of wisdom! Rarely do we encounter a true master. Do you wish to understand these two 'unequals'? All of you have measureless faults; Xuedou also has measureless faults.
As for Xuedou’s faults, he is capable of examining and reproving them himself. But as for you, you lacquer tubs—if I do not strike you now, when shall I?
With his staff, he drove them all away at once."
Form arises before substance; names emerge before the named. Once form and name have manifested, the wandering vapors disturb the clarity.
The Master picks up his staff and says, "O assembly, this staff—this is the simultaneous raising of both form and name. Is there any fault in this? If there is, it is like the moon in the water;
if there is not, it is the manifestation of form and name. If you can investigate this to the end, it is truly said that the kindness is too great to repay."
Before even emerging from the mother’s womb, he saw the public case (gong’an) accomplished. Having taken seven steps while walking about, his transgressions filled the heavens.
Entering the Deer Park once more was like branches and vines growing further upon branches and vines. Then, picking up his staff, he said, "Hūṃ! Hūṃ! and immediately descended from the seat.

O virtuous ones! When a patriarch proclaims the Way, he is like a distinguished guest upon the vast blue ocean, alone drifting in a fragrant boat upon the moonlit islets and misty waves, roaming freely at his pleasure.
To cast forth the fragrant bait, one must wait for the great leviathan; even if there were a tiny scale, there would be no hope [of success].
"A straight hook catches the *kūn* and *jīng* fish; a curved hook catches turtles and tortoises. If a curved hook were used for the *kūn* and *jīng*, it would logically be unsuitable;
if a straight hook were used for turtles and tortoises, they too would find it distasteful. Now, I cast my hook: whoever dares to risk their life, come to the hook!
After a long silence, he said, "Toil without merit," and then descended from his seat.
Day after day the sun rises in the east; day after day the sun sets in the west. It revolves through three hundred and sixty degrees.
How many can understand its hidden lair? Let it loose and it is brilliant and profound; hold it fast and it is a blur and a haze. Do you not see?
In the city of Vaiśālī, that Superior Man’s single room is vast and empty—what thing is there within? The Master calls to the assembly: "Keep your eyes wide open! Then he descended from his seat.
Seated, he addressed the assembly by way of the snow: "Above the head, it is white; beneath the feet, it is white. The Golden-Colored Honored One alone ascends the high platform.
With eyes open, he commits offenses; with eyes closed, he suffers calamity. How strange! How strange! The net of Heaven is vast and wide."
One whose standing ground is firm and secure—neither patriarchs nor Buddhas dare approach him. Why is it that he cannot lift his foot? Again it is said:
One who plays with spiritual powers—neither gods nor ghosts can fathom him. Why is it that he cannot set his foot down?
Even if one were to strike three thousand blows in the morning and eight hundred in the evening, regardless of how one moves through the world in all directions.
The spring mountains layer upon layer in wild green; the spring waters shimmer in empty azure. Vast and silent between heaven and earth, standing alone, what limit can one’s gaze reach?
He then descended from his seat and looked back at his attendant, saying, "Just now, was there anyone looking at the Abbot's quarters? The attendant replied, "There was.
The Master said, "The heart of a thief is always fearful."

Great, there is nothing outside it; small, there is nothing inside it. Half-closed and half-open, forming spheres and masses. The Old Barbarian has long since been cut off, and many monks have gone astray.
Let him remain for ten thousand ages, stretching on and on; filling the ditches and blocking the ravines, no one understands.
He struck the ground once with his staff and said: "Return to the hall. First, it is not fixed;
second, it is not possible. Above, below, and in the four cardinal and intermediate directions, the spring wind envelops all; peach and apricot blossoms vie with one another to bloom.
The willow branches and mulberry twigs are all broken through. How pitiful was Lingyun of old, who bluntly said he had met Bodhidharma while lost.
The Master picks up his staff and says, "Lingyun’s nostrils have been pierced!"
In a small-scale sermon (xiaochan), it was said: Subhūti sat in meditative seclusion within a mountain cave, and the devas rained down flowers in praise of him.
The Venerable One asked, "Who is this person raining flowers from the sky in praise? They replied, "I am Brahmā. The Venerable One asked, "How do you praise me?
The deva said, "I revere the Venerable One’s excellent exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. The Venerable One said, "I..."
"Regarding the Prajñāpāramitā, not a single word has ever been spoken. How can you praise it? The deity replied, "The Venerable One has said nothing, and I have heard nothing.
This absence of speaking and hearing is the true teaching of the Prajñāpāramitā. Furthermore, the earth shook and flowers rained down.
The Master remarked, "To seek stillness while avoiding clamor—there has never been a way to dwell in the world [that achieves this]. He remains in meditative seclusion within his mountain cave."
This was also smeared over by that same group of fellows. Furthermore, there was an old man who could not hold his composure and asked, "Who is this person showering flowers from the sky in praise?
He had already seen the point of failure. [The Master replied,] "I revere the Venerable One for his excellent exposition of the *Prajñāpāramitā*.
[The other] splashed foul water over his head, saying, "Regarding the *Prajñāpāramitā*, I have never uttered a single word."
"He runs through the grass. The Venerable One has nothing to say, and I have nothing to hear. What good or evil could one recognize?
If everyone were like this, where would there be a 'today'? The Master again called to the assembly, "Xuedou is fortunately a man of no affairs.
What do you all come here seeking? With his staff, he drove them all away at once.
Ascending the hall, [the Master said]: "Without the spring breeze, the flowers would not bloom; yet once they have bloomed, they are blown down by the wind.
If you can clearly understand this verse of praise and blame, it is not necessarily the case that a good cause will bring about an evil result. Return to the hall.
The long-beaked bird does not perch upon fragrant trees; it chatters alone. Mo-she-tuo does not enter the vast ocean;
trembling, he turns back. Thirty years later, he attained awakening. Raising his hand, he said, "Hūṃ, hūṃ! and then descended from the seat.
At times, he raised his staff and said, "The great opportunity is in the palm of one's hand. He then pushed aside [the staff] as if splitting the peak of Mount Taihua with the giant spirit Hongji.
Again, he placed the staff horizontally across the desk and said, "A bright mirror stands upon its stand; it cuts off the path of Yanruo as he pursues east and west.
Then, drawing a line with the staff, he said, "Even a comparison to a captured unicorn leaves no trace of the rabbit. Thereupon, he descended from the seat.
Nests know the wind; burrows know the rain. Even a sharp-witted monk cannot yet be granted such approval.
If you ask how it is, alas for Buddha! Enter!
Snow covers the reeds as the day nears its close; the family of the Xies is not at their fishing boat. Having let loose the white ox, there is no place to find it;
one can only hold the iron whip given to the mountain boy in vain.
Śākyamuni has already passed away, and Maitreya has not yet been born; it is precisely at this very moment that the Buddha-Dharma rests entirely upon this Green Peak.
Whether letting go or gathering in, everything depends on this point. To let go: moving freely in all directions, filling every ditch and valley.
To gather in: all the old monks of the world are right here on the tip of the staff, requiring not even a single stroke.
Where the wheel of the sword flies, the sun and moon lose their luster; when the precious staff strikes, heaven and earth lose their color.

From this, the many demons’ hearts burst with fear, and by this, the thousand sages open their eyes. Yet, alas, if one’s two ears are not fully attuned, one will fail to perceive even a thunderclap that shakes the world.

The solitary root is on the verge of perishing; it does not receive the nourishment of the spring rain. Consequently, ordinary beings and sages have diverged, and the paths of enlightenment and delusion have branched apart.
They rush through the seven realms of existence and are submerged in the four currents, bound by heavy karma with no day of respite. You who possess the virtue of meditation—
I hope you will examine and deliberate this well. It is like people climbing a mountain; each must exert their own effort.
To establish guest and host is to carve flesh and create sores; to cite the ancients and the present is to scatter sand and dirt. Directly beneath, there is nothing to do.
This is precisely an iron hammer with no holes; it possesses a separate mechanism that would surely consign one to the Avīci Hell.
A monk with clear eyes must examine this for himself:
it cannot be formed by characters, nor is it the eightfold word. The Udumbara flower is in full bloom, yet though one smells it, there is no fragrance—this is why I laugh.
"A guest on a fishing boat does not love the Southern Mountains; he loves the snout of a turtle.

[He pauses for a long time and] says, "Is there anyone who can emerge from the midst of the bustling marketplace? After a long silence, he says, "It is better to take up my staff and return to the mountains;
with one long cry, the mist and clouds deepen. He then descends from his seat.
The Words of Master Tiantai Yihuai. Recorded by his successor Xuedou Xian.
Ascending the hall, he raised the teaching, saying: "Since the beginning of kalpas, observing the world, it is like a dream. He then picked up his staff and said:
"Look! Look! This staff is dreaming; it dreams of swallowing up the mountains, rivers, the great earth, light, darkness, and form."
"Empty. Furthermore, you have dreamed of becoming Buddhas and Patriarchs; have any of you ever had such a dream?
If you have dreamed it, I, this mountain monk, am utterly defeated today. If you have not dreamed it, each of you return to your hall and settle yourselves there."
"Do not let him lose his pillow. With this, he struck the incense stand with his staff and descended from the seat.
Monks may speak horizontally or vertically at will, yet they do not know that there is an eye upon the crown of the head. At that time, a monk asked, "What is the eye upon the crown of the head?
The Master said, "The robe is worn through, revealing the bare bones; the roof is broken, and one sleeps gazing at the stars."
Clouds arise from the valley mouth; water droplets fall from the precipice. Monkeys howl atop solitary peaks; wild geese traverse the azure void. The eyes blink and move;
the nostrils reach toward the heavens. Like an arrow released from the bowstring, he immediately descended from his seat within the kingdom of Silla.
King Ajātaśatru killed his father, yet Yuanwu realized birthlessness; Śunakṣatra left the home life, yet fell into hell alive. Each of these great men—do not let yourselves be discouraged or cowed.
Your entire body is eyes, yet where you look, it is biased and withered. To cut off all streams is precisely to follow the waves and drift with the current.
O worthy ones, do you wish to understand? The winter melon is long and blunt; the bottle gourd is curved and bent. [He] then descended.
[The assembly] sat.
The Bodhisattva Anantagātra had exhausted the entire Dharma-realm, yet he could not see the mark of the Tathāgata’s crown.
"O virtuous ones, let us set aside for a moment the fact that the Bodhisattva Anantagātra could not see the mark of the Tathāgata’s crown; how about this: did Śākyamuni himself see it?"
"Is this the cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of the Bodhisattva Prabhūtaratna?

If there were a monk with clear eyes today, not only would his cranial protuberance be visible, but the minds of all Tathāgatas throughout the ten directions of the world would all appear before him. After a long silence, he said, "Do you see it?
Then, as if adding mud upon the earth, he descended from his seat.
"Under the Gate of the Great Sun, every day is the third autumn; before the Hall of the Bright Moon, every moment is the ninth summer.
When the ancients spoke thus, they were merely carving flesh to create sores. How many under the Gate of the Great Sun have actually trodden upon it?

Before the Hall of the Bright Moon, people merely receive echoes and respond to hollow sounds. I, this mountain monk, am not like that: fire does not wait for the sun to be hot, and wind does not wait for the moon to be cool.
The plantain opens at the sound of thunder; the sunflower turns with the sun. If you proceed in this manner, it is as if India were moved to this land.
*Chan.* One tongs and one hammer—pulling out nails and extracting wedges. The bellows of Great Tang, the smithing of Silla. O worthy ones, all of you!
Heaven and earth and the great earth are this mallet; where is its handle? If you further ask me for the tongs, you and I, monk, will both suffer defeat at once.
At Shaolin for nine years, he imparted but a single phrase, which has persisted until this very day. Everywhere it is misquoted;
if you wish not to be misled, I, this mountain monk, shall recite it once for all of you. He then said: "Oṃ bhu-bu-he-ga-ta-ri-svāhā," and immediately descended from his seat.
Prajñā has no knowing; there is nothing it does not know. Last night, the lantern swallowed the Buddha hall—let us not speak of that for now.
But tell me: when the Prince of Silla sits at court, what words does he speak? After a long silence, he said: "Long rains have not cleared."
Within each bubble is a Mañjuśrī. Look, look: as the bubbles vanish, they return to the water. "Venerable Elders," [the Master said], "you are all bubbles;
heaven and earth, the great world, are all bubbles. Where is Mañjuśrī? After a long silence, he said: "South of Tiantai, North of Wutai."

Clouds shroud the ancient hall; Kāśyapa knits his brows. Dewdrops fall upon the steps; Śūnyatā-janman sheds tears. The myriad phenomena raise their voices in song—who among them is a true connoisseur?

Water and milk are difficult to separate; only the king of geese knows how to distinguish them well. Suddenly, when the eye atop one’s head opens, do not say that this mountain monk has forced the noble to become base.
Master Xiu asked a monk, "Where have you come from? The monk replied, "From Cuiyan. The Master said, "What words or phrases did Cuiyan use to instruct his followers?
The monk said, "The Master usually says: 'When you go out the door, you meet Maitreya; when you enter the gate, you see Śākyamuni.
The Master said, "Even so, how could that be right? The monk then asked, "How about you, Master? The Master said, "Go out!"
"Who do you encounter when you reach the gate? What do you see upon entering the gate? At these words, the monk attained realization.
The Master said, "Though you have won one victory, you have lost a pair of feet. Now tell me, does this fall on the side of the guest or the side of the host?
If you can determine this, then in sorrow we shall share grief, and in joy we shall share delight. But I, this mountain monk, am not like that; when I go out the door—

Amidst the mountains of Wu and the waters of Chu, upon entering the gates, one encounters the Buddha hall and the corridors. Should there be a monk who comes forth and asks, "What is the Master’s meaning?
then one may grant that he possesses a single eye.

After a long silence, he said: "When one engages in such contemplation, the Buddhas of the ten directions all appear. Now that the contemplation is finished, the Buddhas of the ten directions immediately vanish.
To turn back and contemplate the Buddhas of antiquity is truly like being no man of stature. Why? This world is so vast and expansive;
for what reason, then, do you manifest jewel-king lands upon a single hair-tip and turn the Great Dharma Wheel while sitting within a mote of dust?"
The Dharma Wheel. To examine it closely, its intensity is enough to kill a man.
The teaching says: "The Buddha emits light from between his brows, manifesting all manner of rare and wondrous events.

When the light is emitted from the incense altar at Chongshou, with its three gates, Buddha hall, front corridors, and rear galleries, the sound resounds vast and grand—is this not a rare and wondrous event? Do you understand?
The Western Heaven is not the same as this land. *Chān*. [The Master] cites a verse by Fayan:
"A nine-jointed single staff is fit for observing great function; he says to his sons: 'Is this a staff, or is it not a staff? The Master said:
"Fayan was like one who bathes while clinging to a bridge pillar, or one who holds the mooring rope while letting the boat go. As for me, the mountain monk..."
"So it is. He then picked up his staff, struck once, and said: "A nine-jointed cane; its roots grow from above.
Before it entered my hands, it possessed no skill at all. Now that it is in my hands, it may go down or up.
If one cuts off the path of the thousand sages, Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra will be terrified, losing their seats and their elephant-riders. Even the saints of the ten stages..."
Having attained the three-by-three and two-by-two [realizations], he then descended from his seat.
"The Buddhas are not my path; who is the one who is the supreme path? My parents are not my kin; who is the one who is the supreme kin?"
Since neither the Buddhas are the Way nor one's parents are kin, what is the place where power is gained?

He then picked up his staff and said: "Sometimes it coils like a dragon, sometimes it crouches like a tiger; sometimes it extends, sometimes it spans. Its myriad transformations and applications depend entirely on the occasion.
If it transforms into the Vajra King’s precious sword, it will stabilize the eight directions and forever extinguish the smoke of war. If it transforms into..."
The lion crouching on the ground: if you look directly into its eyes, you will lose your body and forfeit your life.

If, however, it transforms into a probing pole or a blade of grass to test the waters—knowing that the ladle-handle of the eastern house is long and the ladle-handle of the western house is short—it leaves nothing unknown. In heaven, it becomes the five stars.
On the earth, it is like the Five Peaks; in Mañjuśrī’s hand, it becomes a wish-fulfilling jewel; in Samantabhadra’s hand, it is a sacred scripture;
and in this old monk’s hand, it is nothing more than a many-jointed *wan-sui* rattan cane.
Even so, joint upon joint grows further, and branch upon branch sprouts further. Thirty years from now, do not mistake its meaning.
Entering a weedy field, one does not discriminate; one simply picks up whatever grass comes to hand. The entire universe and the great earth are but a single blade of grass.
You all, tell me: what kind of grass is this? If you can recognize it, then curing illness requires no donkey-load of medicine.
If you do not recognize it, then sit for now within the weedy field. *Chan.*
The realms of boundless lands are not separated from one another by so much as a hair’s tip. Tell me:
what Dharma does the Immovable Tathāgata preach in the World of Wondrous Joy? Throughout the ten periods of time, past and present, beginning and end do not depart from the present moment.
As for the first assembly of the Buddha King of Majestic Sound—how many beings did he deliver? If there is anyone who is a master of the universal way, please try to speak on this.
After a long silence, he said: "Difficult is the journey, difficult is the journey. Before the ten-thousand-fathom peak, look with eyes fixed.

Within the shadows of a thousand peaks, in the ancient field of Buddhas, host and guest meet; a glance suffices to recognize the one who knows the sound. Yet even this is merely gouging flesh to create a sore.
To further claim that there is another profound gate beyond this is entirely to deceive the worthy and mislead the sages. After a long silence, he said: "All..."

If you people wish not to deceive one another, consider this: the *zhilu* staff of Tiantai and the ten-thousand-year-old rattan cane of Nanyue—these subtle words remain stuck in the mind's forefront, constantly serving as a field for discursive thought;
the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) dwells right before one’s eyes, yet it is instead turned into a realm of names and forms.
When the old monks of the world open their mouths and move their tongues, they merely use a "special stone" to block it up—this is True Suchness.
"Buddha-nature," "bodhi," and "nirvana"—strike them all through with a single stroke. Throughout the entire earth, there is not even a hair’s breadth of fault or affliction.
Yet, from within this state of no-affairs, there arises yet another affair. I dare ask you all:
why did Yunmen ride the Buddha hall backward? And why did Zhaozhou pluck the willow blossoms?
Empty clarity illuminates itself; there is no need to exert mental or physical effort. When those of superior capacity see this, ghosts and spirits become mere tea and rice.
When those of middling capacity see this, their wild minds are instantly stilled. As for another person—take care not to speak of it at all.
The body manifests the form of the full moon to represent the essence of all Buddhas; the preaching of the Dharma has no fixed shape, serving to distinguish that which is neither sound nor form.
He then raised his voice and said: "O Great Assembly, do you see the life-force of Bodhisattva Nāgārjuna now in the hands of this mountain monk?
If I let it pass, then let them speak of 'Perfect' and 'Sudden,' or argue about right and wrong. But if I do not let it pass, it will not take even a single [breath]."

Squeeze! Examine! How can the myriad dharmas differ from the mind? Why labor further to seek the meaning of the scriptures? When the ancients spoke thus, it was much like washing a clod of earth in the mud;
it was not yet talk that transcends the conventional. Nevertheless, to interpret the meaning according to the scriptures, throughout the three periods of time...
To deviate from a single word of the Buddha’s sutras is to speak like a demon. Yellow is the paper; black is the ink.
That which discriminates is the karmic consciousness. Shutting up the throat, lips, and mouth—where is the sutra? Investigate!
When the great assembly had gathered and settled, he said: "The 'Not Well' (*fǎnshěn*) struck above can digest ten thousand taels of gold;

the 'Take Care' (*zhēnzhòng*) struck below can likewise digest the offerings of the four continents. If you try to understand this as a discourse on the Buddha-dharma, even a drop of water will be difficult to digest;
if you discuss it as a matter of non-action, it is like putting grit in your eye. So, what is it? After a long silence...
He said, "Do you all understand? Take care!
He then cited the Teaching, saying, "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one sees the Tathāgata. Fayen said, "If one sees that all marks are non-marks, then one does not see the Buddha.
"All you people," [the Master] continued, "if you have attained it, you have indeed attained it; yet for now, you only know how to look ahead, without knowing..."
Looking back, I, this mountain monk, am not like that. If one sees that all marks are no-marks, where then is the eye?
These words contain two points of defeat. If anyone can examine them thoroughly, I grant that you possess the eye of discernment. *Chan*.
The Words of Chan Master Caoshan Ji: When he took his leave of Master Dongshan, Dongshan instructed him, saying:
"If you wish to discern the truth or falsehood of those who come before you in the future, there are three kinds of leakage (*shenlou*).
If you encounter someone directly in the moment of action, it is vital that you investigate and interrogate them thoroughly; do not be negligent or superficial, for fear [of error]."
This misleads future generations; such erroneous confirmations corrupt and destroy the ancestral lineage. I urge you most earnestly, I urge you most earnestly! Regarding the three types of leakage:

first, the leakage of view, wherein the faculty does not leave its station and one falls into a sea of poison. Second, the leakage of sentiment, wherein one is stalled by preferences and aversions, and clarity becomes lopsided and withered.
Third, the leakage of speech, wherein one investigates the subtle but loses the source; the faculty is muddled from beginning to end, and turbid wisdom wanders on. At this point...
You should understand these three types. Those who have not yet reached the source of the Dharma often stagnate within these three, falling entirely into extreme positions.
You must protect and uphold this; let this serve as your verification.
Three Summary Verses:

When striking and chanting proceed together, the golden needle and double lock are both prepared; the hidden path encompasses all, the precious seal is wondrous in the wind, and layer upon layer of brocade seams are opened.

Second, the two golden chains and the dark path alternate between light and darkness; when one's effort reaches its limit, progress becomes difficult to perceive, and when strength is exhausted, one forgets whether to advance or retreat. The golden chain forms a net that covers everything.
Third, do not fall into the realms of the ordinary or the sage.

Neither phenomena nor principle are involved; the returning illumination transcends the subtle and the minute. Against the wind, there is neither skill nor clumsiness; like a flash of lightning or a spark of fire, it is difficult to pursue.
The Master then paid his respects and took leave of Dongshan the following day. Dongshan asked, "Where are you going? The Master replied, "I am going to the place where there is no change.
Dongshan said, "In a place of no change, how can there be going? The Master replied, "Even going does not change."

[The Master said: "Different. [The student] asked: "Before one is fully formed in the womb, are there still words and phrases? The Master said: "There are. [The student] further asked: "I request you to speak them. The Master glanced sideways and said: "What do you use to hear? [The student] replied:

"As for a deaf person, would they still be able to hear? The Master said: *Note: This dialogue is from the *Wumen Guan* (Gateless Barrier), Case 30, concerning the story of Mazu Daoyi and his disciple Baizhang Huaihai.*

"If one hears it, one immediately possesses both ears and eyes. The student asked, "I do not yet understand: what kind of person is it that can hear it? The Master said, "One who has not yet entered a womb."
Jingqing (who succeeded Xuefeng and was also known as Daofu) asked, "When the principle of pure emptiness ultimately has no body, what then?
The Master said, "The principle is indeed thus; but as for phenomena, how is it? Jingqing said, "It is just like the principle and just like the phenomena.

The Master said, "You may succeed in deceiving Cao Shan alone, but what about the eyes of the various sages? Jingqing said, "If there were no eyes of the various sages, how would one know it is not so?"

"Is it so? The Master said, "The public authority does not permit even a needle; in private, one may pass carts and horses. He asked again, "As for the 'younger child,' does he still carry [the burden] or not?
The Master said, "He does not pity the younger child; though old, he has forgotten to return. Qing asked, "What is it like when he does not carry it?"
The Master said, "It does not abide. Qing asked, "What is it like when it does not abide? The Master said, "Neither correct nor incorrect.
Qing asked, "Does this matter still involve the passing on of the hand? The Master said, "It must be the matter; it must be the matter. Qing asked, "At such a moment, how is it?
The Master said, "Moment after moment, they continue in succession. Qing said, "In that case, one penetrates through the very lifeblood. The Master—
Yun said, "It penetrates the blood vessels; it is not obtained from others. Qing said, "If it is not obtained from others, what is the matter?
The Master said, "Right here, one does not even see another person. Qing then bowed.
Ascending the hall, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Everywhere, people merely apply restrictive standards; why do they not simply tell them [the truth] so that they may be free from doubt?
Yunmen stepped forward and asked, "In the midst of the profound mystery (*mimi*), why is it that one does not know what exists?

The Master said, "Precisely because it is profound and mysterious, one does not know what exists. Yunmen asked, "How should one approach such a person? The Master said, "Do not seek it in the profound mystery."
Dongmen asked, "How is it when one does not approach in a secret place? The Master said, "Only then do you understand approaching.
Dongmen said, "Yes, yes. Dongmen asked again, "What is the practice of a śramaṇa? The Master said, "Those who eat the crops of the monastery's permanent endowment.
Dongmen said, "If one goes about in this very way, what then? The Master said, "Are you able to maintain it?"
Mendun said, "I am able to keep it. The Master asked, "How do you keep it? Mendun said, "Wearing clothes and eating food—what difficulty is there in that?
The Master asked, "Why do you not say, 'I wear fur and carry horns'? Mendun then bowed in prostration.
A monk asked, "The wasteland stretches far and wide; where can one establish a livelihood? The Master said, "Do not prick your feet in the wilderness.
The monk pressed further, "What about a place that is not a wasteland? The Master said, "It is not desolate. The monk pressed further, "If smoke should rise all at once, who would dwell there?
The Master said, "Go to where it is bustling. The monk pressed further, "I do not yet know: what is one's original livelihood?"
The Master said: "The thorny weeds are deep. A monk asked: "I, the monk Qing, am poor and destitute; I beg the Master for relief. The Master called out, "Monk Qing!
The monk responded, "Yes? The Master said: "Qingyuan’s Bai family wine—after three cups, one still says it has not even touched the lips."
A monk asked, "Is it not the case that a śramaṇa is one who possesses great compassion? The Master said, "Yes. The monk pressed further, "What if you suddenly encounter the six thieves?
The Master said, "One must still possess great compassion. The monk asked, "What is it to possess great compassion?
The Master said, "To strike them all down with a single stroke of the sword. The monk asked, "After they are all struck down, what then? The Master said, "Only then is there harmony."
[The monk] asked the same question: "When the bright moon is suspended in the sky, what is it like? The Master said, "It is still a man standing at the foot of the stairs.
The monk stepped forward and said, "I ask the Master to lead me up the stairs. The Master said, "Come see me after the moon has fallen. [Another monk] asked, "I do not yet know who this person is."
[The Master said: "Then you will not be swallowed by impermanence. The Master said, "It is burning within impermanence;

can it still swallow [you]? A question was asked: "What is the solitary and steep place of Cao Yuan? The Master said, "The ladder does not reach there. He further asked, "Is there anyone who reaches it?
The Master said, "One obtains it without even treading upon the ladder. He further asked, "I do not know what it is like after reaching it."
The Master said, "I do not see anything solitary or lofty. A questioner asked, "What is it like for one who is within [this state]?

The Master said, "Though the kingdom is offered, there is no one who knows him. The questioner pressed, "Is there anyone at all who can recognize him? The Master said, "There is. The questioner asked, "Who is this person? The Master said, "Earth, wood, tiles, and rubble.
A questioner asked, "Furthermore, since there is no obstruction, why is it that one cannot cross over to that side? The Master said...
[The Master] said, "If there were no obstruction, there would be no 'over there' either. The monk asked, "In that case, the entire great trichiliocosm is his house?
The Master said, "The great trichiliocosm is indeed his house; but who is the person within the great trichiliocosm?
The monk was speechless. The Master spoke on his behalf, saying: "One who does not sit within the great trichiliocosm. The Master asked the assembly, "The mountain..."
The Great Master of He (Heshang Moheyan) once came and asked, "What kind of person can answer this? The assembly remained silent.
The Master spoke on their behalf, saying, "One who does not possess the six sense faculties. The Master then asked Senior Monk Qiang, "The Buddha’s true Dharma-body is like empty space;
it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water. How do you explain the principle of this 'responding'? Qiang replied, "It is like a donkey."
[The Master] looked into a well. The Master said, "To speak is to speak too much; you have spoken but eighty percent. The monk pressed him, saying, "I do not yet understand how it is with the Master.
The Master said, "It is like looking into a well and seeing a donkey. A monk asked, "The scriptures say that the great ocean does not harbor a dead corpse."
"What is the great ocean? The Master said, "That which encompasses all existence. The student asked, "Since it encompasses all existence, why does it not harbor corpses?

The Master said, "That which has ceased its breath does not adhere to it. The student asked, "Since it encompasses all existence, why does that which has ceased its breath not adhere to it? The Master said, "All existence is not its achievement; [it is] cessation..."
Qiaoxi was possessed of virtue. A student asked, "Is there anything further above this? The Master said, "If you say 'it exists' or 'it does not exist,' that will suffice.
But what can you do about the Dragon King brandishing his sword? A student asked, "How is it before the sun has risen?
The Master said, "Caoshan also comes in this manner. The student asked, "How is it after it has risen? The Master said, "It is still half a step behind Caoshan."
Yuecheng asked Master De, "When a Bodhisattva is in meditative concentration and hears that an elephant-king crosses a river, from which sutra does this come?

De replied, "The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. The Master said, "Did he hear it before entering concentration, or did he hear it after emerging from concentration? De replied, "Venerable Sir, you are being flowery."
The Master said, "As for 'the Way,' it is far too much of the Way; you have only grasped half of it. Deyun asked, "How about the Master?
The Master said, "Catch it at the bottom of the rapids. A monk asked, "How should a student maintain [this state] throughout the twelve periods of the day?

The Master said, "It is like being in a region where the water is poisoned by *gǔ* (vermin/toxic substances); you must not let even a single drop touch you. [Another] asked, "When one ox drinks water, five horses..."
[The monk] did not sigh. [The monk asked: "What is the situation at that time? The Master said, "Cao Shan understands how to guard his mouth.
He also said, "Cao Shan’s filial piety is complete. A monk asked Xiangyan, "What is the Way? Xiangyan said, "A dragon’s cry within a withered tree.
The monk asked, "What is one who is on the Way? Xiangyan said, "Eyes within a skull. Later, the monk raised this question for Shishuang, asking, "What is the withered tree?"
Fengxue said, "A dragon’s roar within a skull. Yangshan said, "There is still something left to be recognized.
The monk then raised this question for the Master: "What is a dragon’s roar within a withered tree? The Master said:
"The bloodline is unbroken. The student asked, "What is the eye within the skull? The Master said, "It never dries up.
The student asked, "I wonder if there is anyone who can hear it? The Master said, "Throughout the entire world, there is not a single person who does not hear it.
The student asked, "As for the dragon’s roar within the withered tree—what verses are these? The Master said, "I do not know what verses they are."
Those who heard this were all struck dumb. The Master then offered a verse: "The dragon’s cry from a withered tree—truly seeing the Way;
The skull has no consciousness, yet its eyes are first enlightened. When joyful consciousness is exhausted, all news and messages cease; How can a person distinguish the clear within the turbid?

A monk asked, "When snow covers the thousand mountains, why is the solitary peak not white? The Master said, "You must know there is that which is extraordinary within the extraordinary. The monk pressed further: "..."
"What is 'the extraordinary within the extraordinary'? The Master said, "Not falling into the forms of the various mountains. Question: "What is it like when a poor family suffers a robbery?
The Master said, "He cannot empty the bottom out. The questioner asked, "Why can he not empty the bottom out? The Master said, "The thief is a member of the family.
The questioner asked, "If he is a member of the family, why does he instead become a family thief? The Master said: *Note: The text provided ends abruptly with the Master's response.*
"Since it cannot be so internally, it cannot be done externally. The student asked, "What is it like when one suddenly captures the culprit?

The Master said, "Internally and externally, all news is cut off. The student asked, "When the culprit is captured, where does the merit reside? The Master said, "I have never even heard of a reward being given."
The monk said, "In that case, it is laborious but without merit. The Master said, "Merit is not lacking; it is accomplished, yet not dwelt upon.
The monk asked further, "Since it is accomplished, why is it not dwelt upon? The Master said, "Have you not heard it said: 'Peace itself was brought about by the generals'?"
The General was not permitted to see Tàipíng.
As the Monk in Paper Robes was paying his respects, the Master said, "Are you not the Monk in Paper Robes? The monk replied, "I dare not say so.
The Master asked, "What is the reality beneath the paper robe? The monk replied, "Once this single garment is hung upon the body, the myriad dharmas are all..."
"Everything is as it is. The Master said, "What is the function beneath the paper robe? Daoyi stepped forward, joined his palms, and stood there motionless.
The Master said, "You only know how to go like that; you do not know how to come back like this.
Daoyi suddenly opened his eyes and asked, "When the singular, numinous true nature does not rely upon the womb, what then? The Master said, "That is not yet marvelous. Daoyi asked, "What is it?"
"Excellent," the Master said. "I shall not borrow from you. Take care with your robe. He then returned to his quarters, sat beneath his seat, and passed away.

The Master then composed a verse: "The nature of awakening is perfectly luminous, the formless body; Do not mistakenly draw near or distance yourself through intellectual views. If thoughts differ, one is obscured from the profound essence."
The mind falters and does not accord with the Way; its emotional attachments cause the myriad dharmas to sink into the realm before it. With manifold discriminations, one loses one's original truth.
If you can fully understand these words, you will clearly see that you are the person of old, free from all affairs.
The Monk Ju of Mingxi in Lizhou addressed the assembly, saying: "I have a great illness that cannot be cured by the physicians of this world.
I do not know what kind of illness it is. The Master said: "It is an illness that cannot be gathered together or pinned down. The monk asked: "Do all sentient beings have it as well?
The Master said: "Everyone has it. The monk asked: "Does the Master have it too? The Master said: "I am currently searching for its point of origin."
"No. The student asked, "Why then are all sentient beings not ill? The Master said, "If all sentient beings were ill, they would no longer be sentient beings.
The student asked, "Do the Buddhas also have this illness? The Master said, "They do. The student asked, "Since they have it, why are they not ill?
The Master said, "Because they are fully awake. A question was asked: "One brings his uncut jade to a master; I pray the master [will polish it]."
[The Master] said, "Carved. The student asked, "Does not carve? The Master said, "One must know that Cao Shan is a master craftsman.

A student asked, "What thing in the world is most precious? The Master said, "A dead cat's head. The student pressed further, "Why? The Master said, "One must know that Cao Shan is a master craftsman."
"The head of a dead cat. Why is it so precious? The Master said, "Because no one will pay its price.
A monk asked, "The ancients said, 'I am always at this point. What is the meaning of this? The Master said, "If you want Cao Shan’s head, cut it off and take it with you.
Bitou asked Dongshan, "Where have you come from? Dongshan said, "From being close [to the Master]. Bitou said, "If that is so..."
"Approaching and using these two pieces of skin to move about—what is the use? Shanshan went to rest. Later, when the Master heard of this, he said, "My son has truly attained it."
Four Verses on the Prohibitions:
Do not travel the path of the mind; Do not don the garment of originality. There is no need for it to be exactly so; Above all, avoid the time before birth.
Two verses shown to students.
A student must first recognize their own school; do not confuse true nature with inert emptiness. When the essence of wondrous function is fully realized, one knows how to avoid injury or offense.
The power lies in meeting conditions without relying on effort. Let your speech be such that even fire cannot burn it; let your hidden practice be identical to that of the ancients.
To have affairs while having no body transcends the crossroads; to have no body and no affairs falls back into the cycle of beginning and end.
Using names to summon things reveals that they are not the names themselves; who would have thought that, deluded by form, one would instead recognize the sound?

Grasping for a head in a mirror is but a futile distraction; reaching for the moon in water is a waste of a thousand lifetimes. Pointing toward the home-path while returning to the village, once you reach the house, you have lost the way.
Do not blame the fisherman for repeatedly raising his oars; he beats the wind and stirs the waves, awaiting the dragon’s passage.
The Words of Master Touzi Qing: Successor to Dayang, entering the monastery.

Having finished offering incense to pray for the Emperor, he next held up the incense and said: "Does the assembly know the origin of this single portion of incense? It is neither heaven nor earth..."
That which is produced is not formed by yin and yang. Before the time of Vīradhvaja, it did not fall into any ranks;
after Dīpaṃkara, it was transmitted through the seven Buddhas until it reached Caoxi, where it branched out into the great halls.

Early in the Zhiping era, this mountain monk personally received the transmission from Master Fushan Yuanjian, who entrusted him with the verses on the lineage and clearly explained the compassionate intent of the Patriarch, saying: "I shall represent [the teaching]."

I shall continue the tradition of Dayang. Although this mountain monk does not personally know Master Dayang, I recognize him through the lineage of Fushan Zongfeng and thus accept him as my successor.
In this way, I dare not violate the grace of Master Fushan’s entrustment of the Dharma.
I respectfully serve as the attendant for the Great Master Dayang Ming’an of Yingzhou. Why? Because [he is] one's parents and all Buddhas.
Not by kinship, but by the Dharma, do we become kin.

Ascending the seat, the Master said: "If one were to discuss this matter, how could it be found in the lofty elevation of the Dharma-seat, in the formal arrangement of the wise and worthy, or in the exchange of questions and answers between host and guest as a means of transcending the world?
Furthermore, the thousand worthies have closed their mouths and the ten thousand sages have ceased their speech; from antiquity to the present, the Buddhas and Patriarchs have [remained thus]."
The Snow Gate: The Three Baskets and Five Vehicles cannot be pointed out or explained away. Nevertheless, one must not simply go on until the bow is broken and the arrows exhausted.
Thus it is said: "A thousand peaks lock in their colors; ten thousand trees [stand silent]. The moon shines upon the ancient cliff."
The wind arises in the secluded caverns; the clouds part on all four sides. The dragon roars from the withered tree; the phoenix soars through the azure heavens.

The stone ox bellows, cleaving the vast sky; the wooden horse neighs, opening the golden gates. Spiritual sprouts compete to flourish; auspicious grasses vie for the spring. The sun and moon shine together in brilliance.
A thousand rivers pour forth together; it truly reaches such a state. Yet this is still but a matter on the periphery of the world-transcending—fallen into the present moment.
O worthy ones, how can you avoid falling into the present moment? After a long silence, he said: "The stone path of ten-thousand-year antiquity is locked by a thousand clouds;
a single range of green mountains is sealed at midnight."

Ascending the hall, [the Master] said: "If we discuss this matter, it is like a fish fleeing into the deep abyss—it inevitably attracts the fisherman. A jade buried in the Jing Valley—how could it resist those seeking it?
Thus, the feet were cut off in the city of Chu, and the misty waves of the Wei River arose; this was because he failed to maintain his ordinary state, leading to such consequences as these.
On this day, white clouds fill the valley, green waters float with mist, auspicious birds startle at dawn, and the mountain's radiance dazzles the eyes."

To act without partiality in every matter—what could be improper? Nevertheless, even so, you must further be able to shield the sun with handless hands and catch fish without touching the pole. [Descend from your seat.]

Master Xie Huaru said: "The pavilion atop the green peaks is empty; the white clouds naturally differ from one another. The numinous sprout stands alone in its excellence; how could profuse weeds grow there?
Where the golden cock crows, the moon has fallen at the third watch; when the jade hare sleeps, the sun’s wheel is at midday. This is the Upper Garden of the Jasper Forest."
Withered trees welcome the spring; moss grows upon the jeweled halls. The songs of joy resound for ten thousand miles. Although this is so, tell me:
how would you express the phrase that accords with the time and the season? After a long silence, he said: "Last night, amidst the deep snow; at dawn, several branches have blossomed. *Chan.*
Silence sinks into the realm of darkness; speech falls into a deep pit. To attempt to grasp it is like the vast distance between heaven and earth;
to cast it aside is to be lost for a thousand births and ten thousand kalpas. The vast waves roll on, white surges overflowing the heavens. Who holds the bright pearl that subdues the ocean?
After a long silence, he struck his staff once and said: "Reduced to a hundred fragments!"
When Master Yún arrived, [Zhaozhou] said: "In the Hall of No Shadow, who is the one who knows this? Beside the ancient path, there are illusory men and wooden horses.
A thousand peaks lock in their emerald hues; ten thousand trees hold the mist. Where white clouds arise, the gates of the pavilions open;
when blue mists roll away, the summit of the Wondrous Peak is revealed. Now tell me: how would you express the single phrase of meeting at the absolute peak? After a long silence—
It is said: "Without declining the distance of the mountain path, you have come specifically through the pine gate.
Do not sit amidst the white clouds; do not rest within the green peaks. You must directly realize the fragrance of flowers upon withered wood and the blazing of flames upon the icy river.
When the whirlwind does not linger, it strikes the eye with sorrow. In the space of a single deliberation, all further progress is but toil. Reaching this point, you must simply hang [yourself]..."
Letting go at the precipice, one must personally accept it; only after death can one revive again—this cannot be deceived.
Zen Master, what is this matter of acceptance? After a long silence, he said: "The stream is deep and the falling flowers drift far; the mountain is high and the tree shadows stretch long."
In a solitary village or a humble shop, do not hang up your flask or bowl. At the profound gateway of the Patriarchs and Buddhas, pass straight through with your body laid across it.
Already, Su Qin has encountered the barrier; seeking a path, he finds it difficult to turn back. When Xiang Yu faced the river, how could he escape his fated end?

O Zen Master, when you arrive here, to advance is to fall into the realm of celestial Māras; to retreat is to sink into the destiny of ghosts. If you neither advance nor retreat, you are right in the midst of death.
"Within the water. O worthy ones, how can one attain stability? After a long silence, he said: "Let the three-foot snow fall as it may;
it cannot suppress the single inch of the numinous pine."
If the vehicle of the school is raised, both ordinary and sage leave no trace. When the gates of the multi-storied pavilion open, one meets another through a separate door.
Even if one rolls up the curtain and awakens to the Way, how can one avoid being a bystander? Encountering peach blossoms in spring only further aggravates the diseased eye.
Therefore, the ancients said: "The path that points upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages. Friends, since it is not transmitted, why then is there the Iron Ox of Shanfu?
Having traveled through the land of Silla, he let out a shout and said: "The adept must know that there is a shock in the darkness.

He then raised various illusory transformations, saying, "All these arise from the Tathāgata’s wondrous mind of perfect enlightenment. Picking up his staff, he said: "It is just like this monk’s staff;
it certainly does not arise from those [transformations]. Why? If it were to arise from them, how could it be so?"
"It is in the hands of this mountain monk. Zen masters, if you know the place of birth, the Patriarch will beg for his life at the heels of everyone here.
If you do not know it either, I cannot help but provide an annotation for you all. Having said this, he threw down his staff and returned to the abbot’s quarters.
The Master raised an instance: A monk asked Luopu, "When a student wishes to return home, what then? Luopu said, "The house is ruined and the people are gone;
where would you, my son, go back to? The monk said, "In that case, I shall not return. Luopu said, "The remaining snow before the courtyard is melted by the sun;
who will sweep the red dust inside the room? The Master commented: "Tell me, when Luopu answered him in this way, what was his meaning?"
"Where? refers to the path by which this monk returns home. If you can understand it here, you may be said to have cast off your hands and returned home.
If you do not understand it, you must be even more careful with every step you take. Descend from the seat.
Snow covers the ten thousand mountains; white clouds drift in vast tranquility. Pines endure the cold for a thousand ages; mountain streams flow with ice.
The Patriarch did not sit at Shaolin in spring; those who come need not seek the seamless stupa.

On the first day of the year, it is said: The Primordial Beginning inaugurates the reign; all things are renewed. A thousand mountains display their lush greenery upon misty peaks; emerald waters pierce through clouds amidst azure mists.
Stone oxen set forth their paces; auspicious grasses shine with brilliance. Wooden horses hang their ribbons; numinous sprouts burst into bloom.
At the ancient Buddha’s stūpas and temples, Sudhana encounters Mañjuśrī; to the west of Kukkuṭapāda Mountain, Kāśyapa meets Maitreya once again.
"Le! Hanshan adds to his longevity; Shide increases his years. Together we celebrate the Great Peace; together we support the transformation of Yao. O virtuous ones, tell me:
how many years old is the Great Image of Jiazhou today? After a long silence, he said: "The thousand-year-old man’s countenance is like jade;
the ten-thousand-year-old boy’s hair is like silk."
Mist and clouds embrace the emerald peaks; phoenixes and peacocks lose their tracks. Cold rain strikes the mountains as woodsmen return late at eve.
At the beginning of the kalpa, who was it that shook the bell? When there is nothing left to be picked up on the road, the gentleman praises it as beautiful.
Last night the moon was full over Shaolin; on the west of Xiangling Mountain, he carried away a single sandal. O virtuous ones, the Patriarch has yet another sandal—have you all ever seen it?
"Have you captured it? If you have captured it, it is not worth half a penny. If you have not captured it, what can you rely upon as a standard?
[The Master] struck the meditation seat with his whisk and descended from the seat.
Xie the Head Seat said: "The ancients said: 'Accumulate stones and they form a mountain; accumulate water and it forms a stream; accumulate earth and it forms a wall;
accumulate learning and one becomes a sage; accumulate practice and one achieves virtue. Now tell me, what does a patch-robed monk accumulate? After a long silence, he said:
'Though Shaolin speaks not, there is a distinct springtime here.'"
In the past, when the World-Honored One was at the assembly on Vulture Peak, he entered immeasurable samādhi, his body and mind unmoving.
