At the hour of the third watch last night, stone men fought to prostrate themselves. As for this talk, do not say that you cannot understand it;
I, too, cannot understand it.
The head of offerings and construction requested, saying: "Today, Baiyun shall take the world of the Great Song as a single chessboard.
First, he shall fix the five directions with Mount Tai of the East, Mount Heng of the South, Mount Hua of the West, Mount Heng of the North, and Mount Song of the Center.
Next, he shall use Mount Wutai, Mount Emei, Mount Jietuo, and Mount Luofu as its borders."
Assistance! On the left side, there is a slanting formation of flying geese; on the right side, there are the tiger’s mouth and the double gate.
[Baizhang] then raised his hand and said: "Tell me, where does this move land? If you know where it lands, you may be considered a worthy opponent.
If you do not yet know, let me try to convey a message for you: On the nineteen paths of level ground, the struggle for merit shows no sign of ceasing. Do not let..."
"One single mistake ruins the child; it is ultimately difficult to retrieve.
Question: "I have heard your words, Master: 'A single plot of land before the mountain—just as before King Bhīṣmagarjitasvara, who was the master?
Master, you say: 'Ask the person who wrote the deed. Monk: 'Why did the Master trouble someone else to come for this?'"
The Master replied, "It is precisely because you teach others how to ask. The monk said, "I have already departed on equal terms with the Master.
The Master said, "That is still very far off. He then said: "Five eyes cannot behold his countenance; two ears cannot hear his sound. Those who have merit are punished;
those without merit are rewarded. He picks up Mount Sumeru and weighs it at only two taels. Suddenly, someone says: 'One...'"
Only then did he realize it. Why? When weighing people and affairs with a great scale, he said himself: "In official matters, not even a needle is permitted;

in private dealings, one may pass carts and horses. He thanked the neighbor, saying: "Yesterday, neighbor, you brought a handful of sand to the front of the abbot’s quarters. As soon as you saw this old monk..."
It was thrown directly at his face; fortunately, the old monk saw it first and shielded him with the sleeve of his robe, so that no harm came to him.
Today, I bring this up for the assembly and dare not conceal it. Why? To commend his great courage—how he could deploy such a move.
Suddenly someone asked Baiyun, "How can one simply rest like this? Baiyun replied, "It is not said that old age relies on physical strength for its capability.
Although it is thus, the roles of guest and host remain distinct and clear.
If you wish to roam freely throughout the world, go see the Old Monk when he beats the drum and ascends the hall.

At seventy-three or eighty-four, he will suddenly strike you over the mouth with his staff. Even so, only by removing the mounting block at the gate and cutting through the five-colored ropes can you finally attain peace and happiness.
Today is the Dragon Boat Festival. Baiyun has a divine talisman that possesses a measure of efficacy.
Not daring to conceal it, I present it to you all. First, may the Emperor and the Empress Dowager enjoy ten thousand years of imperial longevity.

Second, the high ministers and officials of the court, the civil and military officers of the hundred ranks, and the subordinate functionaries of the prefectures and counties shall always dwell in their positions of emolument.
Third, the myriad people shall delight in their vocations, with timely rain and favorable winds. Then there was a messenger who came to report to Baiyun:
"I have traveled everywhere to all places, yet because my spiritual powers were small, I could not manage one particular matter. Baiyun then asked him, "What was that matter?"
He then said: "Zen students, your nostrils point toward the heavens! Baiyun said to him: 'Do not speak of you; even I cannot do anything about it.
Although this is so, a vast marsh conceals mountains, and principle can subdue a leopard.
But in the end, what is it? One draws out three; two adds four. The horns of the yellow ox point toward heaven; eight legs hang down past the nose. Hurry! Descend from the seat!"

"One who has throughout their life brought everything to a hundredfold completion and a thousandfold certainty is precisely the one who deserves to be struck with a staff. But tell me, where does the fault lie?

From the very beginning, having brought everything to a hundredfold completion and a thousandfold certainty—Śākyamuni and Maitreya are still his servants. But tell me, who is he? Then he descended from the seat.

In a small-scale sermon (*xiaocan*), a monk asked, "What is the Buddha? The Master said, "Fatness enters through the mouth. He then cited: Deshan said, "Tonight I will not answer questions. Anyone who asks a question shall receive thirty blows of the staff. Many among the assembly have raised this case, and few have truly understood it. Now, consider this: * *Fei cong kou ru* (Fatness enters through the mouth) is a colloquial expression meaning that what one consumes directly affects one's physical state. * Deshan’s statement is a classic example of a "deadly barrier" (*shengmen*) used to cut off conceptualization and force a breakthrough into direct realization. It is not merely a threat, but a pedagogical device intended to shatter the student's reliance on intellectual inquiry. The Master’s response, "Fatness enters through the mouth," functions as a pivot. It implies that the very act of seeking the Buddha through words or concepts is itself the source of spiritual "fatness"—a dulling of one's innate clarity.

By pointing back to the source of the seeker's own activity, the Master cuts off the dualistic pursuit of an external object. This is the "thirty blows" in action: a sudden, total negation of the seeker's habitual mode of being. To understand this is to realize that the Buddha is not found outside of oneself; rather, the obstacle to seeing him is the very effort to find him. Thus, the "fatness" is the accumulation of conceptual effort, and its entry through the "mouth" represents the gateway of speech and thought. To let go of this is to be "lean" and clear. This is the true meaning of Deshan’s staff.
"Where do you see Deshan? Let there be a man who disregards his very life and step forward to speak!
If there is none, I, this mountain monk, shall go to meet Deshan on behalf of the assembly. When Deshan says, "Tonight I will not answer questions;
those who ask questions shall receive thirty blows," simply say to him: "I do not ask for a word, nor do I seek a blow."
"Eat! You say, 'Do you understand old man Deshan? To reach this point, one must truly be a man of substance.
Furthermore, for over ten years I have sought the Way upon the sea, meeting several venerable masters under whom I considered myself fully realized;
yet when I arrived at the assembly of Yuanjian of Fushan, I was utterly unable to open my mouth. Later, arriving at the gate of Baiyun, I bit through [the shell]..."
A single iron-sour paste contains all a hundred flavors. But tell me, how would you express the phrase for that paste?
He then said: The cockscomb flowers bloom, lovely in the early autumn; Who can dye their purple silk tips?
Sometimes the wind stirs and they lean against one another, As if vying on the steps, never ceasing.
Question and Answer. Question: “What is the Buddha? Answer: “A single-plank bridge. Question: “How does one proceed toward it? Answer: “Tightly laced straw sandals. Question:
“What is the house style of the Master? Answer: “Iron banners and iron drums. Or, when a guest arrives, how does he receive them?
“Wait. [The Master] said, “Dragon liver and phoenix marrow; wait for another time. [The student] asked, “What is the point of Baiyun’s intimate instruction for people?
He said, “I love twisting people’s nostrils around. “What is Baiyun’s ‘one drop of water’? He said, “Pounding rice in the mortar;
grinding flour in the mill. “If one drinks it, what then? He said, “It leaves you with nowhere to put your face. “What is the Way? He said, “Wait.”

[The Master] was treating the matter of Pingjun. [A monk asked: “What is it to be a person on the Way? [The Master] said: “To take sincerity as one’s master. [A monk asked: “How far apart are the Way and the person on the Way?
[The Master] said: “Their names are transmitted throughout the world. [A monk asked: “What is the Buddha? [The Master] said: “The mouth is the gate of calamity. [A monk asked:
“The teachings of a lifetime are all ‘cutting feet’ (rhymes). I do not know what character they cut. [The Master] said: “*Bharaṇī* (鉢囉娘).”
The ancient verse says:
"Not associating with the myriad dharmas; the Buddha of the Sun’s Face and the Buddha of the Moon’s Face swallow the waters of the West River in a single gulp.
The peony buds newly emerge in Luoyang; tossing up dust and raising clouds of earth, there is no place to dwell."
Investigating, he raises his head and strikes upon his own ground:
A girl with parted hair paints her蛾眉 (eyebrows); Before the phoenix-mirror stand, her eyes are like those of one in a daze. She says of herself that her jade-like countenance has no peer;
Yet she goes to the rack to put on her silken robes.
The dog has Buddha-nature;
Zhaozhou reveals a sharp-edged sword. Its cold frost and blazing flames flare on high. Should you further dare to ask "How is it?"—your body shall be split in two.
(A lament for Master Sengyuan, the Fourth Patriarch.)
This one is ill, that one has entered parinirvāṇa; what gain or loss is there for our school? Birth and death are like flowers in the sky;

going and coming are like the tracks of birds. Rising suddenly in the east, they vanish in the west; their shadows hang upon the walls of the cold hall. The gods of the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven strike the celestial bell;
let all together recite the Prajñāpāramitā.
Lamenting Master Yuanjian of Fushan:
Before the cliffs of Fudu lies the green, slender cypress; rising above the monastic groves, it displays a noble character.
Last night its cold shadow fell upon the western lane—who could have played the eighteen variations of the *hugu* flute?
Lamenting Touzi Qing, who dwelt in silent stillness atop Flower Garland Peak; his clouds scattered the waters of Caoxi, hoisted the sail of Fudu, and sailed straight into the vast ocean.
The carriage has already reached the end of its journey. Last night, a wild wind arose. A girl with horned hair carries a jade flower;
an eighty-year-old old man wears embroidered shoes.
In praise of the true master Baiyun: In praise of Master Fourth Patriarch Yan.
The single moon is in the sky; its reflection is contained within all waters. The true essence of the Master is neither moon nor water.
Blue, yellow, azure, and green—these chaotic smears, when viewed, evoke a mixture of half-anger and half-thieving joy.
Osmanthus flowers wrap around old yellow plums; they do not bloom upon the ground of yin and yang. How could bees and butterflies know the distance of their fragrance?
Their traces are difficult to find as they go and return.
Self-commendation (3):

To grasp characteristics by means of characteristics results entirely in illusion and delusion; to seek the True by means of the True only serves to distance one further from it. When seeing itself becomes the public case, [the truth is revealed].
There is no matter that is not discerned. Throughout the three hundred and sixty thousand days of a hundred-year life, turning over and over, it has always been this very person.
This is my true self; I praise my own self. Only one knows oneself. Face to face, staring at one another, when will there ever be an end?
Blind in his eyes and deaf in his ears, limping as he walks, he forces a smile before others and folds his hands across his chest.
He takes leave of the assembly and ascends the hall. [The Master] cites the Venerable Zhaozhou: "I have a final phrase; how do you understand it? Come forward and speak!
If you can understand it, you will be free and at ease without hindrance. If this is not yet the case, it would be well [to continue practicing]."
"How shall one speak of this matter? After a long silence, he said, "It has already been spoken; it is simply that you all do not know. Do you wish to understand?
"The wealthy lament that a thousand mouths are too few; the poor resent that a single body is too many. Adieu.

On the twenty-fifth day of the sixth month in the third year of the Chongning era, the year being Jia-shen, he took leave of the assembly. That evening, he shaved his head and bathed. On the twenty-sixth...

On the day before the morning gruel, he passed away with auspicious signs. He remained at the mountain gate for seven days. After his cremation, the fourfold assembly collected his relics, which were beyond counting.
A stupa was erected to the south of Mount Dongshan.
The Words of National Teacher Xing of Nantang A small assembly lecture by his successor, Wuzu:
"Tomorrow, this mountain monk shall lead the assembly down the mountain to do battle for the sake of the nation.

I request that the Head Seat act as the vanguard, the Rector serve as the rear guard, and the novice monks be arrayed on the left and right to assist this old monk as the Commander-in-Chief. I ask you all to attend.
May all people don the armor of patience and grasp the sword of wisdom to destroy stinginess and greed.

May they open the inexhaustible treasuries within every household and bring forth the jewels from within their topknots. May they take and discard as they please, entirely free from regret or parsimony.

Thereafter, may the myriad subjects delight in their vocations and the four seas be tranquil and clear, so that together we may sing of the era of Yao and Shun and chant high the melodies of Great Peace.

"You may now withdraw your ranks and lower your banners; each of you should attend to rest. We shall beat the drums of victory, cook the white oxen in the open air, and provide rewards for the three armies to celebrate this joy.
The old monk shall let out a lion’s roar, and the assembly shall perform the gait of the elephant king."
"I venture to ask the great assembly: tell me, what can the Buddha Dīpaṃkara possibly do? After a long silence, he said:
'At the place where the curtain is rolled up and the seat is spread, the fourfold assembly all look up in reliance.'"
Universal labor for road repairs. Ascending the hall: Old Teacher Mugan is skilled at requesting the moving of stones;
he provides people with the true path and enables them to recognize the path. All the bodhisattvas of this monastery nod their heads in agreement, yet there is only one who does not nod.
Tell me, which one is it that does not nod? After a long silence, he said: "Wait until the day is done, and I will give it to you."
Verse spoken by Mazu:
"The mind itself is Buddha. In response to Venerable Shun of Wangchuan Mountain.
"The very mind is Buddha. An iron ox has no bones; a fierce dragon plays in the sea; a magnificent hawk soars to the heavens.
To drink dry the Western River is not yet considered marvelous; a lotus blooming within fire emits a fragrant scent.
The crimson sun has already reached three poles, yet I still dream; Who can share this single pillow of pure breeze?
When people come to ask what practice I cultivate, I reply that these years my two ears have grown deaf.
Song of the Staff: How wondrous! This staff is no ordinary wood. It possesses mountain streams and has its knots and joints. Neither short nor long, it supports heaven and upholds earth;
neither fine nor coarse, it pierces through clouds and penetrates valleys. Sometimes held while walking, the black dragon leaps forth. Too...
Majestic and fierce: sometimes he seizes hold, the golden-maned lion’s brows raised and bristling; sometimes he carries it across his shoulder, the two wheels of sun and moon intermingling;
sometimes he holds it horizontally, the seven stars bursting forth in brilliant splendor; sometimes he leans against it, swallowing the myriad phenomena of the constellations.
Probing the waters, he strikes through the head of the golden tortoise; piercing the clouds, he knocks off the paws of the tiger.
The Words of Chan Master Foyuan: Ascending the hall as the successor of the Fifth Patriarch, [the Master said]:
“The World-Honored One held up a flower; Kāśyapa smiled. Intimate, intimate! Essential, essential!
If your eyes flicker and move, you will be left wandering in confusion. To report this to the Master: do not beat about the bush. Why? Because no dot has been added to the text.”
Descend from your seats. [The Master] raises the case: A monk asked Zhaozhou, "All phenomena return to the One; where does the One return?
Zhaozhou said, "I am in Qingzhou, making a cotton robe that weighs seven catties. O assembly, the ultimate sound transcends melody, and the wondrous tune is beyond noise; it pervades the entire body.
Not a thread of silk hangs upon him; his naked body is entirely without inhibition. All of you, do not pick at the food and lick your fingers.
You must simply cut off the tongue and let go of body and mind; then you will naturally be joyful. If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of themselves.
If the mind does not differ [from its true nature], what else could it be called? Joyful! Joyful! Return to the hall and drink tea.

On the road to Mount Tai, travelers are few indeed. Before the Hall of the Broken Oven, there is no ground upon which to express gratitude. Snow buries the cypress trees in the courtyard; ice locks the winding stream.
Though one may stand at the head of the furnace in the South, one does not enter the pickle-jar of another’s household. Look, look!
On the thirtieth day of the twelfth month, it is as if it were still cold in the early spring. You all must each exert yourselves and press forward;
take care not to give way to self-defeat or despondency.
The practitioner says: "The incense pillar has been ordained for many years; the lantern has long since shaved its head. The Buddha Hall strictly maintains the prohibitive precepts;
the triple gate has recently attained rest. The Great Matter is fundamentally equal: the Unattached Coolness is like the full moon.
Having brought all grasses, trees, thickets, and forests across, it is just as the warmth of spring causes them all to sprout together."
When awakened, this matter is fundamentally easy; after delusion, this gate is truly very difficult. At every place, green willows are fit to tie a horse;
at every household door, one passes through to Chang’an.
Case: Once there was a scholar who visited Master Changsha while he was reading the *Sūtra of the Names of the Thousand Buddhas*.
The scholar asked, "I have heard the names of so many buddhas, but I do not know in what lands they dwell.

Changsha said, "After Cui Hao inscribed his poem on the Yellow Crane Tower, have you, scholar, ever composed one yourself? He replied, "No. Changsha said, "It would be well to compose a poem on this occasion."
The scholar was at a loss. The assembly [asked]: "The scholar asked where the Buddha dwells; why did Changsha speak in such a manner?
Why was it that this scholar, who usually composed verses on the wind and the moon, could not utter a single word before Changsha?
If it were the Yellow Crane Tower, what would be so difficult about it? Listen as the mountain monk breaks through the mystery for you. Thereupon—
It is said: "His countenance is most wondrous; his radiance illuminates the ten directions. I have already made offerings to him in the past, and now I come once more to draw near.

Descend from your seat. If you attempt to deliberate, in what kalpa will you attain awakening? If you do not deliberate, you will remain forever muddled and confused. When you wish to think and yet do not think, at that moment [the barrier] is shattered. Ten thousand [realms].
The village is cloudless and ever manifest. Ever manifest! Its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges, not limited to morning or evening.

You masters of dhyāna, it is precisely now that you should cease your expeditions and lay down your arms, forever laying aside the halberds and spears. By the water and by the mountains, accomplish the Great Matter.
Moreover, human life is easily exhausted; how long is one’s lifespan? Should birth and death manifest before you, what will you ultimately rely upon for support? No!

I have seen the ancient worthies say: "If you do not settle yourself in dhyāna and samādhi, when you arrive here, you will be utterly bewildered. Standing for a long time at Longmen, there was nothing particularly marvelous;
they merely claimed it was the "single transmission of the mind-essence. Not only is there no fish in shallow water, but their probing and searching reveal no openings or seams at all.
At the two times of the day, they unfold their bowls and spread their mats; day after day, they defecate and urinate; all matters are just like those of ordinary people.
"Generally speaking, if one examines it closely, it is quite laughable. Since all things are the same for everyone, why is he called a 'Good Knowledge' (Kalyāṇamitra)?
After a long silence, he said, "I too cannot fathom it."
Jǔ: Master Zhìgōng said, "I observe that people in this world each cling to their own particular divergent views.

They know only to seek cakes by the side of the griddle, yet they do not understand how to return to the source and contemplate the flour. The cake has always been flour; its myriad transformations are brought about by human effort."
"Is there an assembly? The wildcat and the white ox recite the *Mahā*. The cat and the dog see one another constantly. All you Zen practitioners, do you realize it or not?
If you say that the self-nature is originally perfect and luminous, it is much like feeling for the sky and chasing a flash of lightning.
Do you understand? To seek Chang'an from atop the Hanyuan Palace; to wish to be born in the Inner Court within the palace of Maitreya."

On the fifteenth day of the third month at Longmen, the great drum beats its call again and again. It calls everyone to come together at once, yet this gives rise to extraordinary confusion. O Assembly:
since everyone has been called to come together at once, why does it give rise to such extraordinary confusion?

This is a fine opportunity; how will you all resolve it? If you do not know how to resolve it, you will become even more confused. If you know how to resolve it, you have already gained half the advantage. Truly.
Jiur said: "This single segment of causes and conditions has no one to sever it; I leave it for all quarters to sever together and examine.
Throughout the ten directions, at Longmen Monastery, the great earth, mountains, and rivers are its disciples. By following along with all conditions, liberation is accomplished;
when calculated, it does not require any effort at all."
Fluttering and drifting are the willow blossoms; Red and crimson are the distant clouds at the edge of heaven.

Winding and twisting is the road to Longmen; Secluded and still is the dwelling of a wild monk. If one does not yet harbor resolute understanding within the mind, Who can calculate the grains of sand beyond the kalpas?
The prescription for abstaining from grain is rice porridge and vegetarian meals; Moving spontaneously toward one's hometown is bitter and astringent tea. Good brother, drink!
The tea was served.
The attendant said, "The mountain monk has thus ordained one junior disciple. He then picked up his staff and showed it to the assembly, asking, "Do you see it?
The dharma name is Chongmu; his secular surname is Ge. After a long silence, he spoke again: "Since you have already surrendered yourself to me..."

[He] went forth into homelessness. Now, for your sake, I shall administer the Three Refuges and the Five Precepts. He then said: "Chongmu, take refuge in the Buddha; take refuge in the Dharma; take refuge in the Sangha.
Having already performed the Three Refuges for you, I shall now reverse the ten evils for you and confer the Five Precepts.

You should listen and receive them. These concern the body, speech, and mind. Regarding the body, there are three transgressions: namely, killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct. Regarding the mind, there are three transgressions.
These are greed, hatred, and delusion. Regarding speech, there are four transgressions: false speech, frivolous speech, divisive speech, and harsh speech.
To commit these ten is called the ten unwholesome actions; to refrain from these ten is called the ten wholesome actions. You have now received the precepts within the gateway of the three karmas.
These are the characteristics of the five precepts: namely, not killing, not stealing, not lying, not engaging in sexual misconduct, and not drinking intoxicants. You—
"Rely upon my teaching; believe it, accept it, and practice it accordingly. He then struck his staff once and said, "Chongmu, having heard my instruction, he addressed me, saying:
'What the Master has taught—Chongmu has from the beginning had no body, speech, or mind, nor does he know what constitutes upholding or violating [the precepts].
Even if I hear of the Three Refuges, I do not know what is meant by Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha. Having heard the Five..."

Regarding the characteristics of the precepts: from whom are they received and maintained? Although the Master troubled his *upādhyāya* in this way, Chongmu had no place to take them up or examine them.
The Master set down his staff and said, "This one is truly my disciple; this is true refuge; this is truly receiving the precepts.
Therefore, as an ancient said: "Why does the *upādhyāya* not keep a *śrāmaṇera*? The elder replied, "There is one who has no eyes."

"Regarding 'the ear': it is for me to seek out one person; this is precisely that meaning. It is also well-suited to be effective. Little masters and great assembly, do you understand? [He] raised his staff and said:

'Supported across the waters of the broken bridge, we return together to the village of the bright moon. [He stood for a long time."*] *(Note: "久立" (jiǔlì) is a formal expression used when a speaker has stood for a long duration, often indicating the conclusion of a discourse.)*

The general and the particular, identity and difference, as well as formation and destruction—these are nothing other than the mountain monk and the multitude. The lofty and vast Mount Sumeru enters a mustard seed;

the boundless ocean of lands resides within a single speck of dust. Day turns again to night; autumn follows spring. When the environment is still and the mind is harmonized, every phenomenon is true.
Since the great chariot of the seven treasures is thus, do not be negligent regarding coming and going, speaking and remaining silent. Zen practitioners, having heard this—
He finished speaking and laughed loudly, saying, "I know it too! I know it too! The Master then laughed and said, "You know it, indeed.
But tell me, who is there now upon the solitary peak behind Nālandā Monastery in Western India?"
Cultivating practice therein—do you see it? Do you see it? [The Master] descended from his seat.
He hung the portrait of Master Lin of the Four Quarters. "Empty space has no form, yet it does not refuse the manifestation of all forms.
A precious mirror has no shape, yet how could it obstruct the sudden appearance of myriad shapes? Form and shape are always false; emptiness and the mirror are always true."

Therefore, the false is itself the true; it is neither born nor extinguished. Great assembly, suppose the void were suddenly to vanish and the precious mirror no longer faced its stand—when both light and mirror have perished, what thing remains? Let us set aside those sixty-three years for a moment; tell me, what do you say?
"Where, then, is the Old Man of the Four Quarters right now? He then raised up the whisk and said: "What does one possess in their life?
From ancient times to the present, it has been transmitted to people."

Since Master Bodhidharma entered China until the present day, nearly a thousand years have passed. Those who have attained his Way are very numerous, and those who have grasped its essential meaning are truly many.
It is much like the saying: "One person transmits a falsehood, ten thousand people transmit it as a truth. O Great Assembly, idle rumors cease when they meet the wise.
After thirty years, none of you should say that you have come from Longmen.
The Master cited a monk asking Deshan, "What is the extraordinary matter of the School? Deshan replied, "In my school there are no words or phrases;
truly, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. The Master said, "He has let it all slip away!
A monk asked Xuefeng, "When you visited Deshan, what did you obtain that you returned home with? Xuefeng said, "At that time, I went empty-handed and returned empty-handed. The Master [said], "..."
He said, "He has let it slip. Muzhou called to a monk; the monk turned his head. Muzhou said, "A fellow carrying a wooden board. The Master said, "He has let it slip.
First let it slip, second let it slip, third let it slip. Do not use your intellect to anticipate or lag behind;
do not form enmity or kinship with the patriarchs and Buddhas. Behold well the jewel in your robe, always free from defilement. The family members run about, vying with one another. Huai.
"South of here, the old man at Longmen is laughing to death. If anyone can understand the reason for this laughter, their eyes will be like bronze bells and their courage like a peck-measure.
Heh heh heh! Return to the hall!"
The people of Jambudvīpa in the south are mostly noisy and chaotic; those in the Heaven of No-Thought (asaṃjñisattva) of the fourth dhyāna have the most sluggish faculties.
Their slowness and speed are not of the same class, and their defilement and purity are difficult to exchange. Two coins of five hundred each are originally but one string of a thousand.
"Penetrating, penetrating! The mute claps his hands and calls out at the top of his voice. The deaf hear it, yet pretend not to care.
When the sky is bright and the sun has risen, it is midnight. Great Master Zhizhe discusses *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*. Assembly, what is this principle? After a long silence, he says: 'Look!'"
A letter arrived from Master Sīxin of Huanglongshan. He ascended the hall and said: "The mind of Sīxin is already dead; the death of the mind arises from life.
He breaks off the horns of Huanglong and turns his body to walk while lying on the ground. This old fellow has always worn his robe inside out and carried his traveling hat upside down;
his speech is coarse and blunt, yet his heart is gentle and harmonious. He inspects the monastic communities and scolds those in training."

Although he transmitted the Way of Huìtáng, he favored the Chan of Yúnmén. He used "reviling the wind" and "reviling the rain" as his method for training disciples, and took "planting vegetables" and "growing greens" as his daily tasks.
He brought about calamities and inflicted misfortunes; he was seldom joyful and frequently wrathful. When fools saw him, they knit their brows;
when the wise saw him, they nodded in agreement. When he wished to leave, he left immediately—truly a master indeed! His leaping forth was originally just Mò.
The common laborer, in his sleep, has lost the heart of death. Alas, how lamentable! A misfortune for the Dharma-gate.

Empty names and empty forms—like echoes in a valley or reflections in a mirror—are abandoned and not cultivated. How can one clarify the nature of illusion? If one does not exert oneself while young, it will be too late.
Old and full of regret, I ponder this in stillness and weigh it according to conditions. An ancient worthy said: "It is like a hundred-year-old man performing a song and dance;
how could this be the play of a small child? "Great assembly, do you understand why he spoke thus?

He was born with eyes staring and mouth agape. When the staff is wielded and the shout is let loose, he sets it aside. Clouds, moon, streams, and mountains—this is letting go of one move.
Once you penetrate one place, a thousand and ten thousand places are encompassed; once one mechanism is clarified, a thousand and ten thousand mechanisms revolve.

The Blue Cliff does not depart from this very place; this very place does not depart from the Blue Cliff. It gathers the great trichiliocosm within the tip of a hair and merges the mustard seed with the dust mote.

Within the ocean of lands, flowers and birds pass by; monkeys return with their young. That which is profoundly still and unmoving, where the realization of truth is not borrowed—let that be set aside for a moment.
But tell me, on this ground where there is neither yin nor yang, what kind of matter can be accomplished?

While the myriad plants are just now nourished by the power of harmonious energy, the green cliff has already sent forth the fragrance of a single branch. Again, it is related that Master Ma asked Youshan, "Disciple, [what is it?]"
"In this state for so long a time, what is the fundamental matter? The Mountain said, "When skin and flesh have fallen away entirely, there remains only the single reality.
The Patriarch said, "According to what you see, it may be said that it accords with the body and is spread throughout the four limbs."
"Why not take three strips of bamboo to bind your belly and go to dwell in the mountains wherever you may be?

The mountain man said, "What kind of person am I that I would dare speak of dwelling in the mountains? The Patriarch said, "Not so. There has never been one who travels far without dwelling, nor one who dwells long without traveling.
To wish to benefit others when there is nothing to benefit, or to wish to act when there is nothing to do—this is futile. You should instead become a vessel for crossing over; thus, you shall dwell."

Shan: "The Master said: 'O assembly, after the ancients attained their realization, they did not forget to benefit sentient beings; they entered deep mountains directly to uphold the essentials of our school.
This mountain monk is ignorant and dull-witted—how could I dare to aspire to such heights? Thus, there is no need for a bamboo strap to bind my belly.
Yet I have a broken-legged cauldron with which to maintain a life of quiet solitude together with those who come later. If you can believe this...'"
In the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, some may not yet be fully conversant; listen then to this final phrase: The lofty peak towers abruptly against the gates of heaven;
The green ridges are vast and empty, fit for planting one’s feet. Fortunately, the broken-legged cauldron remains; One need not hesitate to carry it away to hide deep within the clouds.
Even so, you must all lend a hand before it can be accomplished. But tell me, in the end, how is it? It is wondrous!
In the dance, one must display the shifts in the beat; in the *santai* (three-platform) performance, all must urge it forward together.
Entering the hall, he points to the abbot’s quarters and says: "This is the seat where Vimalakīrti sat; it is precisely the same as when the command was issued in Magadha."
At the summit of Jia Shan, Ningtong has a single aperture. He lets forth the ancient, veteran Zen master Tianpeng. Now that he has been let out to show his head, tell me:
what kind of artifice can he perform? A splendid fish breaks through the waves and enters the net; as the vast celestial net is raised, there is no room for him to escape.
Upon entering the monastery, he said: "Beyond the gate, the green mountains are like drenched ink; along the road, the fine rain falls like rich manure.
On Lingyun’s path, peach blossoms bloom; everywhere, their fragrance overflows the eyes. At Xiangyan’s crag, emerald bamboos stand; constantly, they sway their shadows in the wind.
Truly, one strike causes all knowledge to be forgotten; a single sight cuts off all doubt. Yet, one cannot help but still linger in seeing and hearing, having not yet penetrated sound."

Form: if one can see form that is not seen, hear sound that is not heard, turn back at the head of the path, and kick over the pivot—then every phrase transcends Buddhas and Patriarchs, every speck of dust shines through antiquity and vibrates into the present, everywhere detached from form and name, each and every one cutting through nails and severing iron.
There is no dharma outside the mind; there is no mind outside dharmas. Wielding the sword from the royal armory, one releases a thousand-jun weight.
The crossbow stands upright like ten thousand fathoms of cliff, severing all directions; one may thereby enter the gate of great liberation and transmit the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye.
Toward the era of Yao and the sun of Shun, we shall together enjoy peace and prosperity, drumming our bellies and singing songs of joy, returning home to sit in stability.
As for this single phrase of "arriving home," how would you express it? I only wish that the spring breeze would exert its full strength, blowing all at once into my door.
Later, Fu Ming remarked: "In the past, [Fayan] possessed a strategy that penetrated the heavens and a divine ingenuity that spanned the seas.
He caused a tongueless man to speak words of no meaning; he gathered Lopu and welcomed Qingfeng; he discerned Shishuang and honored Furi. His phrases were perilous and his sentences steep."
The mechanism for trapping the tiger is profound; like lightning striking and stars flying, pearls whirl and jade turns. This precious temple was established, its exemplary style fully preserved.

Yet, this mountain monk is mediocre in all matters; how could I continue such lofty footsteps? Since I cannot decline the request, and there is no door through which to escape, I have no choice but to borrow a path:
to discourse with words where there are no words, to create affairs where there are no affairs. No...

Where there is no Buddha, he manifests as a Buddha; where there is no Patriarch, he reveals himself as a Patriarch. What is valued is that the beginning and end correspond, so that the head is straight and the tail is straight.
I dare ask you all: do you see this old man Jia Shan? Do not seek him at the tips of the hundred grasses; face-to-face, there is no private bias, pervading past and present.
Opening the hall and holding up the memorial address, he said: "Every word is brocade; every phrase is a pearl. It praises the Unsurpassed Vehicle and reveals the True Dharma Eye.
You must realize it before the words are even raised; you must take responsibility beyond the patterns of the text. If this is not yet so, then please proceed with the reading."
Ascending the seat, he said: "The *śakara* eye emits a great radiance from its crown; Maheśvara manifests a wondrous sign before him. A single word contains all phenomena;

a single phrase accords with the capacities of all beings. How could it merely mean lying across the mouth of a cave in a fierce place, or planting one's feet precariously before a ten-thousand-fathom peak?
Therefore it is said: 'Revealing the great capacity and clarifying the great function—both gain and loss are lost.'"
This is the profound forgetting of both is and is-not; transcending dust and tracks, penetrating form and sound, layer upon layer without end, every matter perfectly integrated.
It is like the Flower Treasury Dharma-realm, where boundless seas of fragrant water and unspeakable numbers of Floating Banner King lands all manifest simultaneously within this very place.
This is realized right here; this is enjoyed right here—not by seeing with the eyes, nor by...
Hearing with the ear, not speaking with the mouth, and not knowing with the mind—can you still realize it?

If you can realize it, there is no need to first see Mañjuśrī at the eastern outskirts of the City of Enlightenment, nor wait for the tower-gate to open before attending to Maitreya. I dare ask the assembly: [Can you do so?]

Right now, whose realm is this? Raising his whisk, he said: "The original body of Vairocana is fully manifest; for one who meets the occasion directly, there is not even a hair's breadth of anything left behind."
One Ding, two Zhuo. This is the tongs and hammer of one's fundamental nature: grasping and releasing. It is the utilization of a master:

where one is covered in dust and ash, there one stands ten thousand fathoms high; where one stands ten thousand fathoms high, there one is covered in dust and ash. Thus, one naturally both releases and gathers.
Everywhere there is auspiciousness and good fortune. Do you understand this thoroughly? Gathering water, the moon is in one’s hand; playing with flowers, their fragrance fills one’s robes.
The great void is vast and empty, yet the myriad phenomena are dense and manifold. When the true eye is clearly penetrating, not even a hair’s breadth can be established.

In its solitary loftiness, even the Patriarchs cannot approach; in its level simplicity, it is known by all humans and devas. Strike open the gate of great liberation, and recognize that which has no face.
Look at this fellow! But tell me, what is a faceless fellow? The peony blooms on the Bodhisattva’s face;
the palm fronds scatter upon the Yakṣa’s head.
To be consistently "not thus" is to gaze at the clouds and stars, refusing to conform to human sentiments.
To be consistently "thus" is to have a head like ashes and a face like dust, trailing water and mud. To be "not thus" within being "thus" is to level the high by following the low.
To be "thus" within being "not thus" is to let go from the void. If there is someone who, amidst both "thus" and "not thus," cares for neither and is without delusion, that is it.
There is neither darkness, nor letting go, nor gathering in. Tell me, how is it? At last, the frosty night moon falls naturally into the stream before one.

Under the first phrase, one attains realization; the patriarchs and Buddhas beg for their lives. Under the second phrase, one attains realization; humans and devas lose heart. Under the third phrase, one attains realization;
one places oneself across the jaws of a tiger. This is neither following established paths nor altering tracks and routes.
If you penetrate it, you possess six arms and three heads; even if you have not yet penetrated it, you are already among humans and gods. Now tell me: what are these three phrases?
An external phrase: How would you say it? "One’s livelihood lies solely upon the fishing line; under the bright moon, a small boat drifts across the Five Lakes.
Residing at Daolin, he ascended the hall and said: "The Great Way has no front or back; the ultimate principle transcends words and explanations. It stands far beyond the Three Vehicles."

Transcending the ten stages of the bodhisattva path, where the myriad dharmas cannot reach, there is a singular brilliance. Before the distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas arose, the numinous light shone alone, falling neither into hearing nor seeing, nor following form or sound.
Directly beneath, there is not a single thread or hair’s breadth of duality; throughout the entire realm, this extraordinary matter is fully manifested.
Even if one were to attain realization through the staff or take responsibility under a shout, it would still be a mere expedient for the present age.

Furthermore, there may even be instances where both light and objects are forgotten, and the mind accords with equanimity; yet ultimately, this is not the definitive point. Thus it is said: "The upward path is not transmitted by the thousand sages;
students weary their bodies, like a monkey grasping at a reflection. When one arrives here, principle is cut off, phenomena are cut off, practice is cut off;
illumination is cut off, function is cut off; the provisional is cut off, the real is cut off. It is truly like a long sword leaning against the heavens—majestic and awe-inspiring.
The divine majesty and the mechanism of the iron ox cannot be confined. Today, fortunately before those with clear eyes, I dare not hide it within a covering bag;
I shall open it wide in eight characters. Holding up his whisk, he said: "Do you understand?

Shining through antiquity and surging through the present, lively and agile, the entire great thousandfold world-system reveals its whole body. He spoke again: "O Great Assembly! In days of yore, Xue..."
Xuefeng held up his staff and showed it to the assembly, saying, "This one of mine is for those of middling and lower capacity.
At that time, a monk came forward and asked, "What if someone of the highest capacity should arrive? Xuefeng raised his staff.
Yunmen said, "I am not like Xuefeng, who beats this broken web of complications. He then held up his staff and said, "This one of mine is for those of middling and lower capacity."
Regarding "The Mechanized Man": Once, a monk suddenly asked, "When a person of the highest capacity arrives, how do you deal with them? Yunmen immediately struck him. The Master comments:
Generally speaking, to support the school and establish the teaching, one must possess the eye atop the head and the talisman behind the elbow.
Observe these two venerable elders; their mastery over killing and giving life, appearing and disappearing, rolling up and unfolding—how truly extraordinary! Examine this closely.
To speak of "the future" is still to produce branches where there were none. According to my own view, I pick up my staff and say:
I shall employ this very thing for all people, regardless of whether they are superior, middling, or inferior. If you wish to lift it up, feel free to lift it up;
if you wish to take it up and bear it, feel free to bear it. At every turn, I block off the essential passageways, so that everyone is left facing a wall.

Standing at a height of a thousand *ren*. Now tell me: what is it like when someone from within that assembly suddenly arrives? When the ten thousand nations have intoxicated their hearts tasting the great cauldron, they meet and take each other’s hands up onto the high terrace.
In the deepest depths, nothing can be compared to it. In the shallowest reaches, it is handed over with both hands.
Unifying the one within the many, it pierces all apertures at the tip of a hair. Shortening the long and lengthening the short, it holds the scale and the ruler within the palm.
Having replaced the skull and the foundation, set it aside for a moment; bring forth the bag for boots and shoes—what do you say? When spirit does not follow [external forms]...
Heaven and earth attain it; how could heroes rely on the shifting of the four seasons?
Leaves fall and one knows autumn; a string is plucked and one distinguishes the melody. Dingguang held up his hand; the Wise One nodded his head.

To take responsibility before the patterns have yet manifested, to reflect upon one another beyond right and wrong, gain and loss—uninvolved in the slightest attachment, how can one transmit this message?
Ten thousand scenes possess only empty forms; the solitary cloud is fundamentally without intention.
The profound mystery of the profound is too vast and indistinct; the clarity of the clear has no boundaries. Birth and extinction are, by their very nature, a state of deliberate contrariety.
Neither going nor coming—this reveals further leakage. Without arising from the samādhi of cessation, one manifests all modes of dignified conduct;
without abandoning the dharmas of ordinary beings, one cultivates all sublime practices. Tell me: is this letting go, or is it holding fast?
Recognizing one's nature as it flows along, there is neither joy nor sorrow.
Master Taishou rose to appoint a monk, saying: "The great person possesses great vision; with great wisdom, they attain great function. One flight takes six months to rest;
one promise weighs as much as ten thousand pieces of gold. That which floods the heavens must be the rivers and seas; that which rises steeply must be the mountains and peaks.

The one who knows first awakens those who do not yet know; the one who has awakened first awakens those who awaken later. Opening the inexhaustible treasury, they bring forth priceless jewels—without relying on anything."
"A single thing reveals the person of primordial origin.
Xuedou said, "When there is plenty, righteousness emerges; when there is scarcity, unfiliality arises. Within the school of patch-robed monks, is this letting go? Is it holding fast?
If anyone can speak of it, I will divide my monastery in half and give it to them to live in. The Master said, "Xuedou suffers from many ailments."

He was well-versed in the natures of medicinal herbs, and after his efficacy had been proven through practice, he began to transmit them to others. Among those disciples, there may have been some who understood abundance and scarcity, who knew how to let go and how to hold fast;
for such individuals, what harm would there be in sharing half the monastery with them?

One need only burn incense and make a vow, hoping only that they might soon have a courtyard of their own to live in, so that they might taste something of the flavor [of the Way] and, for the time being, be spared from the torment of poverty and the scorching heat of hunger.
Protruding and difficult to discern; even those of long standing cannot avoid hesitating. Picked up at random by the hand—how could later students know its true point?
The golden wind fans all things; the jade dew hangs like pearls. Geese pass through the vast sky; crickets chirp upon the secluded steps.

Each and every one is pierced through from top to bottom; clearly manifest, they are layered a hundredfold and a thousandfold. Why need one rely on the mutual exchange of staff and shout to discuss illumination and function? Directly beneath [this very moment]...
"Letting go from a precipice"—is there such a person? To see what is right and not act upon it is no true hero; only by remaining unchanging in the face of peril does one startle the multitude.

With nothing to grasp or collect, realization is perfected at every point of contact. Application is free from discrepancy; do not exhaust yourself seeking form or appearance. Turn toward the thousand...
Upon the crown of the Sage’s head, there are times when the mechanism that neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs can fathom is revealed.
Within the tip of a single hair, there are times when the patterns of the shifting roles of host and guest are displayed—spanning heaven and earth, turning like jade and revolving like pearls.
Let this be set aside for a moment. [The Master] raises his whisk and makes a dotting gesture, saying: "Where does this one dot fall? Only the Sea God knows."
Though precious, its value is not recognized; it remains among humanity to illuminate the night.

Baoning received the official decree and thereafter dwelt alone upon solitary peaks, gazing toward the clouds and the heavens. While he did not fail to uphold the ancestral tradition, was he not perhaps too aloof?
On the other hand, there are those who remain at the crossroads with dust on their faces and ash on their heads, responding to the needs of beings and benefiting all.

The capacity for awakening, though it may be buried and obscured within oneself, is not perhaps too much of a humiliation for one’s life? Furthermore, those of clear realization possess the eye upon the crown of their heads and the talisman behind their elbows;
they come and go, roll up and unroll as they please, attaining great sovereign freedom. Their movement is like drifting clouds, and their stillness is like the spirit of the valley.
They may dwell alone on a solitary peak, unimpeded even by the dust on their faces and ashes on their heads; or, while with dust on their faces and ashes on their heads, [they remain free].
"Unimpeded, dwelling alone on a solitary peak. Within suchness, there is non-suchness; within non-suchness, there is indeed suchness.
Now, as for the phrase that accords with the time and the season—how do you speak it? After a long silence, he said: "Auspicious vapors meet a fortunate destiny."
The numinous sprout brings spring wherever it touches;
the ancient Buddhas have a thoroughfare. It stands manifest throughout past and present; one who can let go at the precipice—each word is worth a thousand pieces of gold.
Brandishing the staff and shouting "Ho!"; dragging stones and carrying earth; the elephant-bone roller and the ball; Heoshan striking the drum; Weiling tending the oxen;
Xuansha seeing the tiger; Zhaozhou drinking tea; Lu Zu facing the wall—how can these compare to Old Yunmen on the twenty-fifth day of the twelfth month?
Li Shanyou became a monk and said: "The three realms offer no peace; the four modes of birth are constricting.

Desiring to escape the net of craving and take a great stride toward the vast expanse, one ought truly to don the armor of patience, wield the sword of wisdom, exercise the highest state of mind, and resolve upon a most excellent aspiration."
To wage war against the Māra of the aggregates, the Māra of afflictions, and the Māra of death; to extinguish the three poisons and shatter the net of Māra—only then is one a true great man.
Have you not seen it stated in the teachings: "There is no peace within the three realms; they are like a burning house, filled with manifold sufferings"?
It is truly terrifying. Furthermore, it is said: "This house has but a single door, and it is moreover narrow and small.

Yet, despite being so narrow and small, all the Buddhas of the past, the Buddhas of the present, and the Buddhas of the future have all departed through this very gate. Now tell me: how do you explain this?
Ultimately, how is it? After a long silence, he said: "How does it compare to a falcon from the distant heavens? Ten thousand miles of clouds, pierced by a single swoop.
Regarding the opening of the furnace, he said: "Dry grass near the fire ought logically to burn first; a drop of water forming ice—these matters do not intersect.

If one can suddenly penetrate birth and death, clarify cold and heat, dissolve movement and stillness, and transcend coming and going, then directly the mind will cast off its objects and emotions, becoming as if— [The text ends abruptly here.]
Be as dull-witted as a pillar. Only then can you eat when hungry, walk in meditation when vigorous, seek coolness when hot, and turn toward the fire when cold.
Even so, Zhaozhou said: "For thirty years in the south, I have had this 'Guestless and Hostless' koan;
until this very day, no one has been able to bring it forth. Now tell me: where does this Guestless and Hostless koan lie? At the head of the brazier.
How can one bring this forth? Do you understand thoroughly yet? "The patched robe covers the head, and all affairs cease; at this moment, even this mountain monk knows nothing.
Zhuanan said when he was invited for a vegetarian feast by Foyan: "In this realm, his conditions have ended; in another realm, he manifests his transformation. In this world, his body..."
Death: appearing in another realm. The Great Spiritual Friend (Mahā-kalyāṇamitra) takes boundless empty space as his true body;
he takes the unspeakable number of lands within the oceans of fragrant water as his field of transformation; he takes the sun and moon as his bright torches;

he takes the physical form as a transient lodging; and he takes birth and death as day and night. When he comes, it is like the dazzling flash of lightning; when he departs, it is like a spark from a flint.
It flies. Although it manifests to worldly people as having coming and going, when its fundamental essence is examined to the utmost, it is unmoving and unchanging.
Thus, in the past, when Nanquan was preparing a vegetarian feast for Master Mazu, he asked the assembly: "Today we are holding a feast for our late teacher;
tell me, has the late teacher come? Some said, "Cover your bowl. Others said, "Add another lamp before the True Hall."
"One part of food. This clearly illustrates that this very thing is immovable and unchanging, supremely spiritual and wondrous, each possessing its own extraordinary quality.
Yet, for now, we see only the sharpness of the awl's point, but not the squareness of the chisel's head.
Today, Elder Baoshan Gui is hosting a vegetarian feast for Master Foyan. I dare ask the assembly: has Master Foyan come? Is there anyone who can say so?
"Come forth and try to say it! If you have nothing, you will not even merit a single offering for the universal assembly.
Why? Because before the eaves, drops of water fall one after another; the five-petaled flower transmits petal by petal. Now tell me: what is this single phrase that flows on without interruption?"
"How do you say it? The Patriarch’s moon soars into the void, his perfect supreme wisdom; on what mountain are the pines and cypresses not lush and green?

Releasing the matter once more for the sake of the monks, he concludes with words of gratitude: "The God among gods, the Sage among sages. Abiding as the greatest within the realm, transcending as the most honored beyond the mundane.
Holding the precious tally to govern the people, commanding the golden wheel to rule the throne. He has cleared away [all obstructions]..."
Having cleared the six directions and halted the poisons throughout the myriad regions, imperial edicts were issued to once again revive the Buddha-dharma.
Consequently, the śramaṇas under heaven were restored to their monastic decorum: the wooden tablets were returned to Minister Pei, and the crowns and hairpins were surrendered to Dashi Fu.
The cranial protuberance (*uṣṇīṣa*) of the Arhats was once more made whole, and the *kṣaumika* robes were donned anew. In the space of a brief moment, the ancient splendor was restored. The Emperor—
The weight of this grace is ten thousand times greater than a mountain. How could something as insignificant as a blade of grass or a stalk of vegetation ever hope to repay it?

I have now poured forth my very heart and soul, offering but a mere fraction of my capacity. O Great Assembly: the ultimate pivot of the Buddhas of the past is like sparks struck from stone, like the flash of lightning.
The Patriarchs have a final phrase that swallows the thorny chestnut and leaps through the diamond ring;
it can rival all others and startle the multitude, and it can transform the ordinary into the sacred. It soars through the present and illuminates the past, transcending form and mounting sound.

Now, as I bring it forth before this assembly, I do not violate the path already laid out. Do you understand? The wondrous power of the great forge existed before heaven and earth; it covers and sustains all.
"Gratitude is due to the Great Sage.

An invitation for the anniversary of his passing. It says: "He wielded the tongs and hammer of the Buddhas and Patriarchs and controlled the furnace and bellows of the masters; he smelted and forged all things of the past and present."
To verify a patch-robed monk, one employs nothing but the ultimate pivot of the upward path—the Vajra King’s Precious Sword.
The Patriarch Linji transmitted this very essential pivot from Huangbo and Mazu; north of the great river, he alone shook the true lineage.

With a single shout, he distinguished guest and host, and the functions of illumination and application were exercised simultaneously. He cut off the tongues of all people under heaven and caused the cloud-dwelling monks of the four seas to hasten toward him.
Thus it continues, down to sons and grandsons, who transmit this right view and employ this true mechanism.
Were one not a person of great liberation, how could they possibly undergo verification in the presence of reality? In the past, the Great Layman Wujin made this matter his lifelong pursuit;
there was no master throughout the seas whom he did not consult. Upon reaching the foot of Mount Doushuai, he encountered an old monk with whom he discussed the "final word."

At this point, he finally attained the complete reality of the whole body; all verbal explanations and intellectual understandings were cast off at once. He then composed a verse: "The drum is silent, the bell has ceased;
returning with his alms bowl, Yantou’s single thrust was like a clap of thunder. As it turns out, he could live for no more than three years."
Is it not that he has received his prediction from him? Like jade struck and metal clashing, like tigers leaping and dragons soaring, he possesses great capacity and attains great function.
With this authentic seal, he stamps the good spiritual friends throughout the world. When I, this mountain monk, first met him in Hubei, we were like lightning rolling and stars racing;
in one word we reached mutual realization, as our inner and outer natures were identical. Your achievements, Layman, are inscribed [in history].
Though his deeds were recorded on bamboo and silk, his enduring virtue lies with the living people. On this very day, he lets go of his hands over there. Tell me, where does he go?
Do you understand? Throughout the myriad lands of the Buddhas across the great trichiliocosm, in every realm and at every speck of dust, his supreme body appears.

This Dharma discourse for Zhang Chiman, the Court Gentleman, concerns the ancients’ use of the metaphor of "herding the ox. How true it is! It is precisely what is required for those who seek long-term stability—a direct and essential shortcut.

First, one must forget the view of self, allowing for emptiness, stillness, tranquility, and harmony, so that one proceeds spontaneously and carefree. Regarding all phenomena, there is neither grasping nor rejecting;

amidst every sense organ and every sensory object, one is at that moment suddenly liberated and abides in oneself. Moving alone and shining solitary, the essence of illumination stands independent. Subject and object are as one;
one goes straight through to the very bottom, where no illumination can be established—like cutting a single strand of silk. One.
"Cutting off everything, cutting it all off—then one simply goes about making a living for oneself.

If even the view of Buddha and the view of Dharma are not permitted to arise, then worldly afflictions and karmic consciousness will naturally melt away like ice and crumble like tiles. One nurtures this until it becomes fully realized;
like a fool, like a pillar, yet with such sharp resolve that one cannot be confined within the ranks of the patriarchs and Buddhas. How could one be willing to enter the womb of a donkey or a horse?"
Zhaozhou said, "I have seen billions of people; they are all seeking to become Buddha-men. Among them, it is difficult to find even one who has no bottom.
He further said, "In the south for thirty years, except for the two times of eating porridge and rice, this was where my mind was distracted and active.
Xianglin [only] after forty years finally became a single piece. Yongquan, even after forty years, still..."

Moving about. Nanyuan’s eighteen [cases] demonstrate the activity of a true adept. One can truly know that among the ancients of old, there were none who did not practice in this manner—stepping forward in dense intimacy.
How could one calculate gain or loss, long or short, or engage in the conceptualizations of acceptance and rejection, right and wrong?
Among my fellow students, only Longmen Zhikai has in the past thoroughly investigated and clarified this with me. Yet, whenever encountering conditions or meeting circumstances, do not...

Do not take anything with you. Not only for this life, but throughout the bounds of the future, even if you were to realize immeasurable holy bodies, that would still not be your place of ultimate rest.
Simply retreat one taste; by all means, do not set any limits.
As the conditions of past karma have not yet exhausted themselves, one must deal with such manifold entanglements and interactions in the human world;
only by managing them with ample ease and leisure can one succeed. Each person follows their own karmic lot; there is no need to loathe clamor and seek solitude.
Provided that the mind is empty within and one conforms to circumstances without, one will remain tranquil and secure even amidst the bustle of a marketplace or a boiling cauldron. As soon as...
If there is even a hair’s breadth of a view acting as a thorn, one will not be able to strike through it.

To the Dharma-keeper Liǒngzhī, the late Master Wǔzǔ said: "Throughout my life, I have been solitary and austere, seldom granting approval. I am dry and parched; standing like a sheer cliff, I rely solely on this."
Once he attained realization, he would often say: "It is like leaning against a single Mount Sumeru; how could one possibly engage in empty talk, playing with slick words to deceive others?
Taking this flavorless iron tart, he thrusts it right at the face of the student to have them chew upon it.
One must wait until their 'bottom of the bucket' falls out, until they lose all such evil knowledge and evil views, so that not even a thread of attachment remains and they pass through into purity."
Only when [delusions] are exhausted can one begin to apply the furnace of refinement; only then can one restrain their fists and feet.

Thereafter, one shows them the Vajra King’s Precious Sword to test whether they are truly capable of practicing it and bearing its burden. When all is pure and still, without a single thing remaining, mountains are simply mountains and waters are simply waters.

Furthermore, you should turn toward that other side—the place where a thousand sages cannot enclose you. There, you will accord with the Treasury of the True Dharma-Eye (Shōbōgenzō) realized and transmitted by your ancestors since time immemorial.
When it comes to its practical application for the sake of sentient beings, you must still drive the plowman’s ox and snatch the food from the hungry man.
If you can verify this through ten stages of realization without any leakage, you are truly a follower of the Way.

The Head Seat Shiming showed that when Bodhidharma traveled through Liang and Wei, he went deep into the grasses to seek out people; he sat coldly at Shaolin for nine years, and amidst the deep snow, he sought out one person.
