Huizhao said, "This is the treasure of a sovereign; who would dare to offer a price for it? The Master said, "Elder Xinghua, you have encountered the Emperor in a single moment to discuss Chan.
Yet, when scrutinized, this does not yet accord with the Sovereign's intent. I, a monk, have a short verse: 'Our Lord has reclaimed the Central Plains.'"

Treasures! Beyond the frontier, the dust and smoke have been swept clean; throughout the ten thousand nations, songs of joy celebrate the Great Peace. At every household gate, the road leads to Chang’an.
A letter from Póngān arrived, saying: "The spring breeze blows through and shatters the rock at the mountain peak; Yan has descended East Peak and left no trace."
When the sun is at its zenith at midday, it reveals its entire body; yet one might cast a red-hot iron caltrop directly in its face.

Thus it is said: "Coming, there is not a single word; departing, there is nothing to be said. The monasteries throughout the four seas sigh in admiration: "How could the turtle have ever been lost within the jar?"

Accepting the invitation from Drum Mountain, he took leave of the assembly, saying: "For three years I have resided within these mountains; throughout the community, both high and low, let us value harmony.
Today, at the head of the stream, do not begrudge parting; De-yun (Cloud of Virtue) remains ever present upon Mount Miaogao."
The Chief Administrator (Kanjishi) said: "The head is covered in a hundred wrinkles and the hair has turned white; with both hands supporting the plow, he comes forth once more.
Taking up his old felt clappers, let us all watch him perform the *Santai* dance. *Rarari, rarari!* Where there is no place, the moon reflects in the clear waves;
where there is a place, windless waters rise in ripples. I recall Ba Ling asking a monk: 'Have you come from traveling the mountains? For...
When the Buddha-dharma arrives, a monk says, "In this world of peace and tranquility, what need is there to speak of the Buddha-dharma? Lingyun says, "What a fine 'non-active' monk you are.
The monk says, "That is already quite a lot of activity. The Master says: "Baling spreads a net across the heavens to catch fish leaping through the waves;
yet alas for this monk—he is a golden-scaled dragon that has passed through the net. In the end, the net cannot hold him. This is indeed so.
This is correct; those with coarse minds will miss it. Now tell me: does it fall on the side of the guest or the side of the host?
Let those with the eye of discernment distinguish this. As Master Baiyun Cundao said: "When opening one's mouth, the very last word hits the mark; when taking a step..."
He took one step forward and stepped right on top of it. Why, then, is his nostril crooked from morning until night?
It is simply because he has been accustomed to being dull-witted; therefore, he does not arouse the aspiration for enlightenment. Now I urge everyone to arouse it. The Master said:
"Baoyun speaking in this manner not only fails to save himself, but moreover is laboring in vain without merit. He does not realize that..."
When opening one's mouth, a single phrase has already been spoken; before taking a step, a single stride has already been taken.
From morning until night, the nostrils hang down with their great heads pointing downward. To report it thus is already a matter of necessity;
if you do not further arouse the aspiration for enlightenment, how can you blame this mountain monk?
A monk asked Touzi, "Is it true that all sounds are the voice of the Buddha? Touzi said, "Yes.

The monk said, "Master, do not let the sound of a boiling pot drown out the noise. Touzi then struck him. Again he asked, "Is it true that coarse words and subtle speech both return to the primary meaning?
Touzi said, "Yes. The monk said, "May I call you, Master, a donkey? Touzi then struck him.
The Master said: "Mount Hall does not think so. When he says, 'Venerable Sir, do not let the hot water boil and the bowl ring,' you should say to him, 'Yes.
And when he asks, 'Is it permissible to call the Venerable Sir a donkey? you should say to him, 'It is. Do you wish to know?
Cutting down generals and seizing banners—Touzi is a master craftsman. Subduing an enemy's army without fighting—you must know that Mount Hall is a skilled hand."

At Gushan, we observe the summer retreat; there is no other principle than this: gazing at the clouds atop Mount Dading and drawing from the waters of Lingyuan. To seek further deliberation beyond this would be like burning paper money to lead ghosts away.
The National Teacher’s Memorial Day verse says: "Of old, a man with three arrows settled the Tian Mountains; He claimed himself a hero surpassing all in the world.
How can he compare to Xuefeng’s single arrow, Which casually pierced through the Stone Gate Barrier?

It reached the point where the mountains and rivers of the great earth No longer possessed a single inch of soil, And throughout the ten directions and three periods of time, There was not a single person at all. At such a moment as this, those of all quarters know only the 'Holy Arrow'."
The place where the seed fell is unknown; one does not know where the holy arrowhead broke. Tell me, where is the place where the holy arrowhead broke?
(He lets out a shout and descends from his seat.)
To establish knowledge within knowledge and vision is the very root of ignorance. To have knowledge and vision without [clinging to] seeing—this is *nirvāṇa*, the untainted and truly pure.
How could anything else be admitted therein? The Old Man Śākyamuni, for no reason at all, has placed all people of the world upon ground where they must inevitably die.
Today, this mountain monk, not begrudging a single hair on his eyebrows, shall provide a footnote: "Knowledge and vision without seeing."
This is *nirvāṇa*. It has deceived and ruined an entire shipload of people. Being untainted and truly pure, how could it allow for any other thing within it?
Heaven above, you add only more grievous suffering! If you can realize this beneath the words of Śākyamuni, I grant that you may sit upright and secure atop a hundred-foot pole.
If you can realize it beneath my own words, I grant that you may set foot within a thicket of thorns.

Moving crosswise, the moon cannot bear to break the five. The patch-robed monk takes it up with fierce vigor; he strikes and stirs the fish of the Eastern Sea, causing the tiger of the Southern Mountain to lose its way.
If you ask what school this belongs to, do not speak of it mistakenly when meeting others.
The skull is crushed to pieces; the eyes are cold. At once, one takes the Southern Dipper and looks toward the North.
With infinite elegance, there is no need to peddle it about. Seizing the moment, one topples Mount Iron-Circle (Cakravāḍa). O sharp-witted ones!
Before the bell has tolled and the drum has sounded, at the Great Summit Peak, we have already met you. Why come here again to seek what bowl? Even so, do not—
"It is strange that you have frequently urged me to drink since we sat together; since our parting, I have rarely seen you.
The Small Session for the Summer Retreat says: "The Great Monastery of Non-characteristic Dwellings—do not inquire about the three before or the three after. Within this,"

A single thought may arise; dragons, snakes, monkeys, and birds intermingle of their own accord. If one proceeds in this manner, dragons and snakes are mixed together, ordinary beings and sages dwell side by side.

Amidst the myriad phenomena of the forested universe, there is immediate solitude and peril. Where the phoenixes and qilin call out to one another in resonance, the entire Dharma-realm is my monastery.
This very body of mine has no place of attachment; the atoms of all lands are my companions on the Path.
I seek a person to sweep the ground, yet there is none. One sees only the Lingxi stream flowing steadily, merging its current with the four seas;
the snow-capped peaks stand towering and jagged, breaking through the gates to enter alongside the ten billion Mount Sumerus. At Baoyu Peak, one turns a hand to create clouds.
Turning his palm downward, he brought forth rain. The Stone that Pierces Heaven arrives in the Western Heavens in the morning and returns to the land of Tang by evening.

If one understands clearly this principle, Śākyamuni never appeared in the world and Bodhidharma never came from the West; the Buddha-dharma pervades all under heaven, yet those who discuss the profound do not open their mouths.
Great assembly: Since Śākyamuni did not appear in the world, what did Mahākāśyapa see when he broke into a smile? And as for Bodhidharma...
Since he did not come from the West, what did the Second Patriarch see when he cut off his arm to find peace of mind?
If you can say it, I shall dwell in peace with you upon the tip of a single hair. If you have not yet realized this, I, this mountain monk, shall speak for all of you.
He held up his whisk and said: "The Elder Śākyamuni, Master Bodhidharma, and Layman Pang the Old—all reside together upon the tip of this whisk.
One person says: 'The ten directions gather together; each and every one studies non-action. This is the field for selecting Buddhas;
with an empty mind, they return as top graduates. Another person says: 'Externally, cease all conditions; internally, let the heart have no gasping. The mind is like..."

A wall or a fence can serve as an entrance to the Way. One person’s Way is to take Great Perfect Enlightenment as one’s own monastery (*gālaya*), dwelling in peace within body and mind with the wisdom of equanimity.
When three people act for the sake of the community, disaster arises from private interests. Under the gate of Ling Shi, if you let it pass, you have failed.
[The Master] strikes the meditation seat and says: "Where have the thousand sages gone? A long sword leaning against heaven presses down."
People are cold.
If Śākyamuni had not appeared in the world, how many listeners could there have been among his forty-nine years of teaching?

If Bodhidharma had not come from the West, how many people could there have been who saw the wondrous secret at Shaolin? O men of keen intelligence: when the patterns and colors have not yet manifested—
Prior to this, it was already seen through and broken open—purely naked, vividly bright, lively and agile, firm and unyielding.
At such a time, there were no Buddhas above to look up to and no sentient beings below to deliver. A single path of divine light pierced the side of the Dipper;
a piercing, clear wind stirred the universe. Then, at Vulture Peak, when the flower was held up, Kāśyapa broke into a smile.
They then claim that the Tathāgata had something transmitted and Kāśyapa had something bestowed.
They say that because the First Patriarch faced the wall at Shaolin and the Second Patriarch "settled his mind," Bodhidharma had something transmitted and the Second Patriarch had something bestowed.
Thus they regard the twenty-eight patriarchs of India as nothing but mediocre fellows, and the six patriarchs of the Tang land as people with thick skins. As for the old monks throughout the world...
These are the mere transmitters of words and messengers of speech—hirelings! What is this "Nirvana’s wondrous mind" and "the treasury of the true Dharma-eye"? It is like a broken bowl;
"pointing directly to the human mind to see one's nature and become a Buddha" has deceived an entire shipload of people.

You must utterly exhaust the functioning of the present moment before you and vomit out the contents of your chest. Upon the crown of every person’s head, the bright sun hangs in the sky; every single one stands with feet firmly planted.

Follow along. A pure breeze sweeps across the earth. Not constrained by the patterns of Buddhas and Patriarchs, nor bound by the old nests of monks, it flows forth from within the breast, covering the earth and the heavens. Picked up with a casual hand, it strikes down wind and rain.
To go about in this very manner—then you have immeasurable transgressions, and I too have immeasurable transgressions.
The donor invites [the master], saying: "In the teachings it is said that the Way is profound, firm, remote, and deep, such that no one can reach it;

it is also said that the mark of the cessation of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words. Regarding these two turns of phrase, if you swallow them whole, I dare say you, elder brother, have not yet reached the end.
If you distinguish between black and white, you will make the mouths of the patch-robed monks laugh. Therefore, when Sudhana arrived at this point...
On the summit of Mount Miaofeng, for seven days he did not see the Bhikṣu Dechen.
When the Bodhisattva Puyan arrived at this place, he surveyed all the lands within atoms, yet did not see Samantabhadra. When Deshan arrived at this place, he said:
"The pond is not seen, and the dragon does not appear. When Jia Shan arrived at this place, he said: "Before my eyes there is no Acharya; here there is no one."
This old monk—having arrived here, I cannot help but utter a word where neither Buddhas nor Patriarchs have reached.
Upon the crown of the head, a thousand suns shine together; taking one step further where Buddhas and Patriarchs have not traveled, beneath the feet, ten thousand mirrors face the dais.
Unless one directly accepts this, one will never understand the vast emptiness of the universal path. Pick up a single mote of dust and scatter it...
Facing toward the trichiliocosm, he speaks of lands and speaks of atoms, speaking with blazing intensity without interruption.
He intends to take this trichiliocosm and contain it within a single atom. Thus, one directly attains the emptiness of persons and the emptiness of phenomena;
there is neither one who can speak nor anyone who listens. When both speaking and listening are forgotten, heaven and earth are revealed in their solitary nakedness. This is precisely [the state].
At that moment, tell me: have they arrived or not? Have they spoken or not? If you can clarify this point, the assembly on Vulture Peak will be seen as vividly present as ever.
Recall one day when Linji was walking through the monks' hall with an official;
the official asked, "Do the monks in this hall study the sutras? The monk replied, "They do not study the sutras. The official asked, "Then do they practice Chan?"
Linji said, "I do not practice Chan. The Official asked, "Ultimately, what then? Linji said, "I simply teach everyone to become Buddhas and Patriarchs.
The Official said, "Though gold dust is precious, when it falls into the eye, it becomes a cataract. Linji said, "I took you for a mere worldly man. The Master said:
"Linji saw only the sharpness of the chisel's tip, but did not see the squareness of the chisel's handle. Today, I [shall provide]..."
An official visited the monks' hall and asked, "Do the monks in this hall study the sutras? The monk replied, "They do.
The official said, "Since they are Zen monks, why are they studying the sutras? The monk simply told him: "All that is sought is answered; no wish goes unfulfilled. [The official asked:
"How do you explain the principle of such an answer? [The monk replied: "The wondrous flowers of Bodhi universally adorn all things, following..."
"The place where one dwells is always peaceful and blissful.
Master Gaoxiang said in his general discourse:
"I humbly acknowledge that you all have come seeking [instruction] regarding your own affairs. If we discuss the affairs of each person themselves, they are like a great fire."
A mass of fire. To draw near it is to lose one's eyebrows and hair; it is like a drum smeared with poison—upon hearing its sound, one’s entire lineage perishes.
Reaching this point, the Buddhas of the three periods of time cannot approach it, and the Patriarchs of the six generations have no way to retreat.
Up until the present day, not a single person has ever struck it directly. To speak of it would silence your mouth and shave you bald.
It is your own tongue. Therefore it is said: "If you wish to correctly grasp the guiding principle, you must simply let the great earth fall into ruin.
Should you attempt to charge against the snow-blade, you cannot avoid exposing its sharp edge. If you can see through in this very way, often there will not even be a person to sweep the ground.
"Elder Xu, today you must stretch out a hand; let us all roll together in the wild weeds.
You people must also quicken your eyes before it will do. [He raises his whisk and says: Look, look! Do you see the person themselves?
If you can comprehend this directly, it is much like mistaking a donkey’s saddle bridge for one’s father’s chin."
If you do not see it go, then even your avoidance of it becomes a point of contention. Now, having simultaneously cast aside both seeing and not seeing, one’s own true self has no place to rest.
With nowhere to rest, cease your searching. The eyes are like drumsticks; the head is like a wooden ladle.
Wandering freely throughout the world, let the matter be as you judge it. At times, though one searches all day long, it cannot be found; at other times, it is everywhere.

It can be expressed through the mouth; yet, how much difference is there between hitting the mark and missing it? A majestic qilin has but a single horn. Clearly, clearly! Attained, attained, attained!
Let there be ten thousand distinctions and a thousand differences—clearly, it is only this thief. Alas for people of past and present: how many recognize this debt of gratitude?
Even if one were to take the words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs from of old, with their interlocking patterns and sharp points, turning like jade...
The pearl turns. It is the sword that kills and the blade that gives life. Riding the tiger’s head and gathering its tail; upward and downward, this side and that side;
bodhi and nirvana, true suchness and liberation—all these are but the casting of hooks and the setting of snares.
None of them concern your own fundamental matter. Look! When Deshan arrived at Longtan, he immediately said, "I have long heard of Longtan; now that I have come here—"
The pool was not to be seen, nor did the dragon appear. This old man of the Dragon Pool has years but no virtue;
he simply says, "You have come personally to the Dragon Pool," which is like a servant showing courtesy to a maidservant. One day, the Buddha was preaching the Dharma atop the peak of Laṅkā.
Those without supernormal powers were unable to reach him. A yakṣa arrived and listened to the Dharma, offering various musical instruments and various foods and drinks.
In a mere moment, he no longer saw the World-Honored One, nor did he see the various musical instruments, foods, or drinks.
I turned my head and took a look; I did not see even my own body. What a pity that he let this matter pass!

At that time, had I waited for him to say, "I do not see my own body," I would have given him a shout. This would have not only set his head straight and his tail straight, but also corrected him entirely.
To avoid seeing death midway. An ancient also said: "Contemplating form as emptiness, one achieves great wisdom and does not dwell in birth-and-death;
contemplating emptiness as form, one achieves great compassion and does not realize nirvana. Since one neither dwells in birth-and-death nor realizes nirvana, tell me:
where, ultimately, is such a person placed? [He] lets out a shout and says: "A thousand!"
"Of ten thousand words, none understand; yet it follows the warbling oriole over the low wall.
These are the words of Chan Master Bie-feng Zhen. While serving as the Head Seat (Shouzuo) in the Abbot’s quarters, he received an invitation from Gushan.
Holding up the formal notice, he said: "The green felt mat originally belonged to our own house; for daily use, what [else is needed]?"
There has never been a deficiency. To truly understand the internal regulations of the monastic rules, one must be a gentleman; such a person may indeed attain the eighth stage.

When the Buddha transmitted the Dharma robe, the Master received it and addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma is not transmitted without the robe, and the robe is not conferred without the Dharma.
Now that the robe has been conferred, how is the Dharma to be transmitted? It is like a clear, eight-sided jewel naturally closing together, its steep and lofty peaks forming a single unity."
Who would dare to peer into it?
Pointing to the Dharma seat, he said: "It is high and without superior, beyond limit; it is deep and without bottom, beyond measure.
If you wish to know how every step penetrates the double barrier, look at the pure breeze arising from both armpits."
Ascending the seat, he said: "I am ashamed of my own incompetence and lack of ability; I am but a monk who walks the long path, subsisting on gruel and rice.
Yet, how could I have expected such fortunate circumstances? How shall I bear this burden of a thousand catties? He continued: "The scriptures say:
'I originally had no mind to seek anything, yet now this treasury has arrived of its own accord. To speak in such a manner is very much like a poor man seeing—"
A small profit. Nevertheless, though it be so, I dare ask the great assembly: having set aside the great mountain-stand before the door, where is the treasure-store?
He plants his staff and says: "Vast and boundless is the universe, with countless people; yet alone the barbarian monk smiles and nods his head."
Pointing to the abbot’s quarters, he said: "The Master’s chamber, standing beyond all dependence, is something that those from all quarters cannot fathom. Today it is entrusted to this humble monk;
taking my bedding, I shall enter from this moment on. Will you all accept this? Transcending all, I sit and cut off [all traces] at the very crown of Vairocana."
"A thousand sages teach in unison, yet you stand with your back to the wind. He gave a shout and entered the hall.
That evening, he gave a small *can* (sermon), citing National Teacher Xingxing, who said to the assembly: "Under the gate of Gushan, one must not cough."
At that time, there was a monk who coughed once. The National Teacher said, "What are you doing? The monk said, "I have contracted a cold. The National Teacher said, "A cold is fine.
The Master [Linji] said, "Great National Teacher, you see what is right and yet do not act upon it; what bravery is there in that?"
New Elder, had you seen this monk coughing at that time, you should have asked him what he was doing.
When he replied, "I have a fever," you should have struck him across the spine immediately. Why? Because unless the medicine causes dizziness and distress, the grievous illness will not be cured.
The opening of the hall. A monk asked, "What was it like before the Master had seen the Buddha-mind?

The Master said, "The auspicious qilin has but a single horn. The monk pressed further, "And what was it like after seeing it? The Master said, "The vermilion phoenix indeed possesses nine-fold plumage.
The monk asked, "I do not know whether this is one or two. The Master said, "If you are not Ren Gongzi, your labor over speaking of the fishing rod is in vain. The Master then [continued]:
It is said: "The appearance of the Buddhas in the world is for the sake of one great cause and condition. To point is not to arrive;

the Patriarch came from the West to point directly to the human mind, so that by seeing one's nature one becomes a Buddha. To arrive is not to point. Through the generations, the ancestral masters have wielded staffs like falling rain and roared like crashing thunder.
One person may transmit what is empty, yet ten thousand people transmit it as real. The venerable elders throughout the land raise the banner of the Dharma and establish the school.
The essential point is this: when the ancestors failed to understand, the calamity reached their descendants. Today, the new Elder has already extended what was contracted;
he shall thoroughly sweep away all those idle gates and broken doors that have existed since time immemorial.
As for the infinite dharma-gates of liberation, the treasury of spiritual powers and radiant light that each of you yourselves possesses—[the Master] strikes once with his staff and says: "Today!"

At once it is opened wide. Those who have not heard shall hear; those who have not seen shall see. Should one suddenly attain such insight through hearing and seeing, one will surely find heaven and earth revealed in their entirety.
This is sufficient to repay the unrequitable debt of gratitude and to assist in the transformation of non-action.
After the cremation of the Buddha’s heart, he addressed the great assembly, saying: "A monk once asked Changsha, 'Where has Nanquan gone after his passing?
Changsha replied, 'When Shitou was a novice monk, he studied under the Sixth Patriarch. Great assembly, if you see where the ancients went, you will know where people of today fall.
As for this single phrase, 'The past and present are not obscured'—how shall it be handled?"
"How is it? "The human face is unknown where it has gone; The peach blossoms still smile at the spring breeze. Ascending the hall, he said:
"In the second month, spring is already half-way spent; the peach blossoms bloom in profusion. Amidst this flurry, the seekers of the sword—whom among them is the man free from doubt?
Is there anyone here who is without doubt? If there is, call him forward and let him wash the mountain monk’s feet."
The donor requests: "A hundred years of life pass like a split arrow; impermanence and birth-and-death shift and change daily.
Only Mahāprajñāpāramitā shines through antiquity and rises to the present, without front or back. Whether seen or unseen, when the bowl is dashed to the ground—"

The lacquer tray has been broken into eight pieces; seeing it thus, one transcends the three realms, walks alone in the great square, cuts off the stream of birth and death, and reaches the shore of nirvana. Holding up a whisk, he asks: "Do you see this person?
His entire body manifests eighteen transformations upon the tip of the whisk, such that water flows from his upper body and fire issues from his lower body, for all to see.
Without realizing it and without knowing it, he has departed for the Immaculate World in the south to become a Buddha. Now tell me: what serves as the proof?
After a long silence, he said: "The land trembles to welcome Śākyamuni; precious flowers fill the air to escort Avalokiteśvara."
A Prayer for Rain. A monk asked Xinghua, "What is it like when there is not a single fleck of cloud ten thousand miles away?
Xinghua said, "Even the blue sky must receive a blow of the staff. Gushan said, "It is not so. What is it like when there is not a single fleck of cloud ten thousand miles away?
He raised his staff and said, "The Black Dragon King is coming! "Tell me, after he has arrived, what then? He struck the ground with the staff and said, "Watch out! You might get soaked!"
Your nostrils: before the fifteenth day, you hide your body where there are no traces; after the fifteenth day, do not hide your body where there are no traces.
On the fifteenth day itself, the mouth of the cloth bag is opened and your entire being is revealed. But how about this?
Not pitying the goose that guards the snow, and rejoicing in the waxen man in the ice.
Retiring from Gushan, he said: "Years of chasing after the dust of the world, I have won only a reputation for idleness that burdens this body.
How can this compare to the summit of another peak, Where I lie high in a single hut, a neighbor to the clouds?"
When Suireng received Yue-lin, he took leave of the assembly, saying: "Only when I follow you through the crags and valleys shall I find peace.
Again, carrying my flask and staff, I respond to the conditions of the times; Fengchuan is not far from here. If inspiration arises, what prevents me from visiting Dai on his boat?
An ancient said: "What others call 'staying,' I say is 'leaving'; what others call 'leaving,' I say is 'staying. To leave.

Though their dwellings differ, their ultimate aim is one. To speak in such a manner is very much like lashing a boat to a stake while rowing, or casting off the mooring ropes while the boat is still at anchor.
Yet, how can one say it without falling into the extremes of "leaving" or "staying"? How would you say it? "The green mountains cannot hide it; the bright moon, however, allows it."
The Master entered the hall and said: "Decrepit and old, I am incapable of anything; I carry my head into the bustling basket.
What remains of my life? Maitreya shares the same shrine. The Patriarch of this mountain said: "Maitreya is truly Maitreya;

he manifests in thousands of millions of bodies, constantly appearing to people of the age, yet people do not recognize him. The Master said: "Son of Changting, why do you act so foolishly? Right now—"
"A new elder has arrived! You must step back; you must allow him to establish his own ground before you can succeed.
The Great Way is right before one's eyes, yet for the moment it is difficult to behold. If you wish to know the true essence of the Great Way, it is not apart from sound, form, and speech.
He struck the meditation staff on the ground and said, "This is sound. Then he held it upright and said, "This is form."
What do you call the Great Way? Even if you were to see it right here, it would still be like leaving Zhengzhou to go out through Cao Gate.
To seek the ox, one must follow its tracks; to study the Way, one must seek the mindless state. When the tracks remain, the ox is still there; when the mind is absent, the Way is easy to find.
He held up his whisk and said: "This is the track; where is the ox? Even if you can see its horns and head clearly, what can you do?
Its nostrils are still in the hands of Yuelin."
Transcending the four propositions and severing the hundred negations—who is this whose head is three feet long? Ask the Old Man Wang whether it is north of the river or south of the river;
one doubt resolved, another doubt resolved.
The Buddha is not far from people; he realizes it within the very mind. The Dharma is without attachment; all encountered objects are thus. Holding up his staff, he said:
"If you call this a staff, you are still attached to phenomena. When none of this applies, he said: "A blind donkey chasing the great herd. After all, how is it?
He then leaned the staff against [the wall] and said: "Seeking cleverness results in clumsiness."
While presiding at the Dharma Stone Hall, he said: "The one path that leads upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages. He struck the meditation staff and said:

"If you can understand it in this way, you have traversed eighty thousand miles. But in the end, what is it? The peach is red, the plum is white, and the rose is purple; yet when asked about the spring breeze, none of them know."
Spring has already departed; summer is now at hand. When meeting others, do not speak of the original mind. At Haishan Temple, we partake of rice and gruel according to circumstances;
let us simply listen as the grass before the hall grows ever deeper.
The quiescent mark of all dharmas cannot be proclaimed in words. Thus, when a monk asked Fengxue, "Speech and silence both involve transcendence and subtlety;
how can one pass through them without transgression? Fengxue replied, "I always remember the third month in Jiangnan, where the *shàgū* cries and the hundred flowers are fragrant.
Which of these is the proclamation in words? Which is the quiescent mark? [Fengxue] struck his staff and said, "There is no need to lower it."
Head. Difficult to fathom through deliberation.
The donor examines the Tripitaka and says: "Manifesting emergence and manifesting entry, it pierces through the skull; the entire canon and the partial canon exchange the eyes.
The yellow base is not paper; the black base is not ink. The blue-eyed barbarian monk cannot discern it, for it does not constitute written characters."
The eight characters are not it. Those of the hundred-seam Zen school are not sharp and clever. If they were sharp and clever, they would lift their robes and go immediately;
they would give a high bow to Śākyamuni and not prostrate before Maitreya. They would call Bodhisattvas "slaves" and call Śrāvakas "maidservants.

He lets out a shout and gives a clap, then descends from the seat.
In the way of the ancients, there were countless dead people upon the pure ground; those who could pass through the thorn-brake were considered masters of the craft.

Whether speaking of the thirty days of the long month or the twenty-nine days of the short month, whether the ground is rich with large eggplants or one’s legs are thin while the straw sandals are loose, whether seeking warmth by the fire in the cold or seeking coolness in the heat—one is precisely a dead person upon the pure ground. If you use a probing staff...
Shadow-grass. Concealing the point within the sleeve; shifting the step and moving the body. Host and guest both illuminated.
Churning the long river into butter and milk; transforming the great earth into gold. Yet, one has still not passed through the thicket of thorns.
Tell me, how can you meet Wuping? After a long silence, he said: "Fine jade is not confused by sand and grit; to recognize true gold, one must use fire."
Looking inside: one contains three; three contain one. From immeasurable kalpas until this very day—what, then, is the matter of today?
After a long silence, he said: "The willows are deep in mist as the hundred-tongued bird cries; the feet of the foreign monk crossing the water are wet."
"The Wheel of Dharma was turned three times throughout the great universe; that wheel is fundamentally and eternally pure. I venture to ask all of you:
how would you describe this turning of the Wheel of Dharma? After a long silence, he said: "In the morning there is congee; at noon one eats;
after nightfall, one stretches out both legs and sleeps."
Clouds and mist shroud ten thousand ravines; snow blankets a thousand peaks. The mouth wishes to speak, yet the teeth shiver with cold;

the eyes wish to see, yet the pupils are blurred by glare. Arriving at this point, tell me: by what means do you establish yourself? After a long silence, he said: "O Zen guests by the earthen hearth, do not complain of the cold;
there are still heroes lying beneath their iron armor."
Two do not form a pair; one does not form a single unit. His appearance is like that of an infant, yet his voice is like a thunderclap.

Entering the water, he does not stir the waves; piercing through mountains, he does not move a stone. Flowing on and on, he is ever before the Five Peaks. Do you, O clear-eyed monk, recognize him or not?
He struck the meditation seat, gave a shout, and descended from the seat.
That which can be seen is seen as nothing; that which can be heard is heard as nothing. When there is no hearing, sounds are most vast;
when there is no seeing, forms are most expansive. Since sounds and forms are thus expansive and vast, then seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing are non-existent.
The boundaries are limitless. Nevertheless, why is this so? The Buddhas of the three periods of time turn the Great Dharma Wheel within a single speck of dust;
at every household door, the path leads straight through to Chang’an.
Shattering the void, shouting away the wind and rain; neither in hell nor in heaven is there a place of attachment. Amidst the shadows of floating bubbles, one passes through the years at will;
within the flash of a stone struck by lightning, one debates dwelling for kalpas.
The mud ox roars on the snowy peaks; the wooden horse neighs at Yunmen. Beyond these alone, all things are but false.
Stillness is the sovereign of agitation; agitation is the minister of stillness. When sovereign and minister accord with the Way, agitation and stillness are simultaneously true.
The spring breeze blows through the gardens, Resounding clearly with beautiful sounds. If one does not transcend what is seen and heard, One fails the compassionate heart of the old woman.
A Verse in Response to Chen Chaoqing of Shaoyang, Sent with Tea from Xie Lingquan.
The Elder Chan Master, former Governor of Shaoyang, forgets all conditions throughout the day, sharing my own state of mind. The living beings across a thousand li are his oceanic assembly;

the lutes and pipes within the city are his family tradition. Through the dispatching of official documents he conveys news; through the use of shackles and staffs he clearly demonstrates suffering and emptiness.
Looking back at my single bowl and single staff, I am instead ashamed that he lies high amidst the white clouds.
A single cake of tea takes precedence over the spring; once ground, it is brewed with snow-water. All day long its fragrant aroma lingers upon the teeth;
by the incense burner, unmoving, one beholds the spirit-spring.

Seeing off a Monk on a Journey to the Imperial Capital Seeing off my junior disciple, his nature and temperament are liberated by the spring breeze. A solitary wild goose drifts afar, brushing against the azure heavens. After our parting, the sound of the mountain spring remains ever-present;
leaning upon my cane staff, I still listen to it.
The myriad nations turn their hearts toward you as one family; in an ordinary step, you arrive at the capital.
Next year, when the cuckoo’s call is sweet, you will surely remember the jade pestle flowers of the mountains.

Treading upon stones, I contemplate their loftiness; facing the flowing stream, I reflect upon its clarity. Gazing at the moon, I study its brilliance; observing the pine tree, I emulate its firmness.
These four things may all serve as teachers; whether walking or sitting, they follow me like a shadow. Do not forget my words; recite them once every morning and evening.
Entrusted to the Secretariat Librarian of Tang Seeing Elder Ming Return to Guankxi A bamboo chair and a rush mat lean against a stone screen; Beyond the stream, the new moon shines through the mist.
Ever since Master Tao left the mountains, The solitary monkey’s cry has been silent for several nights.
Pines and cypresses cast overlapping shadows as the path winds and turns; piercing the clouds on his way home, the sound of his mendicant’s staff is cold.
Night after night, one beholds the mountain moon in the human world, yet it is not like gazing upon it from atop the rocks by the stream.
From the Studio of Silence:
Three or four stalks of slender bamboo in the mountains, A couple of strange rocks— There is an old white-headed monk Who comes from time to time to sit facing me.
A single pool of autumn water drenches the moss; when the night is still, the moon enters from elsewhere. The water, too, has no intention to swallow the moonlight;
cold radiance and chilly azure linger together.

The cowherd boy sings as the lush green grass follows the cattle grazing; atop his ox, he lies across and blows a short flute. From within the flute comes a single melody of the Plucking the Plum Blossoms tune.
It requires no power from the spring breeze at all. Amidst the misty rain, he enters a deep ravine; layer upon layer of peaks do not obstruct his coming.
On the road at that time, purple ferns grew fat upon the stones where fists were clenched; within the leaves, the secluded birds sang their soft melodies.

Suddenly singing, suddenly dancing—though one might encounter a true connoisseur, they would not grant their approval. Riding the ox back home under the bright moonlight, the *zhuzhi* bamboo flute struck down the words before the sound itself.
The Words of Master Hujiu Long (Huanglong Xiyun), Disciple of Yuanwu. Ascending the hall, he said:
"The doors and windows are flung wide open; ten thousand miles away, not a single speck of cloud hangs. The bright sun soars into the sky; looking around, a pure breeze fills the assembly."
The lake’s light is vast and boundless; the wild scenery is clear and bright. The myriad phenomena are arrayed in their fullness, fully manifesting the ocean-seal.
Thus, every single point is a wondrous function, and every single thing is a true mechanism. Mind and environment are as one; not even a speck of dust can be established.

At this very moment, when all is thus, the ten thousand functions cease, and the thousand sages carry nothing with them. One sits firmly atop the crown of Vairocana, receiving no instructions from Śākyamuni, and regards sounds as mere maidservants.

Upon hearing this, the slaves cried out to the Bodhisattvas; Deshan and Linji were left staring with mouths agape. Where there are staffs and shouts, not even a single drop is of any use. But tell me:
should one suddenly encounter a person of such caliber, how would you speak of it? Meeting under a spreading canopy, we are as old friends as ever;
why should it hinder us from coming to drink Zhaozhou’s tea?
"Vast and distant are the affairs of the world, floating and sinking in vain. I cherish the white clouds for myself as the years deepen. Looking up, everything is no longer ordinary grass or trees;
I have resolutely severed my arm to seek peace of mind. Although it is thus, matters are not always one-sided. [The Master] picks up his staff and says:
Bodhidharma has arrived; he is upon the staff of this mountain monk, preaching the Dharma-gate of settling the mind for all of you.

Can you believe it? If you can believe it, then at that very moment your mind will be at peace. If not, the ocean may dry up and its bottom be seen, yet when a person dies, they do not know their own mind.
The Emperor’s decree within the realm; the General’s command beyond the frontier. With a single phrase, heaven and earth are settled; with a single sword, the world is brought to peace.
Thus one sees the times prosperous and the Way flourishing, the four seas tranquil and clear. Yet, under the gate of this patch-robed monk, it is not so.
"The staff has swallowed up heaven and earth; it is continuous without leaking so much as a hair’s breadth.

Where else could there be a single thing to serve as a condition or a counterpart for all people? Do you understand? After a long silence, he said, "Each of you, please return to the hall and drink some tea."
The ox-head sinks; the horse-head turns back. He has no land; the true person of no station is difficult to discern when suddenly appearing.
Where do you encounter him? Like the spark struck from stone or a flash of lightning—whether you attain it or not, you cannot avoid losing your body and life.
For now, as for this phrase of calm wind and still waves, how would you speak? After Sudhana’s departure, who recognizes him? The gates of the pavilion stand wide open.

During the day, do not violate the command. Clarify the wind and moon of antiquity and the present; the numinous mechanism constantly shines alone, and the myriad phenomena are all transparent and clear.
What more need be said of the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye? It has been extinguished within the blind donkey. Within the absence of calculation, one instead falls into calculation. There is none.
In the midst of a path, it turns back into a path; at once, I cut it off for you. The scale-weight is as hard as iron. Part by part.
In the autumn of the eighth month, where is there heat?
A drop of water, a drop of ice. Swallowing it, wind and thunder manifest the Great Function. A blow from the staff points out the eyes; once illuminated, all forms are seen as utterly void.
Stepping out the door, one bumps into Subhūti; pressed against the void, the whole body is revealed.
A single mass of clouds gathers, cutting off all conceptual thought; ten thousand miles of clear light, the jade hare soars forth.
Light does not illuminate the object, nor does the object exist; when both light and object are forgotten, what is it that remains?

Let us set aside for now the phrase, “The hundred grasses’ tips have laid down their weapons. Suppose, suddenly, one were to ride a great statue of the Buddha from Jiazhou while mounted upon an iron ox from Xianfu;
with a single blow, one would shatter Mount Sumeru into a hundred fragments. Then, one might gallop a horse through the land of Silla and preach Chan in Jambudvīpa. Furthermore, how would you act?
"How is it? On Mount Wutai, clouds steam rice; before the steps of the Buddha Hall, it is a "dog-urine day.
Whenever there is anything displayed or entrusted, it all falls into the present moment. To neither display nor entrust is to fall into pits and ditches.
Even if one were such that the wind cannot enter and water cannot wet, if one examines this closely, one still cannot save oneself. Have you not seen it said: "It is as if..."
The moon’s reflection in a cold pond; the sound of a bell in a still night. It remains unimpaired by striking and does not scatter when touched by waves.

Yet, this is still merely a matter on the shore of birth and death. [The Master] picks up his staff, makes a stroke in the air, and says: "With this stroke, I sever the many years of entanglements of Dharma Master Sheng.
The Nodding Stone, unable to help himself, claps his hands and laughs loudly. But tell me, what is he laughing at? [He points to] the back of his head.
Seeing his cheekbones, do not associate with him.

Even if the entire nation of Shaolin were to try, they could not restrain the Dharma Master as he departed. Carrying his single sandal westward, he returned home; it must have been the moon over Mount Xiong that cast its cold radiance for a thousand ages.
The Words of Master Ying’an Hua: “Succeeding Tiger Hill, he ascended the hall and said:
‘Nine years facing the wall ruined the descendants of this land; returning to the West with a single shoe left the Old Man of Yellow Face frustrated.’”
[The Master] held up his staff, drew a line, and said: "A stone ox blocks the ancient road; one horse gives birth to three tigers.
Huangbo is a meddling old woman; Dayu is a garrulous chatterer. There is not much to this Buddha-dharma; the orthodox eye is extinguished by a blind donkey.
Suddenly, he seized the staff and said: "Miaoyan suddenly thrusts out the staff; the three men take a tortoise and certify it as a turtle. He then struck once with the staff.
The staff is skilled at discernment; stand firm with your backbone. Do not let it leak away.
Guanyin Bodhisattva buys a sesame cake with money, but when he lets it go, it turns out to be a piece of raw iron. [He] throws down the staff and descends from his seat.
When Master Xuetang Xing arrived, he said: "Linji received three painful blows of the staff and realized his homecoming on the banks of the Gaoyuan Rapids;
Xinghua, under the staff of Dajue, deeply clarified the essential tenets of Huangbo. Although there are not many brothers here in the mountains," [he continued].
Each and every one of us has a disease deep within the vital organs; had it not been for the arrival of you, Master Shishu, Mingguo would not have dared to rashly convey this news.

In a short while, we shall descend from our seats and, together with the various administrators, heads, and the assembly, we shall prostrate ourselves to invite you. We humbly beseech you to look upon us with compassion.
He compassionately administers the medicine:
before the fifteenth day, the water rises and the boat ascends; after the fifteenth day, the mud thickens and the Buddha grows large.
On the very fifteenth day, an East Sea carp receives a single blow of the staff, and the rain pours down like an overturned basin, such that the entire trichiliocosm is filled.
All sentient beings rejoiced and praised him, saying, "To strike this one blow was truly timely and appropriate;
to repay his kindness, he did not even realize his whole body leaped with joy. He then composed a verse and presented it to the great assembly:
"The dragonfly is indeed a fine dragonfly, Flying here and there without ever stopping. Having caught it and plucked away both wings, It is now simply a..."
[He] drove in a large iron nail.

Master Daguang raised up the words of Zen Master Danyuan Zhi, saying: "When everyone gathers together to eat a stalk of vegetable soup, if you call it 'a stalk of vegetable soup,' you will enter hell as fast as a shooting arrow.
The Master said: "Danyuan’s words are excellent, yet they have no point of origin. If one can discern them—"
[He] attained it. [The master] gave him one *liang* of gold.
One day, as recorded in the *Deshan Record*, a monk just looked at him and immediately stepped forward, assuming a wrestling stance. Deshan said, "You are so impolite;
you deserve a blow from this old monk's staff. The monk brushed his sleeves and went out. Deshan said, "Even if you were granted..."
"In this way, you have only attained half. The monk then gave a shout. Shanshan struck him, saying, "It must be I who strike you before it is truly so.
The monk said, "There are those with clear eyes in all quarters. Shanshan said, "You naturally possess eyes. The monk opened his eyes wide with his hands and said, "A cat!
Shanshan said, "The Yellow River clears itself only once every three thousand years. The Master said, "This monk is..."
For one who has passed through the barrier, had it not been for Deshan’s fundamental tongs and hammer, they would have nearly died beneath the words.
As for Deshan saying, "The Yellow River clears once every three thousand years"—how is this so? It is like the岭梅 (lingmei) plum blossoms after the lingering snow.

When the cloud-like hair has not yet been combed, one wears fur and horns, dragging the tail and pulling the plow; one tills the forest of thorns, sows seeds in hell, and opens the flowers of the three poisons.
It binds the fruit of ignorance; therefore, all who see and hear give rise to evil thoughts.

When these evil thoughts arise, they fill the void of space, and within the very substance of that void, one realizes the body of a Māra-king. At such a moment as this, who is the giver? Who is the receiver?
If you can distinguish the black from the white within this state, I grant that you all have a way to manifest yourselves. If, however, you have not yet...
Nevertheless, tell me: are Buddha and Mara one or two? Regarding the meaning of "one" and "two," you all must not doze off.
Why is this so? Because the gods of the Thirty-three Heavens are rolling a breath-ball.

Students of the Way must strictly avoid misapplying their minds. To seek enlightenment and realize the nature is a misapplication of the mind; to become a Buddha or a patriarch is a misapplication of the mind;
to study the sutras and expound the teachings is a misapplication of the mind—even walking, standing, sitting, lying down, speaking, or entering samādhi.
This is a misuse of the mind. Eating porridge and eating rice; defecating and urinating—these are misuses of the mind.
Moving and stilling; coming and going—these are misuses of the mind. There is yet another place that is a misuse of the mind, which Guizong dares not reveal to you all.
Why? "Once a single character enters the gates of officialdom, even nine oxen cannot drag it out."
When Bodhidharma came from the West, he pointed directly at the human mind, asserting that by seeing one's nature one becomes a Buddha.
That old barbarian—if he had known back then there was a "turning-over-the-body" phrase—then all of you here would not have escaped with your corpses sprawled out and bones exposed.
Tell me, when Baolin makes such a proclamation, does he have any standing ground? Do not linger by the green herbs of the cold crags; do not sit within the realm of white clouds.
Not good. Entering the five viscera of the Arhat, it is said: "The yellow-faced old man is a dry dung-club; his attendants are a mass of fire-rotted mud.
His heart, liver, intestines, and stomach are all straight as arrows; his vegetarian meal and tea-flower chill the gall. Although the Buddha-dharma has not yet been dreamed of, [it is thus].
He was seen; his supernormal powers allowed him to enter the clouds. One must deeply lament for Guizong Temple; at times he would descend the verdant peaks carrying his alms bowl.
A monk asked Jingshan, "What is it like when the breath is stilled like ashes? Jingshan said, "It is still merely the effort of ordinary people."
The monk asked, "What about after the task is accomplished? Sanshan said, "The farmer tills the field but does not sow. The monk asked, "Ultimately, how is it?
Sanshan said, "When the grain is ripe, he does not go to the market. The Master said, "Fragrance sinks in the phoenix pavilion; the snow-nest is cold at night. A bright moon fills half the window."
A harmonious atmosphere pervades. At such a moment as this, tell me: does Guizong and Jingshan still have the opportunity to meet one another?
Setting aside for a moment the question of whether they see each other or not—consider simply this monk’s question to Jingshan:
"Do you possess the eye? If it be otherwise, then clouds conceal the seamless robe, and birds nest upon the sproutless branch.
Wanshan arrived and said: "The large is large; the small is small; the long is long; the short is short; the curved is curved; the straight is straight;
the square is square; the round is round; the correct is correct; the deviant is deviant. Is this a Buddha? Is it a Bodhisattva?
Is it an Arhat? Is it a Holy Monk? Is it a ghost or spirit? Is it a celestial being or an immortal? I—
In the past, I heard this Dharma, yet I have never recklessly proclaimed it. To say "this is the meaning" or "this is not the meaning" is to fall into following the meaning.

To say "it is neither right nor wrong, nor is it neither right nor wrong" is to fall into following the phrasing. If one engages in such deliberations regarding the Buddha-Dharma, the single school of Bodhidharma will be swept away like dust.
If one does not engage in such deliberations regarding the Buddha-Dharma, this old monk will remain alive even while trapped in hell. As for you all—will you still wear the black robes?

Do you truly understand? If not, shortly after I descend from the seat, together with the administrative officers and heads of the community, we shall invite the new Abbot of Wanshan to explain it all for the sake of the assembly.
Baizhang raised this case and said to the assembly, "When you have finished clearing the fields, I will explain the Great Meaning to you.
A monk said, "The fields are cleared; I request the Master to explain the Great Meaning," and he spread his two hands wide.
Master Baiyun Yuan commented, "Baizhang’s explanation of the Great Meaning was just like this. As for those who went back to Mazu at that time, where did they go? If...
To say there is more would be no different from drawing legs on a snake. But tell me, how can one know the place where the old man Baizhang stands?
He then said: "When guests arrive, there is no tea or refreshment; mugwort soup serves as the ritual offering. The Master said:
"Baoyun wishes to see the principle of Baizhang’s second visit to Mazu—this is truly laughable! One must laugh for thirty years!"
Furthermore, the Way says: "How can one know where Baizhang stood? To this, he also laughs for thirty years.
'When guests arrive, there is no tea; mugwort soup serves as the ritual. To this, he also laughs for thirty years. Three laughs thus make ninety years."
Is it because my critique of Baiyun was incomplete? Or is there some other principle?

You people—if you can examine this thoroughly, I shall hand over the staff of Guizong with both hands. If you have not yet attained this, how many times have you returned home drunk under the bright moon, led by the sound of pipes and songs into the painted hall?
Muzhou addressed the assembly, saying: "To tear it open is up to me; to fold it back together is also up to me.
A monk asked, "What is tearing it open? Muzhou replied: "Three times nine is twenty-seven. Bodhi and nirvana, true thusness and liberation."
"This very mind is Buddha. I have spoken thus for now; how would you respond? A monk said, "I do not speak in this way.
Zhou said, "The cup falls to the ground; the saucer breaks into seven pieces. Yunfeng Yue said, "If you scold me, I’ll let you stick out your tongue;
if you spit at me, I’ll let you splash water. The Master said, "Let me ask you all: Yunfeng acted in such a manner..."
What is this "Mò niántí"? Is it to grasp the meaning of Muzhou? Or is it to clarify Muzhou’s words?

Guizong said, "While walking, it does not hinder one from swinging one's arms. It is not Chan; it is not the Way; it is not the profound; it is not the subtle. I have stood for a long time. I humbly pray that you will take care of yourself.
Dana was once passing by a temple when he encountered a freezing cold snap. Inside the hall, he saw a wooden Buddha and took it up to burn as a fire.
The temple steward happened to see this and rebuked him, saying, "How can you burn my wooden Buddha? Dana brushed away the ashes with his staff and said: [The text ends here].
I burned the wooden Buddha to retrieve its relics (*śarīra*). The temple master said, "How can a wooden Buddha have relics?
Xuanxia replied, "Since there are no relics, please bring two more statues so we may burn them again. Thereafter, the temple master's eyebrows and beard fell out.

The Master said, "The various quarters of the school debate this, saying that the temple master suddenly gave rise to doubt and thus brought about this calamity. Others say it was because the temple master did not provide him with clothing when the weather was cold."
Danxia pointed his fire-tongs toward [the statue], causing the wooden Buddha to be burned away, whereupon its eyebrows and beard fell off.
Little did he know that the temple administrator had purchased iron and obtained gold—a truly magnificent stroke of fortune.
A monk asked Duofu, "What is Duofu’s grove of bamboo? Duofu said, "One stem, two stems, leaning. The monk said, "I do not understand.
Duofu said, "Three stems, four stems, bent. The Master (Linji) therefore composed a verse:
"One stem, two stems, leaning—its intent is as venomous as a snake. Three stems, four stems, bent—one will undoubtedly enter hell upon these words."
If you know it is not so, the mind attains the first rank in emptiness and returns home. It is laughable that the Old Man of Jiangshan has, for no reason, entered the weeds.

Upon returning from the military expedition, he ascends the hall; having pierced through iron walls and silver mountains, the bustling marketplace of red dust fully manifests the ancestral style of the Buddhas.
Passing through wine shops and tea houses, he brings forth the very core of the patch-robed monk. He coldly laughs at the cold ashes and withered wood of all other quarters.
Muzhou said, "I am sitting in a place where there is no soul and one must surely die. Miaoyan possesses a modicum of spiritual power;
for your sakes, I shall speak out. He struck his staff once and said, "For thirty years I have been riding a horse, yet I have instead been granted a prophecy by a blind donkey.
He struck it once more and descended from the seat.
Great man! You must fiercely shatter all former cleverness. Directly cut through like a nail being driven home.

Cast aside the devices of the Buddhas and Patriarchs; pull out the hitching stake for the donkey. Have you not seen how Muzhou was too intimate with people, pressing Yunmen until his feet were broken?
Since then, the descendants have failed to discern the essential point, instead making distinctions at the very place where the door should be pushed open. If...
If you practice Chan in such a manner, you will not find rest for as long as it takes for a donkey to grow horns. Wuyuan [Miaoyan] does not begrudge his eyebrows;
he brings it forth for you right at the head. He picks up his staff, hurls it down, and says: "The people of Jambudvīpa are always in Uttarakuru."
Bloody and festering amidst the thorns; flies on the back of a broken donkey. When Han Xin ascends the throne, the Buddha of Dongshan has no radiance.
This crew of fellows—three thousand in the morning, eight hundred in the evening—what fault is there in them?
But as for the copper sieve filled to the brim with oil—how will you all handle it? After a long silence, he said: "The large month has thirty days."
Day. A small month with twenty-nine days.
At the tips of the hundred grasses, the weapons of war are laid down; before the ten-thousand-fathom peaks, one plays freely and unrestrained. One sighs in secret for Old Lu.
Facing the wall with single-minded devotion, I did nothing but greedily indulge in sleep. Yet I laughed at Muzhou when he saw a monk carrying a bucket of water for him;
at such a moment, Linji’s shout like a rolling thunderstorm is set aside, and Deshan’s staff like a scattering of stars is likewise placed elsewhere.
Miaoyan has a living path for you all to walk together. Thus, he drew: [Image of a man carrying a bucket]
A single circle says: At the foot of the eastern mountain slope, on the left side—nine times nine.

Śākyamuni did not know it existed; he turned his face around, extended his hairy hand, grasped the vajra-hammer, shattered the old molds, and brought forth the True Person of No Rank. One by one, they face south and gaze at the Big Dipper.
The mountains, rivers, and great earth; the grasses, trees, and forests—all are the number of thousands of Buddhas throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Even if you can believe this, it is much like swinging a staff to strike at the moon: buying at a high price in the east and selling at a low price in the west.
Thirty years from now, where will you put your worn-out straw sandals? You lacquer bucket! Go to the hall for practice.

At the commencement of the summer retreat, he took up his staff and held it crosswise, saying: "I, the mountain-dwelling monk [Name], relying upon the Bodhisattva vehicle, cultivate the practice of quiescence.
Together we enter the maintenance of the pure, true mark (*dharmatā*). Taking Great Perfect Enlightenment as my monastery, I dwell in peace within body and mind through the wisdom of equality.
Two thousand years ago, this old monk was together with the twelve great beings in the Radiance."
Within this treasury, I have personally heard the Tathāgata’s golden mouth entrust this with earnest instructions:

that after two thousand years, for the sake of sentient beings in the final age, one shall extensively expound these essentials. Now is precisely that time. To repay his kindness, I dare not conceal or cover it away;
I shall now unfold it wide open for everyone in eight characters. (He strikes the ground once with his staff and says: First, I invite Mañjuśrī Bodhisattva...
"Good man, just now on the tip of this mountain monk’s staff, I have spoken the verse for the summer retreat for you all:
'To protect life, one must kill; only when killing is exhausted does one truly enter retreat. If you can understand the meaning within these lines, an iron boat will float upon the water.
Now it is this mountain monk’s turn to speak the verse once more: Mañjuśrī seizes the tiger’s head, and this mountain monk gathers up the tiger’s tail; as for the various Bodhisattvas in between—"
Following the custom, he expressed his joy. Then, striking the ground once with his staff, he descended from the seat.

He then thanked the Head Seat (Śrāmaṇera), the Scribe (Karmadāna), and the Librarian (Bhāṇaka). [The Master] cited the case of two monks under the guidance of Zhaozhou who pushed each other aside, refusing to accept the position of First Seat.
When the administrator reported this to Zhaozhou, Zhaozhou said, "I will have them both serve as the Second Seat. The administrator asked, "Who then shall be made the First Seat?"

[The Master] acts as the presiding seat. The Governor says, "Incense is being prepared. The Attendant says, "The incense is ready. The Governor says, "The fragrance of precepts, the fragrance of concentration, the fragrance of wisdom, and the fragrance of liberation."
The Master picked up the case and said: "Zhaozhou’s single blow was indeed enough to startle the multitude and stir the assembly.
Yet, if one examines it closely, it is still like washing clods of earth in the mud. Under the gate of Jianfu, there is no need for such mutual deference;
there is someone for the first seat, someone for the second seat, and someone for the third seat. Nevertheless, one cannot help but follow along."
The first seat: The head pours over it; even iron eyes and copper pupils cannot see through it. The second seat:
A springtime "White Snow" with no one to join in the song. The third seat: True body and mind, identical to Bodhidharma. Now tell me, are these the same as Zhaozhou’s or different?
