Yet, in an ordinary, level stride beyond the azure heavens, one only knows the universe is vast when turning one's head back to look.
Addressed to Layman Rilü: Liang, the Chief Cook, has returned to Zhongfeng Hermitage;
now that he is as immovable as Mount Sumeru, the path of chasing after phenomena and principles has grown ever more remote.
Having directly trodden across the woodcutter’s trail, I know you have not yet reached Ge Hong’s abode.
Mount Taibai is high and the universe is low; the spiritual bones of the former master have never been moved. Every one of his descendants is just like this:
the mouths of those traveling on the road are like stone monuments.
The Tea Ceremony Seeks a Verse:
The spring breeze blows down the emerald peach blossoms; A single petal flows past tens of thousands of households. How does this compare to the temple beneath Flying Eagle Peak?
Where we invite you to come and drink Zhaozhou’s tea.
The Buddha performed the rite of cremation for the eminent monk Shi at Zhongyi. The Venerable Shu entered the stupa.
The spring rain has just ceased; the spring waters murmur, the spring breeze blows vast and free, and the spring birds warble in harmony. Turning my head toward Qutang Gorge—
The smoke-filled oars overturn the mountains and rivers of Wu and Yue. This one monk has his purpose; today is the day for a lifetime of joy.
Amidst the flames of the red furnace, he stirs up waves.
Burn it all away until it is but a heap of ashes; it cannot be kneaded into a ball, nor can it be split apart.
Since these numinous bones still remain, what prevents the wind and thunder from arising wherever they may be?
The Words of Chan Master Cao Yuansheng Succeeding Mian at Yunju, he accepted an invitation from Miaoguo and said:
"By the tree of peace and joy, I hide my ugliness and clumsiness; In this floating life, piercing and carving do not interfere with one another.
This morning, my staff has leaped and bounded forth; Without cause, it smashes through Zhaozhou’s Barrier. He then raised his staff.
"Look! Look! To call it a 'cane' is worlds apart; not to call it a 'cane' is also worlds apart.
Here, the Buddhas of the three periods, the patriarchs of the six generations, and all the old monks of the world—when they arrive at this point, they find themselves in a state of grievance."
There is no place for *huṃ*; thus he goes. When the Dharma is exhausted, there are no subjects. Having already torn his face-skin asunder, he does not avoid the censure of all quarters.
He then lays his staff across his lap, looks left and right, and after a long pause, says: "The three-foot dragon spring sword shines upon the gall;
in this realm of Great Peace, it slays the dull and obstinate. He lets out a shout and strikes the ground once.
Again, he raised an example: One day, Master Baogong sent a message to Chan Master Sida, saying, "Why do you not go down the mountain to teach and transform sentient beings?
Why do you always gaze at the clouds and sky? Sida replied, "The Buddhas of the three periods of time have all been swallowed by me in a single mouth;
where else could there be any sentient beings left to be saved? The Master said, "He sent this message with such earnestness; what was Baogong so concerned about?"
As for the origin of this: it would be a waste of words to explain it in detail; the Great Master’s own tail has already revealed itself.

When the Elder Sheng was walking along with his arms swinging, he was equally descending the mountain; yet, without asking whether it was a Buddha or a sentient being, as soon as it poked its head out, he cut it in two with a single stroke.
Why? Because "once one has begun, one does not stop until it is finished."
The two characters for "Buddha-dharma" are known by everyone. Yet, how could one allow such lethal poison or white arsenic to enter the mouth?

Even if you were to transcend the time before Vipaśyin Buddha, you would still be wandering outside the realm of the deluded and frantic. This mountain monk has already been dragging through mud and water;
how, then, should you all understand this? (He lets out a shout.)
The golden crow flies and the jade hare runs; ten days of the intercalary month have passed once more. The Immortal of Non-abiding cannot be sought;
one night the frosty wind knocks upon the gate.
Śākyamuni said, "Stop, stop! There is no need to speak; my Dharma is subtle and difficult to conceive. [The Master] lets out a shout and says, "How thick is your face?
You do not realize that the great earth and heavens, the myriad phenomena, light and darkness, form and emptiness, the sentient and the insentient—these have all been spoken of in their entirety.
There is no place for you to cover one side or shield the other. This is the staff of Deshan and the shout of Linji.
"Ho! (The Master) raised his finger; Xuefeng rolled the ball—all of these are like scratching an itch through a boot. "Let it go! Do not engage in deluded thoughts.
What is it? Do you understand? It is merely calling a dog and giving it food. Furthermore, he said:

"Water chestnuts from Suzhou, lotus roots from Shaobo, the Flower Peak of Tiantai, the Stone Bridge of Nanyue"—to call these "upwardly maintained" is to be led astray within the gate of the patch-robed monks.
"The straw sandals have not yet been obtained. Is there no one who feels indignant at the side? Come forth and speak a single phrase!
Even if you could speak it, it would still be nothing more than Guo Lang’s nostrils.
Before the fifteenth day, there is no need for further examination; after the fifteenth day, there is no use in bringing it forward.

On the fifteenth day itself, one does not obscure the timing of the occasion. How then can one communicate? One simply sees the imperial wind forming a single expanse, unaware of where the boundaries of the realm lie.
Winter Solstice. Holding up his whisk, he says: "Do you see it? The Way of the superior man grows long. He strikes once and says: "Do you hear it? The way of the petty man wanes.
"The ice-river simultaneously bursts into flame; the stone-needles secretly sprout branches. He lets out a shout:
"Matters from across kalpas of dust and time are found only this very day."
At the invitation of Guifeng, he addressed the assembly, saying: "Clad in fur and bearing horns, I have entered the marketplace; leaping out of the donkey’s womb, I have fallen into the horse’s womb.
The Buddha’s hand is manifest and cannot block it; let the wind and thunder arise from the level ground."
The ancient sail hoisted high, he enters the Cao Yuan source. Thunder rolls and wind blows, mountains and rivers darken.

He personally cuts off the thirty-two peaks; striking his staff once, he says: "Within a single hair-tip, heaven and earth appear. Raising the staff, he says: "Look, look! The ten directions manifest everywhere;
the oceans of lands are all revealed together. Mañjuśrī and Samantabhadra are dispatched as messengers; Śākyamuni and Maitreya are driven forth."
If you grasp it, it is like a silver mountain and an iron wall—no passage can be found. If you let it go, it pervades the earth and fills the heavens, possessing three heads and six arms.
Neither letting go nor grasping, it is like the King’s precious sword, its divine majesty awe-inspiring; should anyone dare to touch its edge, their corpse would lie ten thousand *li* away.
If you can see through this point, you will be worthy of repaying the unrepayable debt of gratitude and shall join in assisting the Unconditioned.
I shall transform it for you; yet, should this not yet be so, I, Guifeng, cannot help but add feet to the drawings of a snake.
Striking the ground once with his staff, he said: "The hawk-bow has been hung up and the smoke of war has ceased; the ten thousand nations sing praises to celebrate peace."
The spring breeze fans eastward and westward; the spring rain is like clearing, yet not quite clear. Pale whites and deep reds are spread out in a profusion of brocade and embroidery;

the warbling of orioles and the chatter of swallows perform in alternation like the music of flutes and pipes. Each and every thing reveals the wondrous gate of universal penetration (*yuantong*); at every turn flows the treasury of the true Dharma eye (*zhengfayan zang*).

If you attempt to direct your mind toward it or settle upon it, you will find as before ten thousand waters and a thousand mountains. Only when you know how to return directly beneath your feet do I grant you permission.
[The Master] pierced it through from every side and poked holes in all directions.

He struck the meditation seat and descended. Regarding the commencement of the retreat, he said: "In the school of the patched-robed monks, there is a three-month period of formal confinement. The vital thoroughfare is blocked off; the paths of sages and ordinary beings are severed.

Last night, amidst the sound of raindrops dripping from the eaves, the true mechanism was suddenly and completely leaked away. He gave a shout and said: "Be careful not to remain tethered like a donkey!"
The Stake.

A Prayer for Rain, combined with an expression of gratitude to the Supervising Collector. It says: "I recall when Muzhou was reading the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, a monk asked him, 'What sūtra are you reading, Master?
Muzhou replied, 'Great clouds of radiant light; azure clouds of radiant light; purple clouds of radiant light. Which one?
"What cloud is on the edge? The monk said, "On the south side is a black cloud. The Master said, "There will surely be rain today.
The Teacher said, "On the south side is a black cloud; there will surely be rain today. It is good for hemp and beans; it is good for rice and millet.
Although the harvest may be bountiful and the year prosperous, how much hardship lies within every single grain! To report this to those who seek the mystery: you must know where it falls."
If you can realize this, its enjoyment will be inexhaustible; if you do not yet know it, there is much trouble for the supervisors and veteran monks to collect and manage it.
To cite Master Changsha Cen: while he was viewing the moon with Yangshan, Yangshan pointed at the moon and said, "Everyone possesses this, yet they simply cannot use it.
Changsha said, "Precisely! I shall borrow it for you to use. Yangshan said: [and so forth].
"How do you apply this? Changsha stepped forward and gave a kick that felled Yangshan. As Yangshan rose, he said, "Right now, he looks like a great tiger.
I have a verse; let me recite it for the assembly: 'The floating clouds have vanished and the moon is in the sky;
the hare is pregnant and gives birth to a tiger. Leaping forth before the wind, it brandishes its fangs and claws, shaking the world to this very day.'"
The Cold Palace.
The eighth month has passed and the ninth arrives; the seasons press on one another without a moment’s pause. Holding up his staff, he says: "Master Yunmen is coming!
*Zha!* It has rained for a long time without clearing; only the nostrils of the patch-robed monk remain as they were before, perched atop [his head]."
[The Master] strikes his staff once and says, "Lips! Good brother! He draws a line and says, "Falling down is not another thing;
drawn across, it is not dust. He sighs, "I cannot bear this thief Linji, who calls him the 'True Person of No Rank. He gives a shout.
Scattering the assembly, he said: "An ancient worthy said, 'The entire Great Canon of the Teachings is a radical for a single character.
I wonder what character it radicalizes? Wuzu said, 'Bolanang. Yuanwu said, 'Faster than a clap of thunder to cover one's ears.

"Those two great elders' way of radicalizing the character is indeed so; however, it is far too much of a local dialect. Suppose someone were to ask Guifeng: 'The entire Great Canon of the Teachings—'"
This is a compound character; I do not know what character it compounds with. He replied: "It is not far from here to Yiyang.
Rain and sun are as swift as a split arrow; in the blink of an eye, a year passes. One first sees Great Heat and Lesser Heat, and then again Lesser Cold and Greater Cold.
Throughout one's entire being, cold and heat never shift or alternate—this makes the old Master Dongshan of yore laugh to his downfall."
From morning until evening, the bells, fish-shaped chimes, drums, and wooden boards have already awakened the highest of high capacities for all of you.
If you can believe this, the Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are leaping beneath your very feet. If you cannot believe it, Guifeng Shide eats his rice with his mouth.
[He] struck the meditation seat and descended from it.
The Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished this gate. The Bodhisattvas of the present have each entered perfect clarity.
Those who practice and study in the future, even if they fall into pits or ditches, should abide according to this;
it is like adding a point to an arrowhead.

In a small assembly (xiaochan), I recall Master Sishin saying: "The small assembly discourse in the monastic groves is called 'family instruction' (jiaxun). Is it not for discussing the profound and explaining the subtle, citing the ancients to clarify the present?
Is it for ascending the hall on the fifth day or entering the room at dawn on the third day? No, that would be mistaken. Is it for walking slowly?"
"Is it walking? Speak with a low voice; maintain a solemn and pure demeanor; is it the meticulous observance of the precepts? No, that is wrong.

Is it perhaps the practice of striking with the staff or shouting 'Ho!'? Is it swallowing the *liji* thorn, penetrating the diamond ring, rolling the Xuefeng ball, or carrying Muzhou’s board? No, that is wrong.
When members of the monastic community leave one grove and enter another monastery, each one possesses the eye at the crown of their head, and every person has [the power] behind their elbow."
There is a talisman: seeing one's own self as if it were a born enemy; hearing of the Way of Chan as if it were the wind passing through trees.

At times, one stands solitary and perilous like a sheer cliff, with no path for the thread of understanding to pass; at other times, one blends water and mud, moving freely in all directions, even killing the Buddha upon encountering him.
Meeting the Patriarch, they kill the Patriarch; they create the karma of hell and bind the causes for the Avīci Hell.

With jaws like a horse’s and a chin like a donkey’s, with heads like gods and faces like ghosts, they sit all day yet have never sat, they walk all day yet have never walked, they wear clothes all day yet have never hung on them a single thread of silk, they eat rice all day yet have never bitten into a single grain. They roll up and unroll, appear and disappear, sweeping away...
Vast and unrestrained, like a gourd upon the water: touched, it moves; pressed, it turns. How can one approach it? How can one settle within it?

Even if the Buddhas of the three periods, the Patriarchs of the six generations, and all the great spiritual friends of past and present were each to manifest three heads and six arms, they would have no choice but to fold their hands in surrender. Examine this closely!
"Come! You are still merely guarding the postal station, grasping at the bottom of horse dung for an interpretation. Under the gate of a true monk, you must buy new straw sandals and travel on foot.
How can you bear to be so utterly devoid of realization, indulging in nothing but empty pretension, slandering the ancient sages and deceiving yourself?
When casually pressed, your two feet find only empty air. He then struck his knee with his hand and said, "Aha! A Great Man!"

Child, who is without their share? The contracts and deeds that accompany one are fundamentally clear. If you understand how to investigate them, you will surely attain solitary mastery in the crimson heavens.
But as for this turning of the body—how is it, after all? "Lifting your head to gaze beyond the heavens—who is there like me? Again, he cited:
A monk asked an ancient worthy, "What serves as the vessel for crossing over birth and death? The ancient worthy replied, "The years..."
Do not burn paper money at all. Here is a verse; I shall present it to the assembly: When the year ends, do not burn paper money; The rat’s burrow has been pierced by a snake.
Even if you understand this with profound insight, You remain face-to-face yet separated from the Western Heaven.
Verse: Inscribed on Mount Lie; Inscribed on the Changgan Stupa Temple.
Boats and ships come and go as one ascends this height. The offering of wine and burning of paper money only deepens my concerns. In general, the human heart is naturally treacherous.
The precipices vanish; when the mind is empty, mountains and peaks naturally subside.
The śarīra appears without cause, responding to thought; the stupa rises from level ground, towering and majestic.
Had it not been for the power of the golden hammer in those days, how could its radiance have illuminated the nine realms?
The Words of Master Tiebian Shao: Successor to Mian, ascending the hall for the summer retreat, he said:
"Today is the fifteenth day of the fourth month; the monasteries throughout the land have entered the formal retreat. Yet, for a patch-robed monk, there is originally no such thing as 'many'."
"Venerable ones, for now let us all follow the established custom. I do not know what principle underlies this 'binding' (knotting), nor what meaning lies in this 'restraint' (regulation).
If you say it is to bind the body, there is nothing within the body that can be bound. If you say it is to restrain the mind, there is nothing within the mind that can be restrained.
If you say that within this state of non-restraint, non-action, and non-stopping, one simply allows everything to be as it is, making it the *circular enlightenment* (*pariniṣpanna-bodhi*)."

Lan. This constitutes the partitioning of empty space. If you say that one must extinguish all seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, and inwardly maintain a state of profound stillness, this is merely taking one’s own body and mind to imprison oneself. To sever these various paths of entanglement, how can one ultimately achieve it?
I tell you all: cease your deliberations; there is no need for the arduous toil of long-term practice. Right now, you shall enter.
Samādhi. Tsk! On the national anniversary of Emperor Huizong’s death, he raised his whisk and said to the assembly: “Do you see?
By the time you blink your eyes, the ancient Buddha has long since passed away. Take care.”
Spring has returned and summer arrives; the scorching breeze sweeps across the earth. Mount Sumeru runs straight into the nostrils of a mosquito;
the waters of the great ocean hide upon the horns of a ram. It reaches the point where vast waves surge and white billows overflow the heavens—this is neither the Way nor Zen.
The cat cries out from next door; the rat scurries away like smoke.
Regarding the intercalary month, it is said: "One five, two five. The mechanical wheel turns without obstruction; clouds rise from the southern mountain, and rain falls upon the northern mountain.

Some say this is like adding embroidery to brocade; others say it is like washing soil with mud. Still others say that by departing from these two paths, one sees oneself walking alone across the crimson heavens.
If you all continue to deliberate and measure matters in such a manner, I, this mountain monk, do not yet dare to join you.
"Agreed. "But ultimately, how is it? After a long silence, he said: "When meeting people, do not fail to speak correctly.

While the Master was residing at Kuangxiao Monastery in Quanzhou, the Prefect invited him to open the hall. After the incense had been offered for the Emperor and the mallet had struck, the Master said:
"What do you call the 'Ultimate Meaning'? Is there anyone here who is dissatisfied with this? Come forward and speak!"
At that time, a monk stepped forward and asked a question. The Master’s brow furrowed and his eyes stared fixedly. Taking up his staff, he struck it and said, "Stop! Stop!

Today’s opening of the hall is no ordinary Buddhist service. Even if you were to engage in question and answer until Maitreya descends to be born—linking rings and hooks together so tightly that not even a drop of water can leak through—it would still be nothing more than empty drumming for the sake of rice and gruel. It has absolutely nothing to do with one's own self."

This is why it is said: "The question does not reside in the answer; the answer does not reside in the question. Question and answer race against one another like a thunderclap crashing through a clear blue sky—those who observe cannot even blink.
How much less can one hope to settle the ultimate meaning within words or clarify the essential principle beneath a phrase?
Such an approach is very much like climbing a tree to catch fish or waiting by a stump for a rabbit. Little do they realize that in our school there are no words or phrases.
Not a single dharma is given to anyone here; one must penetrate through to this point. Thereby, the imperial grace and the Buddha’s grace are repaid all at once.
If you have not yet reached this realization, I shall add more flowers to the brocade. (He strikes the meditation staff once.)
It is said that on the day of the Buddha’s Nirvāṇa, this old man, on the eighth day of the twelfth month at the hour of midnight, went mad;
he forcibly drove a long nail into his eyes, which remains unextracted even to this day. Today, this mountain monk shall deal him a lethal blow.
"For the sake of others, let me pull it out once more for you to see," he said, and immediately descended from his seat.
He then cited the Heart Sūtra: *gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā*. The Master said:
"Śākyamuni Buddha was much like a thief whose heart is empty; it is like a sacred tortoise dragging its tail. Nevertheless..."
So it is. Look further at the commentary: those who slander the Buddha and revile the Dharma shall not be counted among the assembly, and they will ultimately never attain nirvana.
[The text] strikes its own mouth three times.

For the sake of Senior Secretary Meng, he ascends the seat. With a single phrase, the torrent is cut off; ten thousand functions are stilled and eliminated. That which is empty is itself extinguished, and quiescent extinction manifests before one.

He sits and cuts off the heads of the Reward and Transformation Buddhas, utterly transcending the nest of birth and death. With the nest of birth and death utterly transcended, he faces reality directly and is free from self-interest.
In every dust mote and every land, the fundamental light is never obscured; in every thing and every situation, the wondrous function is fully revealed. As for that function:
Thus it is. To bring his sovereign to fulfillment and bestow grace upon the people, to govern the state and discourse on the Way—its realization is empty and formless, tranquil and eternally so.
Dwelling in wealth and honor, he remains free from pride; encountering sounds and colors, he is not deluded. Within the realm of conditioned existence, he manifests the Dharma of non-action.

Yet they do not destroy the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Within the unconditioned realm (*asaṃskṛtadhātu*), they manifest conditioned phenomena, yet they do not discriminate regarding the nature of the unconditioned.
Though born before heaven and earth, they do not become a seed-spirit; though dying after heaven and earth, they do not become old.
Though transforming all day long, they do not become active; though ultimately quiescent, they do not become at rest. Though they arise in profusion...
They exercise great function without disturbing their spirit; even if heaven and earth were overturned, it would not interfere with their concerns.

This is because they have realized that the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* are empty and understood that the single mind has no abiding place. Abiding in non-abiding—abiding in this manner—if one seeks for a mark of abiding, none can be found.
It is utterly unobtainable. There is nowhere to go; one goes in this manner. If one seeks the characteristic of going, it is utterly unobtainable.

Therefore it is said: "Coming and going are not by means of forms; movement and stillness are not by means of the mind. Since there is no mind regarding this or that, how could there be any form regarding coming and going?
Birth-and-death and coming-and-going are merely wandering through gardens and viewing spectacles. Upon reaching this point, it is called "one flavor."

Equanimity. This is the gate of great liberation of purity. The wondrously luminous mind-ground of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions—those who realize this ground are no different from the Buddhas.
Now tell me: after the Minister of the Dragon Diagram has realized this mind-ground on this very day, in what land will he be reborn, and what sublime retribution will he receive?
Do you wish to know? He cannot remain within the realm of true purity; in every atom and every world-system...

Manifesting his entire body, on the first and fifteenth days of every month, he strikes the bells and beats the drums everywhere. If one does not slander the Way of Chan, it is as if one were reviling the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
All say that in compassionately receiving others, nothing surpasses this; yet what about the nostrils of Chengtian?
I laugh at him. Truly, I do not yet dare grant my consent. Why? Because while the tongues of those sitting here are certainly not lacking, how can one make a tongueless person speak?
When the autumn light is clear and shallow, the white egrets blend with the mist upon the islands. How excellent! Avalokiteśvara has entered the wild weeds with his whole body.
The Master’s note says: "The nostrils of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva and the life-force of all people throughout the great earth—this single note has been issued and delivered.
Do you all feel the heaviness upon the crown of your heads?"
Master Yehai requested the ordination of a monk, saying: "The precious sword has not yet emerged from its scabbard, yet its divine radiance pierces the constellations of Dipper and Ox.

Though a thousand soldiers are easy to find, a single general is truly difficult to seek. Now that this sought-after general has been found, we see the soldiers follow the seal and the general pursue the talisman.
He deliberates within the tent curtains and secures victory beyond a thousand miles. Nevertheless—"
It is so. As for this one move—“bending the enemy’s army without fighting”—how do you explain it? Do you understand thoroughly?
Descend from your seats and pay your respects; I invite Master Yehai to specifically break it open for everyone.

The eighth month is autumn. Where is there heat? The wind enters the pines; their sound is rustling. The setting clouds and solitary wild ducks fly together; the autumn waters and the vast sky are one color.
This is not a matter of facing the scenery or responding to the occasion; it is not a matter of conforming to the time or the season. Ultimately, how is it so?
The assembly descends from their seats and proceeds to patrol the hall. "Be careful with your tea; take your rest.
The Master cites a passage from the teachings: "All Buddhas, as well as the *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* dharma of all Buddhas, all emerge from this sutra.
I do not yet know from what place this sutra emerges. I venture to request that all of you pay close attention.
"Look at the true Way. He then shouted loudly, "Stop! Stop! Do not touch it. If you touch it, you will receive thirty blows;
I will not bargain even for a single blow. He then descended from his seat.

The Master called to the assembly, saying: "Do you understand? If one wishes to speak, words are insufficient; let us deliberate well beneath the grove. But tell me, what is it you are deliberating about?
After a long pause, he looked around and said: "One song, two songs—no one understands them. After the rain has passed, the autumn waters in the night pond run deep."
On the occasion of the *xià* (summer retreat) conclusion ceremony, [the Master] brought up a verse by Xuedou from when he was giving a small-scale sermon (*xiǎo cān*) at Lingyin Monastery.

At first glance, it appears extremely cold and flavorless, difficult to understand and difficult to enter; consequently, few have previously picked it up for discussion. However, if one examines it closely...
It was so great that it startled people. Indeed, those ancients attained a profound depth and applied themselves with precise correctness;

there was no further talk of "Chan," "Way," "Buddha-dharma," or "principles. This is not like the Chan and Way-talk, the discourse on the subtle and the mysterious, or the brandishing of spears and swords prevalent nowadays.
Wielding the staff and shouting "Ho! to expose their wind-bone, they discourse on principles that flow like rushing torrents or pass through a blade;
swift as a blazing flame surpassing the wind. To possess such evil knowledge and evil perceptions is to deafen and blind future generations. This old fellow does not act in such a manner;
he uproots everything—ground, seat, and table—and brings it forth, meeting you face-to-face in his naked essence. As the saying goes: "A tiger without teeth; a dragon lying low."
Do not chant. A thousand mountains are shrouded in black moonlight; the six realms are obscured by dark clouds. For a mountain monk, such a favorable opportunity is difficult to encounter;
it would be like adding feet to a snake’s drawing. Yet, I wish for future generations to examine this. Xuedou’s verse says:

The vast expanse of the six realms remains utterly unknown; Passing the summer retreat at Vulture Peak was a great advantage. In the empty hall, the night is still and there is nothing else to do; He leaves the Chan monk standing for a brief moment. Great!
The assembly has already been sufficiently instructed. Long standing, take care of yourselves.
By the hedge, yellow chrysanthemums hold the morning dew; before the courtyard, vermilion cassias spray the autumn fragrance. Clearly, this thing is no other thing;
one must accept it in its entirety, yet not meet it face-to-face. Since you have accepted it, why then do you not meet it face-to-face? You must...
Do you understand? After thirty years, you will realize it.

In the small assembly during the winter night, he said: "The movement of the sun's shadow shifts; the winter solstice has arrived. When the season comes, the monastic groves boil over with activity. He spoke.
Chan speaks of the Way. It cites the ancients to clarify the present; it speaks of "coming from the east" and "coming from the west"; it speaks of the intent of the Buddhas and the patriarchs.

It says that the cold plum blossoms reveal the eyes of the patriarchs; it says that the flying ashes leak the very core of the patch-robed monks. Everywhere there is the pouring forth of white dew and the manifestation of reality;
everywhere there is the emission of light that shakes the earth. Everywhere there is the lion’s roar; everywhere there is the playful sport of the elephant king. To dwell in this is...
Attaining liberation from the senses and their objects, at every step one treads upon solid ground.
Although people everywhere deliberate in this manner, here at Nantai it is not so. After all, how is it? This year’s oranges are ripe; each one costs one copper coin.
The Words of Chan Master Po’an Xian *Successor to Mian, ascending the hall:* "Seeing smoke from across a mountain, one knows it is fire;
seeing a horn from behind a wall, one knows it is an ox. [He] held up his staff and said:
This is not separated by so much as a single hair’s breadth. Ultimately, what would you call it? Sometimes leaning against an ancient screen, it allows the brush and ink to enter the painted picture.
The news of Miman’s passing arrived, saying: "A traveler comes from the south to report to me, the old man of Tiantong: 'He has shattered the vast void;
his entire body has entered the wild weeds. Now, reflecting deeply upon this, it leaves one unable to weep and unable to laugh.
Vast and empty, the thousand peaks are clear at dawn as my gaze is lost."

Deshan’s staff sets a pattern for imitation; Linji’s shout turns into mere lamentation. How laughable that the "True Person of No Rank" enters and exits through the gates of the face, yet loses his pair of old, tattered sandals.

To transcend the standard and surpass the lineage is to bury the former sages; to rely on others for establishment is to betray one’s own spirit. It does not involve the two paths.
How can one communicate? The numinous tortoise leaves no lines or omens; its empty shell need not be bored.

There is no need to stand in the snow at the courtyard gate, nor to cut off one’s arm before the Master. One must believe that within one’s own portion, one already stands shoulder-to-shoulder with the Buddhas and Patriarchs.
If you understand this, you may receive eight hundred blows in the morning; if you do not, you shall receive three thousand blows by evening.
Gautama flaps his three-inch tongue; for forty-nine years he has not spoken a word of Dharma. The Dharma does not establish a single character or stroke;
the branching of lineages has no place to attach. Since it does not establish a single character or stroke, from where did these branching lineages come?
The green mountains do not lock in the soaring momentum of flight; the vast blue sea surely knows the height of its origin.
The donor invited [him]. Juhui Tang said, "The time of departure in the past is today; today, as before, people do not come.
Since they did not come in the past and will not go now, the white clouds and flowing waters are empty and vast.
The Master said, "Huitang is much like one who smears mud to make bricks; what joy is there in that? How can he compare to my great patron, who goes whenever he wishes to go?"
Coming, one simply comes. Originally there are no diverging paths; how could one traverse steps or stages? Ultimately, what is it? After the rain, Mañjuśrī ascends Mount Wutai.

For the memorial service for his mother, he requested [this verse]: "When afflictions are exhausted, the fire of sorrow is extinguished; where parental affection is severed, the river of craving dries up. Pervading all of space...
Emptiness is the fire of sorrow; where can it be extinguished? The entire earth is the river of craving; how, then, can it be dried up? Do you understand?
"The clouds atop the ridge peak never rest; the water flowing down the ravine is far too busy."

In every thought-moment, abandon all evil realms; in every mind, strive to attain the Buddha’s Bodhi. The two paths of grasping and abandoning are like shedding a garment and donning another. Yongjia never even knew Caoxi.
At the request of Master Yin, he ascended the hall and said: "Now, for a wandering monk, having once worn out his straw sandals, he must follow them through to their very end.
He must pass beyond the realm of Wei-yin, and even further beyond that. The patriarchal school and the scriptural teachings are but provisional paths;

Buddhas and Patriarchs are merely forced names. Bestowing teachings and transmitting the lineage are both empty delusions; seeking the true and pursuing the real only results in increasing disparity. If..."
Taking the self-nature of one’s own mind as the ultimate, there must necessarily be other things and other people as counterparts.

Even if one were to cast it directly across the great void, such that internally there is not a speck of dust for flies to gather upon and externally there is not a thread for ants to cling to—when Zen monks brandish their staffs to strike at the moon, what is it ultimately like? Alas, how bitter! Buddha!
Upon the crown of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, there is a great road that pierces the heavens. If you have not yet penetrated the barrier of birth and death, how can you dare to take a step forward?
Or rather, do not take a step forward; throughout the great thousandfold world-system, there is no obstruction. A single phrase cuts off all verbal explanation—like Xingzha lifting the iron pillar.
The mountain stream flowing downward has no intention; the solitary cloud returning to its cave is fundamentally without mind.
If human life could be like clouds and water, iron trees would bloom and spring would fill the entire world.
I invite the Head Seat, the Secretary, and the Librarian to ascend the hall. I have a broken-legged cauldron; three sons lift it together.
With every stroke it rises higher; with every step it widens. From this point on, the livelihood flourishes; the pure wind stirs the profound depths.
At midnight, the black rooster is released; atop its head is a single spot of snow.
Bodhidharma came from the West; Old Lu reached the South. Branches were established and lineages spread, until their descendants covered the earth.
Everyone claims this is the "separate transmission outside the teachings," yet how many have ever even dreamed of it? You smell the stench of sweat beneath Dongchan’s feet.
Tell me, what excellence does Dongchan possess? When meeting someone, speak only three parts of the truth; do not yet cast away your whole heart.
It is the twelfth day of this month; the sound of the drum shakes the earth, and the clouds and waters rise upward. What is the point of seeking such a thing?
Even if the heavens were to rain down the four flowers, how could that compare to returning to the hall to sleep? (He lets out a shout.)
If Bodhidharma had not come to the Eastern Land, and the Second Patriarch had not gone to the Western Heaven;
if Old Lu had not known the Fifth Patriarch—who would say that the robe was transmitted at midnight? Later people listen to matters without truth, calling a bell a water jar.
With mouths wide open, they do nothing but talk of dreams. Let them dream as they please, let them speak as they please; I urge you not to drive nails into empty space.
[He strikes the meditation pillar. *Hè!* [One shout. He descends from his seat.
On New Year’s Eve, he says: "Day after day we rush about, night after night never resting. We run until the end of the year, yet it remains the same fixed point on the scale.
Tonight, this mountain monk, seizing the wind to fan the fire, shall once more recite a verse for you all."
Thus it is. At the end of thirty-six weeks on this evening, the windmill turns upon the pivot of the fixed board.
When you release the place where the crisscrossing patterns knot together, you must believe that the Chan breeze flows from within the house.
Entering a field of weeds, one does not pick; one simply plucks whatever grass comes to hand. Holding up his staff, he said:
"Now, plucking whatever comes to hand—it strikes when the eyes are open, and it strikes when the eyes are closed. Is there anyone here who cannot be deceived? After a long silence, he said:
"Except for the scholar Pan of Mount Hua, I know not who else could ride a donkey backward."
Residing at Xichan, he entered the abbot’s quarters and said: "I have an elder brother, Lanyuan; there is truly something to be found through such karmic conditions.
Going from east to west again, the two places have been settled between us. Departing now, I have no lingering regrets; the only debt remaining is for sleep.
I cannot forget our bond as brothers, so I have come specifically to repay him. But how shall I repay him? Wait until I have woken from my drowsiness, and then I shall tell you."
The Way.
[The Master] raised a case where a monk asked Zhaozhou, "What is your surname? Zhaozhou said, "It is here in Changzhou. The Master said, "It is here in Changzhou, but not in Fuzhou.
The river wind blows fiercely and the waves are rough; there is no need to mark the boat in vain while searching for the lost sword—the single sail has already departed."
Passing through Lake Dongting: "Two-thirds of one's life have already passed. That single point of the numinous mind has not been polished. Greedily pursuing life, one goes about in trivial toil;
when called back, one does not turn—what can be done? Old Xuedou, you are showing off too much! You deserve thirty blows of the staff. Nevertheless...
Even so, there is still a spark remaining on a piece of dead wood; it is solitary and facing outward, such that no one can know it.
A monk asked Master Kuān, "Where does the Way reside? Kuān said, "It resides right before your eyes.
The monk said, "Since it is right before my eyes, why do I not see it? Kuān said, "Because you have 'I,' you therefore do not see it. The monk said, "I have..."
"Because of 'I,' I do not see. Does the Preceptor still see? Guang said, "There is you and there is me; thus, we pass each other by without seeing.
The monk said, "If there is neither you nor me, do you still see? Guang said, "If there is neither you nor me, who is it that seeks to see?"
The Master said: "If you scold me, I will spare you my retort; if you spit at me, I will spare you my splash.
He then cited Zhaozhou’s saying: "Hurry! Hurry! Hurry! Standing on the water wearing boots, one gallops to Chang'an before the tips of the boots are even wet.
The Master said: "A dull bird flying against the wind."
When a single leaf falls, one knows autumn. Vague and indistinct is Buddha-nature. When a single speck of dust arises, the entire earth is gathered up. Blunt and clumsy is True Suchness.
If you are a guest in the gate of the patch-robed monks, there is no need for further hesitation. You have already looked upon the painting of Mount Hua;
now add Pan Lang, riding his donkey backward.
"Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion? The Patriarch said, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River with a single mouthful, and then I will tell you.
If it were Yishan, he would not have said so. Had someone suddenly asked him, "Who is it that does not take the myriad dharmas as a companion?
he would have replied, "Wait until you can suck up all the waters of the West River with a single mouthful."
"Water. I have not yet told you this.
[The Master] cites Zhaozhou’s saying: "People are driven by the twelve hours; I, the old monk, drive the twelve hours. The Master said:
"Even though Zhaozhou 'drives the twelve hours,' he is still a hired laborer at Mount Yi. Since he does not act for the sake of the twelve hours..."
At that time, the messenger was actually a laborer from Mount Gui. Is it not said: "A vast marsh hides a mountain;
principle can subdue a leopard"?
When the news of Tiantong’s passing arrived, it was said: "Dreams, illusions, and empty flowers—sixty-seven years. The white birds vanish into the mist; the autumn waters."
Reaching to the heavens! This is the final stroke of the old monk Hongzhi.
Those who recognize it call it the crown bone of the Buddhas and Patriarchs, the authentic transmission of Caoxi—continuous and dense, dense and continuous. Those who do not recognize it simply say:
"Hand in hand with a single sandal, he departed from Mount Congling in solitude. I, this mountain monk, do not avoid the laughter and suspicion of the assembly; yet, I have not yet...
Do not add feet to a snake’s drawing. (67) Dreams, illusions, and empty flowers—though departing, she still harbors the heart of an old woman;
she embroiders the mandarin ducks and presents them for others to see. Who would have known that originally they never touched the golden needle?
On the eighth day of the fourth month, Jufu Dao says: "Everyone pours a ladleful of foul water to wash away the impurities on the Tathāgata’s pure side.
When the impurities are exhausted, the afflictions of sentient beings are removed, and the foxes then let out a lion’s roar. Yishan, however, does not say it this way:
"Everyone pours a ladleful of foul water to wash away the impurities on the Tathāgata’s pure side. When the impurities are exhausted, the afflictions of sentient beings..."
His agitation was dispelled. The Lion then let out the cry of a fox. Since he was a lion, why did he instead let out the cry of a fox?
He replied, "Who would deign to lower their dignity to conform to the lowly?"

In the *Jianbi kaizang* (Opening the Treasury for My Late Mother), it is said: "To adhere to a single word of the sutras is to be at enmity with the Buddhas of the three periods; to depart from a single word of the sutras is to be no different from the teachings of Māra.
How can a clear-eyed Chan practitioner express this? After a long silence, he said: "How pitiable is the sand-swallowing wild goose, crying out in anticipation of spring."

The Memorial Service for the Deceased states: The Way of filial piety and compassion is a common principle shared by both Confucianism and Buddhism. If one does not contemplate the parents who have passed away, who then shall repay their labor and virtue?
Therefore, the Way of the former sages holds that great compassion encompasses all without exception, and great filial piety extends to all without exception.

To love only those who love me, while failing to love others, is not great compassion. To love the parents of the present moment, while failing to love the parents of the past, is not [great filial piety].
This is filial piety. The Buddha taught the *Ullambana* Sūtra to broaden one’s care for one's kin, thereby honoring parents through successive generations;
and to extend one’s love broadly, thereby rescuing sentient beings in the three miserable realms. In terms of filial piety and compassion, this may indeed be called great.
Yet, as for a mountain monk like me, it is not so. Why? Because that which has form ultimately does not become great; only that which is formless is called the True.
The Verse and Ancient Case: "Dividing the bones to return them to the father"—Baizhang opens the fields;
the corpse is entirely consumed, leaving not a trace. From this point on, the entire world is Nanda. Even if you were to see it, there would be not a single fiber [of duality].
A cataract; it has not yet spared me from adding more flowers to my eyes.
Everyone has exerted their full strength in the communal labor of opening the fields; they are all in a flurry, trailing water and mud. Spread out these two hands—do not ask why.
Last night at the third watch, the moon fell to the west.
A monk asked National Teacher Nanyue Huairang, "In the Western Heaven, people use the *lao* (staff) as a means of verification. In this land, what is used as a means of verification?
Huairang said, "A Korean person’s straw sandals. [The monk] asked, "If one calls them a 'bamboo whisk' (*zhuhui*), it constitutes an offense (*chu*).
I do not know what is used as a means of verification in this land. [Huairang] picked up the Korean person’s straw sandals. Han Zu’s Hall: Fan Kuai.
Anger! Who opened that one step at the Gate of Swans?

The shadows of birds vanish across a thousand mountains; Human tracks are cut off for ten thousand li. An old man with a straw raincoat atop a solitary boat Fishes alone amidst the snow on the cold river.
Hao Yue the Offering-Master asked Changsha: "If one realizes that karmic obstacles are fundamentally empty, then what about the Venerable Siṃha and the Second Patriarch—were they realized or not?
Changsha said: "Virtuous One, you do not recognize fundamental emptiness... (and so forth). Changsha then presented this verse:
"Provisionally existent, yet fundamentally not existent; Provisionally non-existent, yet fundamentally not non-existent."
The meaning of Nirvana as the repayment of debts:

the single nature is no different, and the repayment of debts in Nirvana is likewise no different. Shattering Changsha’s "arm-pit talisman," this one phrase is fully presented—there is no talk or meeting with it.
In the eighth month at Qiantang, the flower-like waves are coarse.
The Words of Chan Master Lan’an Xu A Successor of Dahui, ascending the hall:

Hiding in crags and retreating to valleys, like withered seeds and scorched sprouts; responding to things according to their forms, dragging through mud and water—even if one dwells in such [seclusion],...
Acting yet remaining unmoved by smoke and dust; dwelling in non-action yet not sinking into dullness or intoxication.

Yet one has not avoided the predicament of not reaching the village in front and not reaching the inn behind. If you are such a person, scatter the white clouds with a shout and burst through the azure void;

uproot the spiritual sprouts and strange weeds from their very foundations, and let thorns grow across the great earth as they may. Even so, within the sphere of the patch-robed monk, it is still thus.
"Everyday tea and rice. After a long silence, he said: "Even if the vast ocean were to change, I would never speak for you.
Racing currents passing through a blade—this is not yet a master. A swift flame passing through the wind—even this is but a dull-witted man. Therefore, he clenches his fingers."

Upon awakening to the Way, one’s sense of being scarred by afflictions increases further. Though striking the bamboo awakened the mind, it did not prevent one from remaining in a state of bewilderment.

Even if all skillful means were exhausted and the breath were entirely stilled, were one to examine this closely, it would still be "not yet. Have you not seen it said: "The path that goes upward is not transmitted by the thousand sages;
students weary their bodies like a monkey grasping at reflections"? Since it is not transmitted, how did the school of Bodhidharma come to exist?
It has come to this very day. [The Master] lets out a shout and says: "Be careful not to mistake the bridge of a donkey's saddle for your father’s chin.
If a son can truly inherit his father’s legacy, how many people has he deceived? Once the house is ruined and the family perished, there is no door left to shelter this body.
"Eh? Throughout the twelve periods of the day, where do you establish yourself and find your livelihood? Do not speak of your sorrows to one who is already sorrowful;
to speak of them to such a person is to drive them to despair."
If you wish to attain presence before [the truth], do not harbor thoughts of compliance or resistance. To relieve yourself of excrement and urine is a way to save much effort.
A monk asked, "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants; tell me, who is he? The Master said, "If you try to explain it through intellectual penetration, you are unfit.
The monk pressed further, "Ultimately, what is his countenance? The Master brushed his eyebrows aside with his hand. The monk then bowed.
The Master said: "Excellent! Excellent! He then said: "Śākyamuni and Maitreya are his servants. But tell me, who is he? Majestic and towering;
awe-inspiring and radiant. In hand he carries a staff of rabbit horns; underfoot he treads upon a stone tortoise.
His coming cannot be checked; his going cannot be pursued. Now that he has arrived here, he joins his palms and kneels. *He!* (A shout)"
He shouted, "This wild fox spirit! Even so, what is it that makes you not equal? You have merely tucked in your neck and tucked up your tail to depart.

A monk asked, "There has never been a state of mind without an object, nor has there ever been a mind without an object. When the object is forgotten, the mind naturally ceases; when the mind ceases, the object..."
[The student] asked, "What about when there is no invasion? The Master said, "In the frosty sky the moon has set; the night is already half over. Who shares this cold reflection in the clear pool?
The student continued, "Were it not for the early blooming of flowers along the purple road, how could the yellow oriole descend upon the willow branches?
The Master said, "Be careful not to use a jumble of needles and awls. The student said, "Thirty years from now, someone will bring this up. The Master said, "You are wasting people’s time!"
The Master then said: "I observe a hawk soaring toward the heavens; a tortoise chasing fish at the bottom of the water.
Three old ladies and six nurses; the Diamond Throne is as rotten as mud. You people, do you know or not?
Though Bo Ya was skilled at playing the lute, one who could truly hear him required Ziqi."
A monk asked, "When the great function manifests before one, and no rules or regulations are maintained—what then? The Master said, "The mountain torrents overflow; the peaks collapse.
The monk stepped forward and said, "Looking out from beyond the heavens, who is such a person? The Master said, "From head to foot. The monk said, "How can it be otherwise?
From ancient times to the present, there is no divergent path; those who attain realization share the same way. The Master said, "Have you attained it yet? The monk said, "..."
"Familiarity is the same as being strangers. The Master said, "Stop your drowsy chatter. The Master then said:

"If you wish for the Great Function to manifest before you, you need only suddenly forget all views. When all views are exhausted, delusion does not arise; great wisdom will then shine through with total clarity."
It is understood that this is not some other thing. He then drew a circle and said: "If you say you see it, I will blind your eyes.
If you say you do not see it, I will goad your eyes with blindness. At such a moment, what is it? The bright sun shines in the sky;
the blind man gropes upon the ground.
[The Master] cited Master Baofeng. A monk came from Shitou; the Master then held up his whisk and said, "Those who fall within this mechanism have not yet possessed the eye.
As the monk was about to step forward, Baofeng said, "You have just fallen into this very mechanism.
The Master [Xuedou] said, "When the mechanism is like a flash of lightning, one cannot avoid the ailment of 'nesting in the reeds. The monk returned and related this to Shitou. Shitou said, "I..."
If he sees [the whisk], snatch it away and see what he does. The Master said, "Drawing the bow after the thief has fled.
Baofeng asked, "If I had a whisk, I would snatch it from him; but what if I bring no object at all? The Master said:
"I thought the beard was red, but here is another with a red beard. Shitou asked, "The scale without stars—how can it distinguish anything?
The Master said, "One who has not undergone bitter toil does not know. The Master further said, "Baofeng knows how to blow the holeless flute;
Shitou is skilled at responding with the felt clappers. Is there anyone now who knows how to listen well? With every sound, the melody emerges."
"Before the Ancient Sovereign, who says it is easy for the ears of people of this age to enter?
A monk asked: 'The secluded birds warble their songs; leaving the clouds, they enter the chaotic peaks. What is the state of affairs at such a time? The Master said:

'Darkly inscribing the sorrowful gut, to whom can one speak it? The monk pressed further: 'If that is so, then one does not depart from the present place and remains ever serene; if sought, one knows you.'"
"It cannot be seen. The Master said, "Do not let the water boil over. The student stepped forward and said, "On the stringless lute, those who understand its music are few;
since I have begun to play, the melody has been lofty. The Master said, "Where did you see me, old monk? The student said, "Eye meets eye.
The Master said, "You blind fellow! The Master then said: "One who sits in a deep well does not know the vastness of heaven and earth. To forget..."
As for those with biased views, they fail to suddenly clarify the perfect fusion of the ultimate principle. Thus it is said:

"If one wishes to know the principle of true emptiness, the True Suchness within the mind pervades the external as well; sentient and insentient beings share a single essence, and everywhere is identical to the True Dharma-realm.
Then, raising the whisk, he says: "This whisk horizontally encompasses the Dharma-realm and vertically embraces heaven and earth. One.
All mountains and rivers, as well as frogs and earthworms, are entirely upon the tip of this whisk. They demarcate boundaries and establish divisions;
picking up one, they let go of seven. Again, striking once, he says: "Everything has been completely pulverized into a hundred fragments. Do you all still feel pain and itchiness?
If you say you know it, then the whisk has already pierced through your skulls; yet the skulls neither perceive nor know."
If you say the Way does not know, then the skull has already pierced through the whisk; yet the whisk neither knows nor perceives.
Let us set aside for a moment the question of whether it knows or does not know. Then, tearing open his chest, he said: "Now tell me, how many hairs do I have on my chest that cover the gallbladder?"
He then let out a shout.
Zhao Shou arrived and requested him to ascend the seat. He said: "When sages meet, it is like the spark struck from flint, like a flash of lightning.
To hesitate or not to hesitate is already ten thousand miles away in white clouds. When Confucius met Wen Bo Xue, he was already in a state of disarray."
Fucheng of Taiyuan mistakenly struck Old Xuefeng; it was a total failure on his part.

As for the other masters of the monastic groves and the great teachers of the world who cite the ancients and discuss the present, who discourse on the profound and explain the subtle—they all deserve to be summoned here to be interrogated.
But as for Layman Chaoran, arriving here today, what should he speak of? After a long silence, he said: "When meeting, there are no idle words; simply..."
He said, "I am talking about the growth of mulberry and hemp.
Before the drum has even sounded, why did you not vanish on the spot? Why have you come back here to seek after such dung?
He then seized his staff and leaped down from the rope bed; the assembly all scattered at once.
The Master raised a case where a monk asked Jingqing, “What is the Mohe Mohe sword? Jingqing replied, “Dust covers the sandals beneath the bed; the wind moves the headcloth on the rack.
Later, Layang Heshang said, “Among the assembly, people deliberate upon this as a matter of answering a question.

Since you all do not understand it as an answer to a question, how then do you understand it? After a long silence, he said, “When departing, go by the front street; when returning, [go by the back lane].”

Returning from the back streets later that day, the Master said: "Jingqing was the vanguard; Langye was the rearguard. They lined up their ranks and deployed their divisions, shaking the earth and startling the heavens.
Yet when it came to facing the enemy on the battlefield, they could not avoid falling into a pit or a trench all at once.
If someone were to ask you now, 'What is the Mohe Sword? simply say: 'Tempered until the seven stars shine with brilliant luster; capable of grasping the heavens.'"
Below, he acted with unrestrained freedom.
A monk asked, "When moving, one is turned by circumstances; when still, one is bound by dharmas. Apart from these two paths, how can one be 'just as it is'? The Master said:
"The sleeves of his robe are too short for his long arms; his straw sandals are too wide for his thin feet. The student asked, "Do you permit this disciple to understand this?
The Master said, "How do you understand it? The student replied, "I know that you, Master, are tearing open your belly and gouging out your heart.
The Master said, "Measuring the ocean with a ladle—what a miserable state of affairs! The Master then said: "Movement is turned by objects; stillness is bound by dharmas. This is precisely..."
This is to refute the ordinary person who thinks there is form that can be obscured and sound that can be mounted;

such a one is not yet a master of the craft. Thus the Great Master Yunmen said: "Countless dead people lie upon level ground; he who passes through the thorn forest is a master of the craft. The Master [Zhaozhou] said:
"Great as Yunmen was, he was nonetheless somewhat lacking in courage. If it were Dongchan, he would sit right in the midst of the thorn forest. Thorns...
"What fault is there in lying down in the forest?
A monk asked, "When the spring thunder has already sounded but the sunbird has not yet cried—at such a moment, how should one issue the command? The Master said:
[The Master] pulled the arrow from behind the head. [Zhaozhou] stepped forward and said, "Today you did not get the advantage. The Master said, "A defeated general is not executed.
Zhaozhou said, "I know that the Master is accustomed to gaining the advantage. The Master said, "I spare your life; I let your breath pass. Zhaozhou said, "Hūṃ hūṃ!
The Master said, "Be careful not to deceive with empty words. The Master then said: "One who is skilled in speaking speaks what cannot be spoken; one who is skilled in traces..."
As for "traces," they are traces that cannot be traced; they are words that cannot be spoken. They cannot be grasped through language or conversation.

Since traces cannot be traced, they cannot be pointed out by means of shadows or footprints. Thus, a monk asked Deshan: "The discourse at Vulture Peak spoke of the moon, and Caoqi pointed to the moon;
I do not ask about those, but what is the true moon? Deshan said: "Last night at the third watch, it turned toward the west."
The Master said: "This monk asked in such a way, and Deshan answered in such a way. I do not know how you all will go about grasping this. Listen to a verse:
Last night at the third watch, the moon turned toward the west; In the dimming universe, how many people are lost?
The reflection turns in the clear pool as the wind first subsides; From beyond the ridge, the solitary monkey’s faint cry is heard."
Master Huangbo said: "Since Master Bodhidharma arrived in this land, he has spoken only of the single nature and transmitted only the single Dharma.
He transmitted Buddha-to-Buddha, speaking of no other Buddha; he transmitted Dharma-to-Dharma, speaking of no other Dharma.
This Dharma is the Dharma that cannot be spoken; this Buddha is the Buddha that cannot be grasped. It is precisely the pure source-mind."
The Master said: "Since the Dharma cannot be spoken and the Buddha cannot be grasped, what thing could one point to and call the 'originally pure mind'?
[He gave] a shout and said: 'If you wish not to incur the karma of the Avīci Hell, do not slander the True Dharma Wheel of the Tathāgata.'"

A monk asked, "Discussing the profound and explaining the subtle, citing the ancients and deliberating on the present—all these belong to untimely speech. Without involving the profound mystery, how is it with a single phrase?
The Master said, "The partridge cries where the flowers are fragrant. The monk pressed, "What if one goes forth in this very way?
The Master said, "Dust in the eyes. The monk pressed, "What if one does not go forth in this way? The Master said, "Heavy."
[The Master] layered the mountain paths and entered [the hall], saying: "One melody, two melodies—no one understands them. After the rain has passed, the spring waters in the night pond are deep.
The Master said, "A guest beneath the toad’s robe. Then the Master continued: "In the mundane, one is fully mundane; in the sacred, one is fully sacred.
Each occupies its own fundamental position, having thoroughly mastered both phenomena and principle. It is like there being no sound of a drum within a bell, and no sound of a bell within a drum."
The sounds of bells and drums do not intermingle; in every phrase there is no before or after. If one can penetrate to the root source herein, let the golden-haired lion be called a dog at will.
For those on the busy road who have not yet returned home, take care never to look for the Big Dipper while facing south.
Jujian asked a monk, "Where have you recently departed from? The monk said, "Dongchuan. Jujian said, "Twin caves and solitary pines;
smoke-blue and moon-white. Which of these is your true host? The monk said, "I have only just arrived at Tongan, and I am already being questioned about this.
Jujian said, "This is like marking the sword on the boat or breaking a pearl to seek its reflection. Is this not your own realm? Sit for a while."
A monk asked, "What is the true master of Tong’an? An replied, "A colt on the road cannot surpass a *huālóu*.
The monk then bowed. An said, "The barbarian beats the rhythm, yet there is no dancing to the beat.
The Master said, "The skillful hand of a master of the school is like the majesty of Gūlíng as he splits Mount Tài-huá, or a blue dragon unfolding to seize the *lílú* pearl."
The momentum is such. Nevertheless, if one encounters a man-eating lion, one will never let it pass. Do you all wish to recognize Tong’an?
